It is intended as an overview, showing the scope and the landscape of the subject. Foreword – Curators of Semantic Capital Sometimes, a task (from baking a cake to studying the evolution of stars, planets, galaxies, and other objects in the universe) requires only one speciﬁc agent to be performed. In this case the agent in question, say A (Alice or astrophysics, in our example), is supposed to be both necessary and suﬃcient to deliver the required result. A can be the agent and the only agent for that task, and hence her unique identity as the deliverer is uncontroversial. Because she is both necessary and suﬃcient, she may ﬁnd her role ethically demanding in two senses. Not only must she deliver but she can also deliver by herself. When things develop, this twofold responsibility may become less clear. A may no longer be suﬃcient, perhaps she needs to coordinate with other agents, yet she is still necessary, sometimes even more so than in the past. The debate on the future of Westphalian nation-states seems to suﬀer from such confusion sometimes
===
--- Chunk 12 ---
necessary, sometimes even more so than in the past. The debate on the future of Westphalian nation-states seems to suﬀer from such confusion sometimes. Given the global and very pressing challenges we face, nation-states are far from obsolete. On the contrary, they are even more necessary than in the past. However, they are no longer suﬃcient, since nation-states now need to coordinate their eﬀorts with many more agents required to make things happen, from companies to NGOs and supranational organisations (think of climate change eﬀorts). The digital revolution seems to have brought a similar change in information science too. We need information science to curate our expanding space of information (infosphere) and all the growing semantic capital that we inherit, accumulate, enrich, reﬁne and bestow to future generations. It is a crucial role because semantic capital is the most precious outcome of all our activities, since it is what enables us to understand, make sense, and shape ourselves and our realities. And yet, information science today is no longer suﬃcient to take care of it, but must interact, coordinate and collaborate with many other disciplines (think of computer science) and agents (think of Google and its scholarly services) to fulﬁl its task. This ‘insuﬃcient necessity’ of information science is challenging for anyone who still thinks of its deﬁnition in terms of ‘necessary and suﬃcient’ conditions, and hence seeks to identify a role, a ﬁeld, a subject, an a
===
--- Chunk 13 ---
 anyone who still thinks of its deﬁnition in terms of ‘necessary and suﬃcient’ conditions, and hence seeks to identify a role, a ﬁeld, a subject, an approach, a methodology, a tradition, a canon or any other combination of variables that may establish (for some people, restore) such twofold conditions. But it is an intellectual opportunity for anyone who can embrace a collaborative spirit. From this perspective, information science is one of the necessary curators of semantic capital, has all the responsibility of being increasingly necessary and has the added responsibility of no longer being suﬃcient but in need of being seriously multidisciplinary in its cooperation with a larger group of stakeholders. This means that the epistemological status of information science has evolved. Perhaps there was a time when information science was necessary and suﬃcient and did not have to be but could aﬀord to be self-reliant and unrelated. But now that it has become even more important and yet insuﬃcient, the solution is to join forces, create relations of trust with other disciplines and agents and become a crucial node in a network of curators of semantic capital. The uniqueness of information science is not (or no longer) provided by some necessary and suﬃcient status as a scientiﬁc discipline, but by the speciﬁc contributions that it must provide to the larger context of taking care of our semantic capital and the infosphere. It is a collaborative and ecological task that readers o

Because the world we live in is surely a world of information. Tom Wilson (2010) Introduction The subject of this book is information science. We begin by asking what information science is, as an academic discipline and profession. Obviously, and simplistically, it is the science of information. But this is not suﬃcient, since the multiple meanings and implications of information, which will be discussed in Chapter 5, have given rise to diﬀerent conceptions of information science (Buckland, 2012; Limberg, 2017). One such conception is of information science as being concerned with computing, algorithms and data science, a second with information and communication technologies and a third with information as an entity with physical and biological science. A fourth conception sees information science as concerned with information recorded in documents, with meaning and knowledge, and hence as growing from the older disciplines of librarianship and documentation. We will focus on the last of these in this book, although we will mention aspects of the others at appropriate points. We will therefor
===
--- Chunk 21 ---
documentation. We will focus on the last of these in this book, although we will mention aspects of the others at appropriate points. We will therefore be following the kind of deﬁnition which goes back at least as far as Borko (1968) and is expressed by Saracevic (2010, 2570) as: Information science is the science and practice dealing with the eﬀective collection, storage, retrieval and use of information. It is concerned with recordable information and knowledge, and the technologies and related services that facilitate their management and use. This gives us a general idea of the nature of the subject, but there is still scope for much diﬀerence in viewpoint as to exactly what the subject comprises and how it should be understood; see Bates (1999), Hjørland (2000), Robinson (2009), Ibeque-SanJuan et al. (2014) and Bawden and Robinson (2016). We now examine the nature of the subject in more detail. The nature of information science Information science is an academic discipline which supports areas of professional practice. We will think ﬁrst about the discipline, although we should note that there have always been some doubts as to what extent it is a real discipline, still less a ‘science’ (Robinson, 2009; Buckland, 2012; Furner, 2015). One way to accommodate the wide range of views about, and diverse approaches to, the subject within a coherent framework is to regard information science as a ﬁeld of study, using this phrase in the speciﬁc sense of Paul Hirst, the philosop
===
--- Chunk 22 ---
ct within a coherent framework is to regard information science as a ﬁeld of study, using this phrase in the speciﬁc sense of Paul Hirst, the philosopher of education (Hirst, 1974). A ﬁeld of study is an alternative to ‘disciplines’ based on a unique form of knowledge, such as mathematics or the physical sciences, and to ‘practical disciplines’ based on one of the forms of knowledge but oriented to solving practical problems, such as engineering or medicine. For Hirst, a ﬁeld of study is focused on a topic or subject of interest, using any of the forms of knowledge – sociological, mathematical, philosophical, etc. – which may be helpful in studying it. Bawden (2007, 320) argues that it may be appropriate to regard information science as such a ﬁeld of study, focused on the topic of information, understood as information recorded in documents produced and used by individuals and societies: a multidisciplinary ﬁeld of study, involving several forms of knowledge, given coherence by a focus on the central concept of meaningful recorded information. This is reminiscent of the insistence of Machlup and Mansﬁeld (1983) that the ﬁeld should be described as the information sciences, emphasising the plural, to show the breadth of approach needed. Ibeque-SanJuan et al. (2014) reinforce this, referring to the ‘pluri-, multi-, trans-, meta- and interdisciplinary’ nature of the discipline; see also Bates (2015), Limberg (2017) and Hjørland (2018). Evidence for the interdisciplinary is also

--- Chunk 23 ---
and interdisciplinary’ nature of the discipline; see also Bates (2015), Limberg (2017) and Hjørland (2018). Evidence for the interdisciplinary is also given by the extent to which authors from the information sciences publish in journals outside the subject, and vice versa; see, for example, Chang (2018a; 2018b). We can give some more precision to this general idea by arguing that the focus on recorded information can be expressed speciﬁcally as a focus on the communication chain of recorded information: from its creation, through dissemination, indexing and retrieval, use and archiving or disposal (Duﬀ, 1997; Robinson, 2009). This is implied in earlier formulations, but noting that it explicitly helps to clarify what are the concerns of information science. Details of the chain, and the ways in which it is being changed by new technologies, are discussed in Chapter 13. Information is recorded in documents, and information science has a close aﬃnity with the documentation movement and document theory, as will be covered in Chapter 6. We can also explain more precisely what information science does, in terms of both research and scholarly study and of practice, through the components of domain analysis, as propounded by Birger Hjørland (2002). This will be discussed fully in Chapter 7. For now, we will just note that there are a number of aspects which represent both the activities of the information practitioner and the ways in which research and study are carried out. Exampl

number of aspects which represent both the activities of the information practitioner and the ways in which research and study are carried out. Examples are user studies, historical studies, studies of terminology, research on indexing and retrieval and so on. Considering information science as an academic discipline, comprising the study of the components of the communication chain of recorded information through the perspective of domain analysis, provides the understanding of information science which we shall use throughout this book. Information science is a ͅeld of study, with recorded information and documentation as its concern, focusing on the components of the information communication chain, studied through the perspective of domain analysis. Information science is a vocational discipline, underlying a number of professional activities, including: data, information, and knowledge management; librarianship; metadata and taxonomy management;  records  management  and  archiving;  and documentation in museums, galleries and heritage institutions. What kind of discipline? There is liĴle agreement as to how information science should be categorised as an academic discipline. It has been called, among other things, a meta-science, an inter-science, a postmodern science, an interface science, a superior science, a rhetorical science, a nomad science, an interdisciplinary subject which should be renamed knowledge science, a liberal art, a form of cultural engagement, a sub
===
--- Chunk 25 ---
 science, a nomad science, an interdisciplinary subject which should be renamed knowledge science, a liberal art, a form of cultural engagement, a subject which may assume the role once played by philosophy in mediating science and humanism, and the applied philosophy of information. There have also been national variations in the way the subject is regarded in, for example, the United Kingdom (Robinson and Bawden, 2013), France (Ibeque-SanJuan, 2012; Hudon, 2018), the Nordic countries (Limberg, 2017) and the United States (Buckland, 1996). University departments teaching and researching the subject may be found in faculties of arts and humanities, social sciences, computing and technology, education, science, and business and management. This scaĴer may be a natural consequence of the status of information science as a ﬁeld of study, but it has been held to be a weakness of the discipline. The related question of the extent to which information science has its own body of concepts and theories, as opposed to simply borrowing them from other disciplines, will be considered in Chapters 3 and 4; see Dillon (2007) for some concerns on this aspect. It is clear that many other professions are interested in components of the communication chain: journalists are concerned with creation, publishers with dissemination, computer scientists with information retrieval and so on. Even accepting that information science is a meta-discipline, surely it must have some ‘academic turf’ of its 
===
--- Chunk 26 ---
s with information retrieval and so on. Even accepting that information science is a meta-discipline, surely it must have some ‘academic turf’ of its own? We suggest that the uniqueness of information science lies in its concern for all components of the communication chain and the ways in which they interact with, and impact upon, each other. Other disciplines are interested in speciﬁc aspects, but only the information sciences see their concern as being the totality. We might also name some aspects of information organisation and information behaviour, seemingly invariant to technology or to context, which are the particular concern of information science. But our main claim to a unique area is the totality of the communication chain; for more discussion, see Robinson and Bawden (2012), Robinson (2009) and Robinson and KaramuĞuoglu (2010). Constituents and core There is no canonical list of topics which fall within the remit of information science, despite much debate, supported by bibliometric mapping, about such a list, and consequently about what should be in the curriculum for information science education: see, for example, Robinson and KaramuĞuoglu (2010) and Milojevic et al. (2011). Commonly mentioned topics are: nature and conceptions of information, documents and collections; information theory and philosophy; information history; information organisation and metadata; information behaviour and practices; information and digital literacies; information seeking and 
===
--- Chunk 27 ---
tion history; information organisation and metadata; information behaviour and practices; information and digital literacies; information seeking and retrieval; information architecture, human–computer interaction and user experience; data, information, and knowledge management; information policies and strategies;  document  and  collection  management;  records management and archiving; information law and ethics; information research methodology; information society; information systems; publishing and scholarly communication; and information services of all kinds. A useful model for organising this broad collection of topics is that of the communication chain of recorded information (Robinson, 2009). There is no canonical set of constituents of the chain, but it typically comprises stages of creation, dissemination, collection, storage, organisation, description, retrieval, use, and preservation. The elements of the chain form the core of most academic courses in the subject (Robinson and Bawden, 2010). The subject is delineated by national educational authorities. In the United Kingdom there is a detailed Subject Benchmark statement for the rather broader topic of Librarianship, Information, Knowledge, Records and Archive Management (Quality Assurance Agency, 2019). Professional bodies also list components of the subject, typically for supporting the accreditation of courses and individuals, and generally taking a strongly vocational perspective. The Association for Information Science and Technology (ASIST) also has a set of educational guidelines, specifying broad topics to be included in curricula. Overlaps with other information disciplines Information science as understood here is the central discipline focused on recorded information and documents, but it has overlaps with  other  information-related  disciplines.  Some  of  these, particularly with collection disciplines such as librarianship and archival science, are of long standing. Others are more recent, such as those with the newer disciplines of data science and digital humanities (Casarosa et al., 2020). We can distinguish eight such overlaps with diﬀerent kinds of adjacent disciplines. These overlaps result in the linking of information science with other disciplines in academic departments and faculties, professional bodies, research management structures, journal titles, etc., and the frequency with which  those  with  information  science  qualiﬁcations  ﬁnd employment in these adjacent sectors. Collection disciplines Given its focus on information recorded in documents, and its origins in the special library sector, it is not surprising that there is a particularly signiﬁcant overlap between information science and the collection disciplines, particularly those concerned with libraries and archives. Bates (2007) distinguishes these as the ‘information sciences’ and the ‘disciplines of the cultural record’. There is frequently a conﬂation into a wider discipline of library and information science (LIS) or library and information management (Dillon, 2007; Bawden and Robinson, 2016; Limberg, 2017; Hjørland, 2018), evident in the titles of academic departments, professional associations, academic journals and textbooks, etc. Many people with information science qualiﬁcations ﬁnd employment in the GLAM (Galleries, Libraries, Archives and Museums) sector, further emphasising the overlap with collection issues. This overlap will be discussed later in the book, in sections on digital libraries, collections management, records management and archiving, and others; see Rasmussen and Hjørland (2021) for a discussion of the overlap and convergence of collection institutions. Both are concerned with recorded information encapsulated in documents (in the broadest sense), including datasets, and both are concerned with the creation, curation and use of compilations of data and information. Technology disciplines As already noted, information science originated partly as a response to new information technologies, and the overlap with technology is still very signiﬁcant, as evidenced by the many academic courses in the overlap area, particularly in institutions presenting as iSchools, and by societies such as ASIST. Data science The relatively new discipline of data science, concerned with the extraction of knowledge and meaning from large datasets, is a discipline evidently adjacent to information science (Kelleher and Tierney, 2018; Du and Khan, 2020; Stuart, 2020). In order to support data science’s activities of data and text mining, data and text visualisation and statistical analysis, it is essential to have data curation, management and analytics, including collecting, cleaning and storing data and making it accessible through good metadata; all with concern for the data lifecycle. This is closely analogous to, if not identical with, the information management role (Benzing, 2020; as an example, see Darch et al., 2020). There has been considerable interest in introducing data science and data management issues into information science curricula (Robinson and Bawden, 2017; Wang, 2018; Casarosa et al., 2020; Loni et al., 2020). Social science disciplines Though there is debate as to what kind of discipline information science is, there is no doubt that many of the phenomena it studies are social phenomena, that many of its theories and concepts are social in nature and that much of its research is conducted using social research methods (Roberts, 1976; Hjørland, 2018). There is therefore an overlap with the social sciences, including psychology and law. This is seen particularly with information behaviour and practices (Chapter 12) and the information society and social informatics (Chapter 16), but also in national and international information policies (Chapter 14) and information law (Chapter 15). Communication and media disciplines Technical communication, the writing of abstracts, translation, information design and so on have always been regarded as an area of interest to information science. There is an evident overlap with journalism, publishing and media studies in the creation and dissemination sections of the communication chain, as will be discussed in Chapter 13. This is reﬂected in the structure of academic departments and faculties and in research assessment; for example, the conﬂation of these disciplines in panel D34 (Communication, Cultural and Media Studies, Library and Information Management) in the UK Research Excellence Framework for 2021. Management and policy disciplines Information management and information governance, and to an extent business intelligence, are regarded as important aspects of information science, but equally of relevance to business studies and management science; this is the rationale, no doubt, for some information science departments being located within business schools. Knowledge management also straddles the information science/business divide. National and international information policies, while primarily the concern of politics and social policy, also have signiﬁcant information science input. These aspects are covered in Chapter 14. Domain disciplines – subject specialism Many contributions to the development of information science have been made by those whose expertise is in a discipline where new specialised information systems are needed, particularly in the STEM subjects and within those, particularly in chemistry. Developments in information science continue to be driven by those from such ﬁelds, particularly for information resources and informatics systems for chemistry, biology, and medicine, as will be covered in Chapter 7. History of information science Recorded information in the form of documents, with associated activities of record-keeping and librarianship, has been important for millennia, as will be discussed in Chapter 2, but it was only in the 19th century that a codiﬁed body of professional knowledge emerged, to be developed into an acade
===
--- Chunk 34 ---
ll be discussed in Chapter 2, but it was only in the 19th century that a codiﬁed body of professional knowledge emerged, to be developed into an academic discipline (Hjørland, 2018). The Bavarian librarian Martin SchreĴinger was the ﬁrst to argue for formal training for librarians, and used the term BibliothekswissenschaĞ, which may be reasonably translated ‘library science’, in 1808 to encompass the tasks of cataloguing, classiﬁcation, shelf arrangement and library management. Later treatises by Christian Molbech and Frederich Ebert ampliﬁed the idea that the skills and knowledge needed to manage document collections were distinct from those of the scholar. The ﬁrst professional journal for the information disciplines was published in Germany from 1840: Robert Naumann’s Serapeum. ZeitschriĞ für BibliothekwissenschaĞ, HandschriĞenkunde und Ältere LiĴeratur (Journal of Library Science, Manuscript Information and Older Literature). The ﬁrst formalised educational programmes for the information sciences came with the establishment of courses in librarianship at the University of GöĴingen in 1886 and the University of Columbia in 1887, and at Leipzig and Barcelona, both in 1915, followed by the creation of London University’s School of Librarianship (later aĴached to University College London) in 1919. Graduate studies in ‘library science’ began at the University of Chicago in 1926 and in London a few years later. The history of information science, as distinct from librarianship
===
--- Chunk 35 ---
cience’ began at the University of Chicago in 1926 and in London a few years later. The history of information science, as distinct from librarianship and archival record keeping, is more recent; for overviews see Bawden (2008), Buckland (1996; 2017), Buckland and Liu (1995), Hahn and Buckland (1998), Hjørland (2018), Meadows (1987) and Shera and Cleveland (1977). Its origins are in the communications revolution of the 19th century, which will be discussed in Chapter 2, and with the simultaneous emergence of scientiﬁc and technical disciplines (Meadows, 2004), with a consequent need to deal with large volumes of documents, scientiﬁc and technical literature in particular. Its speciﬁc antecedents were the advent of the documentation movement and the development of the special library sector, both at the beginning of the 20th century; see Williams (1997) for an account of these in the USA. The documentation movement, pioneered by Paul Otlet, espoused a ‘scientiﬁc’ approach to the storage and retrieval of recorded information, with new schemes of classiﬁcation and the use of the new retrieval technology of the card index (Wright, 2014). The increased awareness of technical information as a resource for science-based industries led to the establishment of special libraries, and to the idea of ‘information work’ as distinct from librarianship. These, compared with traditional libraries, had a much more proactive role, a strong subject focus and an interest in all forms of informat
===
--- Chunk 36 ---
arianship. These, compared with traditional libraries, had a much more proactive role, a strong subject focus and an interest in all forms of information, not just formally published materials (Ditmas, 1950). The need to deal with the ‘information explosion’, the very rapid expansion in publications of all kinds dealing particularly with scientiﬁc and technical information during and aĞer the 1939–45 war, was discussed at the inﬂuential 1948 Royal Society conference on scientiﬁc information (Line, 1998). The growing application of new technologies to information handling – initially mechanised documentation techniques and then the digital computer – provided the technological background for the new science (Buckland, 1996; Black, 2007). Vannevar Bush’s inﬂuential Memex concept of personal information management with access to the world’s information, combined with Shannon and Weaver’s Mathematical Theory of Communication and the new ‘informetric’ laws, such as Bradford’s law of scaĴering (all to be discussed in later chapters), held out the prospect of a genuinely scientiﬁc approach to information management. The establishment of a new discipline or profession has typically been recognised, since the 19th century, by the seĴing up of a professional body to represent it. The ﬁrst such body in the area that was to spawn information science was an international body for the co-ordination of the activities of the documentation movement. n science was an international body for the co-ordination of the activities of the documentation movement. The Institut International de Bibliographie, later renamed as the International Federation for Information and Documentation, was established by the two Belgian pioneers of documentation, Paul Otlet and Henri La Fontaine, in 1895. In existence for over one hundred years, it was the ﬁrst recognisable information science association (Rayward, 1997). On a smaller scale, several associations were set up for special librarians. The Special Libraries Association, founded in the USA in 1909, is still thriving as a worldwide body today. In the UK, the Association of Special Libraries and Information Bureaux (ASLIB), was formed in 1924 with the aim of coordinating the activities of specialist information services in the UK and a role as a national intelligence service for science, commerce and industry (Bawden and Robinson, 2017). National groups of special librarians were formed in many other countries. The UK was rather slow oﬀ the mark, perhaps because of the existence of two other bodies catering for a relatively small sector; the Industrial Group of the Library Association was formed only in 1971 (Mason, 1991). It is still active, though now combined into a group also catering for commercial, legal and science librarians. The American Documentation Institute, created in 1937, became the American Society for Information Science in 1968. It renamed itself as the American Society for Information Science and Technology in 2000 (Sonnenwald, Davis and Shaw, 2017). In the UK, the Institute of Information Science (IIS) was formed in 1958, and joined with the Library Association (itself formed in 1877) to form the Chartered Institute of Library and Information Professionals (CILIP) in 2002, whose Royal Charter states that it will ‘work for the beneﬁt of the public to promote education and knowledge through the establishment and development of libraries and information services and to advance information science’. While each association had its particular reasons for the change, the fact that both felt that it was sensible for information science to enter a wider grouping – with technology or with the collection disciplines – illustrates what was said earlier about its multidisciplinary nature. Specialised journals are also a feature of a mature discipline. Of the major information science journals today, the longest-established is Journal of Documentation, the name reﬂecting its origins in the ﬁeld of documentation when it was founded in 1945. The ﬁrst educational provision for information science came with a course speciﬁcally for science graduates in London in 1929, though this closed for lack of interest in 1935. Modern information science education began in 1961, when Jason Farradane set up an evening course in ‘collecting and communicating scientiﬁc knowledge’ at Northampton College of Advanced Technology. Farradane, a British scientist born in Hampstead, London to Polish parents, was originally named Levkowitz and adopted his new name as a tribute to his scientiﬁc heroes, Michael Faraday and J. B. S. Haldane. He was the ﬁrst to use the terms ‘information science’ and ‘information scientist’ (Shapiro, 1995). Although his initial concept of an information scientist was a specialist in the handling of scientiﬁc and technical information, Farradane pioneered the teaching of information science as a distinct subject and was among those who argued for a ‘true science of information’, along the lines of the natural sciences (Farradan

on science as a distinct subject and was among those who argued for a ‘true science of information’, along the lines of the natural sciences (Farradane, 1976). A Masters course in information science was established at Farradane’s Centre for Information Science when the Northampton College became City University London in 1965 (Robinson and Bawden, 2010). Other courses in the subject were developed worldwide in the following years, typically conjoint LIS departments (Um and Feather, 2007; Mezick and Koenig, 2008). Recent years have seen a restructuring of many such departments, some joining with cultural and media departments, others amalgamating with technical and computing departments. Many of the laĴer have, since 2005, been associated with the iSchools movement (Golub, Hansson and Selden, 2016). One recurrent question has been to what extent education in the information sciences should be focused on theories and principles, as against training in practical techniques. We strongly advocate the former, believing that it is much more valuable for students to gain an understanding of principles and concepts on which they can build throughout their professional lives, rather than ephemeral points of practice, and this has been the basis of our courses at City, University of London (Robinson and Bawden, 2010). Librarianship … must abandon the practice of puĴing its students through ‘liĴle fake experiences in the classroom’. We must teach pupils theory, not techniques: principles, not practice. Summary Information science is a multidisciplinary ﬁeld of study, focused on meaningful information recorded in documents, and requiring a variety of perspectives and methods. Growing out of special librarianship and documentation, it has strong links with information technology (IT) and computer science and with the collection disciplines, and overlaps with a variety of other academic subjects. It is a coherent academic discipline in its own right, and educational programmes based on concepts and principles are the most valuable. The focus of information science is the human record, instantiated in documents and processed through the communication chain of recorded information. The uniqueness of information science is in its concern for all components of the communication chain. We will give some historical perspective on speciﬁc topics in several of the chapters which follow. It is sometimes suggested that, since information science is a relatively young discipline, there is no need to think about the history of anything which came before, say, 1950. We strongly disagree. Some appreciation of the history of information and documents, as well as being of interest in its own right, can help give a perspective on current problems and solutions. Although contexts and technologies may change, many information issues remain constant over time, and a historical perspective can be of practical, as well as academic, value. • • • • • • • Historical studies come in many forms and ﬂavours (Black, 2006). For the information sciences, historical accounts have fallen into a number of categories, including: history of libraries, archives and information services history of information policies and infrastructures history of publishing, books and reading history of information technologies (not just digital ones) history of the information disciplines and professions origins of the information society studies of the cultural and social contexts of information communication and use. The last of these has developed into a new sub-discipline of information history, concerned with all aspects of information in societies of the p

The last of these has developed into a new sub-discipline of information history, concerned with all aspects of information in societies of the past; how it was understood, used, organised, managed, collected, disseminated, etc. See, for example, Weller (2008), Skouvig and Andersen (2015) and Cortada (2019). It may be regarded as a branch of history focused on an intangible central object of study; analogous to histories of such things as humour or fear. Very oĞen, however, it will necessarily be studied through a focus on the documents which convey information and how people have produced and used these. We will not follow any of these approaches. We focus on the historical development of documents, and the systems and services set up to deal with them; hence the title of the chapter. The treatment will be brief and informal, and will direct the reader to other works for details of all the topics mentioned, giving just suﬃcient material to set the context for what follows in the rest of the book. Information ages? It is tempting, in trying to present a short and simple account of a complex and long-term development, to write of distinct ‘information ages’ based on ‘information revolutions’. And there is no doubt that a series of developments in the communication of information have largely dictated the information environment which followed. Language, recorded signs and symbols, writing and scripts, printing, mass communications, the digital computer, and the internet a
===
--- Chunk 55 ---
ent which followed. Language, recorded signs and symbols, writing and scripts, printing, mass communications, the digital computer, and the internet are typically taken as deﬁning developments. However, this is too simplistic a viewpoint. No form of history falls into such neat periods, and developments happen at diﬀerent points in diﬀerent parts of the world. In outlining the history of documents, therefore, we will follow the timeline without invoking such distinct categories. For convenience, and acknowledging that this involves gross over-simpliﬁcation, the timeline is divided into ﬁve periods: prehistory and the ancient world; the medieval world; the age of print, including the Renaissance and the Enlightenment; the age of mass communication, roughly approximating to the long 19th century; and the documentation age, to the present day. Luciano Floridi (2014, chapter 1) has distinguished prehistory, when there are no information systems, history, when information systems support society, and hyperhistory, when society is dependent upon, and deﬁned by, information systems. In our timeline, the ﬁrst period sees the move from prehistory to history, and the last the move from history to hyperhistory. A thorough and detailed overview of information in society across all periods is given by Blair et al. (2021), and a shorter account by Gleick (2011). Prehistory and the ancient world Information communication began with spoken language, but we can only speculate how information may have been transmiĴed through oral communication. It is only with the origins of recorded information that we can begin a history of information, based on documents. We take this ﬁrst period as lasting from the ﬁrst records to the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476. For overviews of libraries in the period, see Ryholt and Barjamovic (2020), Nicholls (2017), König, Oikonomopoulou and Woolf (2013), Too (2010) and Casson (2001); for archives, see Brosius (2003) and Delsalle (2018); and for writing, reading and literacy, see Houston (2004), Kallendorf (2013) and Kolb (2018). The earliest artefacts which we might reasonably describe as documents are cave paintings and other forms of rock art, the oldest believed to be more than 40,000 years old; the famous cave paintings of  Lascaux  in  France  are  20,000  years  old;  see hĴps://archeologie.culture.fr/lascaux for video images. Whether it is reasonable to call them ‘documents’ is a moot point; but they show that the people of that time had the means to record signs and symbols, and thereby to communicate across time, whatever their purpose may have been (Bahn, 2010; 2016; David, 2017). It is now believed that writing was invented independently at least four times: in Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Mesoamerica, although some older texts consider that writing systems may have spread by a mechanism of diﬀusion. The earliest accurately dated writings are from Uruk in Mesopotamia (3300 BCE). Mesopotamian writings used the cuneiform script, wriĴen on clay tablets using sharpened reeds as writing implements. In Egypt, the hieroglyphic, hieratic, and, later, demotic scripts were wriĴen in ink on a variety of materials: the stereotypical papyrus, but also wood, stone and poĴery. Because of the nature of the materials used, and the durability of clay tablets, we know much more of collections in Mesopotamia than their equivalents in Egypt. The library/archive at the palace of Ebla, in modern Syria, active between 2600 and 2300 BCE, comprised tablets stored on wooden shelves, with diﬀerent types of materials held in separate rooms. Two ‘archive rooms’ held over 17,000 tablets of commercial, legal and administrative records. Another room held collections of dictionaries, proverbs, epic narratives, myths, hymns, incantations and rituals. Others contained material on botany, zoology, mineralogy and mathematics. There was even what might be regarded as an early form of reference collection. Many tablets were devoted to lists of persons and items, oĞen in order of precedence and importance: gods, kings, professions, animals, stones, etc. The ordering of items in the rooms was maintained by rudimentary wriĴen classiﬁcation tables. The classical world The emergence of the alphabet had a signiﬁcant impact on writing, and on the intellectual tools used to provide access to the writings. An alphabetical script was more readily understood than the complex logo-syllabic cuneiform, or the numerous Egyptian hieroglyphs, and provided a rea
===
--- Chunk 64 ---
 An alphabetical script was more readily understood than the complex logo-syllabic cuneiform, or the numerous Egyptian hieroglyphs, and provided a ready-made solution for arranging materials. The origins of the alphabet are unclear (Robinson, 2013). It is believed that the Phoenician alphabet, ﬁrst seen around 1000 BCE, used a small number of symbols to replace the much larger symbol sets of cuneiform and hieroglyphic writing and could be used to write diﬀerent languages, greatly increasing the ﬂexibility of representation. It inﬂuenced the Aramaic/Hebrew and Greek alphabets, leading to the ﬁrst substantial bodies of alphabetic writings (Steele, 2019) and to the ﬁrst ordering of books by alphabetical order. The derivation of the Phoenician alphabet from earlier scripts remains an incomplete story, although current thinking is that the script developed from Egyptian hieroglyphs via a proto-Sinaitic or proto-Canaanite script. This is based on the discovery in 1904–5, by Flinders Petrie, of inscriptions which he believed to be alphabetic at Serabit el-Khadim (Petrie, 1912). The script became known as Proto-Sinaitic. In 1916, Sir Alan Gardiner concluded that the Sinaitic signs were created by reforming Egyptian hieroglyphic signs (Gardiner, 1916). The earliest known alphabetic inscription in Greek dates from around 730 BCE, but the date of the invention of the Greek alphabet remains uncertain, placed between 1100 and 800 BCE (Robinson, 2009). date of the invention of the Greek alphabet remains uncertain, placed between 1100 and 800 BCE (Robinson, 2009). The Greeks wrote on stone, papyrus, poĴery and slate covered in wax. Libraries and record centres became widespread throughout the Hellenistic world, with evidence for signiﬁcant libraries at Pergamum, Antioch, Pella and Alexandria. There were recognisable royal, private and public libraries, supported by scriptoria and a book trade. Texts were wriĴen on papyrus rolls and stored on shelves, in pigeonholes or chests, with tags or smaller scrolls to identify title and author. Strabo tells us that Aristotle was the ﬁrst to teach the Hellenistic kings of Egypt how to arrange a library. The best-known library of this period is, of course, the Great Library of Alexandria in Egypt, founded by Alexander the Great in the fourth century BCE and developed by the Ptolomaic kings over the following centuries (El-Abbadi and Fathallah, 2008). A centre for scholarship, it was believed at its height to contain over 400,000 Greek papyrus manuscripts: essentially all of human knowledge at that time. Its ﬁrst director, Xenodontus, is said to have created a shelving system, with a subject division derived from that of Aristotle and items arranged within these divisions by alphabetical author names. The famous Pinakes may have been a catalogue of this library, or a bibliography of literature; presented on many scrolls, it was divided according to the classiﬁcation of its creator, Callim

--- Chunk 66 ---

This had sections for philosophy, law, history, medicine, natural history and miscellanea, with literature divided into rhetoric, lyric, comedy, tragedy and epic works. Including a general guide to the literature of the day, it is regarded as the ﬁrst recognisably modern form of bibliographic tool. The Roman world adopted the documentary infrastructure of the Greeks, with many public and private libraries and a ﬂourishing book trade (Nicholls, 2018). The ﬁrst Roman public libraries were initiated by the military commander Asinius Pollio (75 BCE–4 CE) around 39 BCE, and by the emperor Augustus some years later. The codex, the forerunner of the modern book, was developed by the Romans from wooden writing tablets tied or hinged together, later replaced by parchment pages. Considerably more convenient to store, arrange and use than scrolls, codices replaced scrolls for most purposes over the period 100–500 CE. The ﬁrst reference to literary works in the form of a parchment codex is made by Martial during the years 84–86 CE (Reynolds and Wilson, 2013, 35). The impetus for change from the scroll to the codex is thought to have come from early Christians in biblical texts; pagan texts in codex form were rare in the second century CE. The transfer of classical texts from scroll to codex happened gradually and may have resulted in the loss of texts considered less interesting or important at the time. All modern books are technically codices, but the term is generally reserved for handwriĴen books produced from late antiquity through the Middle Ages. Some of the earliest surviving works are parchment codices from the fourth century CE. The Codex Siniaticus, a manuscript of the Christian Bible wriĴen in Greek in the fourth century, is a well- known example. The medieval world Developments begun in the classical period continued throughout medieval times, which is conventionally taken as lasting from 477 to the fall of Constantinople in 1453, although the establishment of Gutenberg’s printing press a few years earlier might be a more appropriate end marker for our purposes. The earlier part of the medieval period used to be referred to as the ‘Dark Ages’, but this gives a quite misleading impression of a loss of all culture and documentation. In fact, there was a rich and evolving book culture throughout the period, based on the manuscript codex, which began with the transmission of classical works but moved on beyond it (Kwakkel, 2018; Reynolds and Wilson, 2013). Initially, the documentary legacy of the classical world was maintained in the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) empire, with Constantinople a centre for scholarship and the route
===
--- Chunk 68 ---
ntary legacy of the classical world was maintained in the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) empire, with Constantinople a centre for scholarship and the route through which many classical writings were preserved (Wilson, 2013). There were three major libraries, which can be categorised as royal, religious and academic. Subsequently,  innovations  in  information  communication continued, in Europe and beyond. Parchment, able to be wriĴen on both sides and beĴer able to accept illuminations, became the norm, with the sheets folded and sewn together in codex form. This was the period of the illuminated manuscript, now the treasures of many national libraries. Other forms of information representation – maps, musical notations and mathematical symbolism – were developed, the last using the so-called Arabic numerals, originally an Indian innovation. The Islamic world was at that time much ahead of the West in document production, having embarked on a major programme of translating Greek, Persian and Indian texts and extending them by original scholarship (Al-Khalili, 2010; Lyons, 2009). This process was pioneered by the ‘House of Wisdom’ (Bayt al-Hikma) established in ninth-century Baghdad by the Abbasid caliph Al-Ma’mun, who wished to collect all the world’s books under one roof. Nothing remains of this institution, and its nature and purpose remain speculative. By the end of the 12th century secular scribes were banding together into guilds and workshops. Works in local languages – as opposed to Latin or Greek – were becoming more common, and treatises on mathematics, logic, philosophy and astronomy began to appear, oĞen translated from Arabic. It is not unreasonable to suggest that, two hundred years before the introduction of printing, a publishing industry had been established. This was promoted by the rise of secular universities throughout Western Europe, stimulating a need for multiple authoritative copies of texts. This was coupled with a demand for popular and professional books, including medical texts, educational books, novels and cookery books. The production of manuscripts aĴained a professional status, with scribal fraternities and apprenticeship schemes. Paper had reached Europe in the 12th century, a Chinese innovation from the second century or earlier (Allen et al., 2010; Zheng, 2014), passed on via the Arabic world aĞer its introduction to Samarkand from China in 751. However, it was initially used only for formal documents, and not for books. The ﬁrst paper mill in England was established at the end of the 15th century, in order to meet the demands of printers. University libraries appeared, some of which survive to the present day, at Oxford, Cambridge, Paris, Padua and elsewhere. Catalogues of this period were accession lists of authors and titles, and served to support an active programme of document loans between libraries and scholars (Reed-Leal, 2020). The ﬁrst union catalogues were created; in 14th-century Paris, for example, the Sorbonne university library had a union catalogue of several Parisian libraries. Secular classiﬁcation was typically based on the classical seven liberal arts: the trivium of grammar, rhetoric and dialectic (or logic) and the quadrivium of arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy. This form of classiﬁcation was ﬁrst devised in the sixth century by Flavius Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus (c. 490–c. 585), a philosopher and theologian living in the last days of the Roman world. The age of print This period from the introduction of printing to the conventional beginning of the ‘long 19th century’ in 1789 saw the introduction of an information infrastructure based on printed documents. Printing with moveable characters had been established in China – where characters of baked clay were used initially – for several centuries before it was introduced into Europe in the middle of the 15th century (Zheng, 2014). The earliest dated printed book is the Diamond Sutra, held by the British Library, printed in Chinese translation in north-west China in 868 (Figure 2.8). Figure 2.8  Frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra (public domain, International Dunhuang Project, via Wikimedia Commons) Credit for the introduction of the printing press into Europe is usually given to Johannes Gutenberg, who established a press in Mainz around 1447, his colleague Peter Schoeﬀer having discovered a viable method of casting the leĴers using an alloy of tin and lead. The ﬁrst printing press was set up in England in 1476, by William Caxton; the ﬁrst product was The Dictes or Sayings of the Philosophers. For more details of early printing and printed books, see Twyman (1998), Wagner and Reed (2010), de Hamel (2013), Dondi (2013) and Mosley (2013). Printing houses spread throughout Europe during the next
===
--- Chunk 73 ---
, see Twyman (1998), Wagner and Reed (2010), de Hamel (2013), Dondi (2013) and Mosley (2013). Printing houses spread throughout Europe during the next century, combining the talents of compositors, engravers and type- casters to give a recognisably modern printing industry, able to produce both text and images, though by a rather clumsy process with images reproduced separately, initially on wood-block carvings and later on metal plates. Printing had two general eﬀects. One was the availability of multiple identical copies of works, calling for bibliographic tools – catalogues, bibliographies, tables of contents and indexes – in which there was a single description for a printed work, rather than for each unique handwriĴen manuscript. The other was that printing led to the original ‘information explosion’, with many more copies of more titles, of an increasingly diverse nature (Eisenstein, 2005; Barber, 2017). The ﬁrst bibliographies in a modern sense appeared at this stage; notably Conrad Gesner’s Bibliotheca Universalis of 1545, which pioneered ideas of selection, arrangement and indexing. Gesner (1516–65), who has been described as the ﬁrst would-be universal bibliographer and the last to have had any chance of succeeding, managed to include 15,000 titles in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, estimated at 20–25% of the total available at the time. The publisher, bookseller and bibliographer Andrew Maunsell (d. 1595) published a Catalogue of English Printed Bookes in 1595, the ﬁrst a

Classiﬁcation schemes, aĴempting to reconcile a philosophical organisation of knowledge with the practical need to arrange books in libraries, were developed by several scholars, notably Francis Bacon (1561–1626) and GoĴfried von Leibnitz (1646–1716) (Schulte-Albert, 1971). A variety of reference tools and techniques were developed for organising and managing information (Blair, 2010; Krajewski, 2011). In the 17th century advances in printing technology led to both a more rapid production process and the ability – through lithography – to print text and images at the same time. This led to the increased numbers and readership of newspapers, magazines and scientiﬁc and professional journals. The ﬁrst scientiﬁc journals were established in 1665, the Paris-based Journal des Savants, ﬁrst published on 5 January, just claiming precedence over the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, which was ﬁrst published on 6 March. The so-called Enlightenment period of the 18th century saw a further expansion of the information infrastructure. Major reference tools, such as Chambers’ Cyclopedia (1728), Diderot’s Encyclopédie (1761), Samuel Johnson’s Dictionary (1755) and the Encyclopedia Britannica (1768), appeared for the ﬁrst time, accompanied by national and subject bibliographies

National libraries and ‘memory institutions’ began to appear: the British Museum and its associated library in 1753 and the Bibliothèque Nationale in 1789. Headrick (2000) shows that many of the conceptual developments in the organisation, presentation and communication of information made during this period enabled the technical advances of the following century. The age of mass communication The advent of mass communication, due to the adoption of the products of the Industrial Revolution for the purposes of information dissemination, laid the foundations of the modern information environment, and the long 19th century (1789–1914) can be regarded as the mass communication age. The ﬁrst steam- powered presses, introduced early in the 19th century, increased the rate of printing considerably, but this soon went up by orders of magnitude; one of the ﬁrst such machines, Koenig’s steam press of 1814, is shown in Figure 2.9 on the next page. Whereas a hand press typically printed 250 pages in an hour, by the 1820s steam-powered presses could produce 4,000, and by the 1850s newspaper rotary presses were achieving 20,000 sheets an hour. Steamships and steam trains provided rapid and reliable transport for this new volume of printed material. An example of the way in which s

A much greater range of books and serial publications was produced, both popular and academic; in particular, many more specialised scientiﬁc and professional journals, monographs and textbooks to meet the needs of the rapidly professionalising and specialising scientiﬁc and technical activities (Meadows, 2004). Communication in general improved, with the introduction of the telegraph in the 1830s, national postal services in the 1840s and the telephone in the 1870s. Photography was introduced in the 1840s, and three decades later photographs were commonly being reproduced in printed documents. Charles Babbage’s analogue computers of the 1830s, although their concept proved to be beyond what the technology of the time could deliver, gave intimations of things to come. Summary This overview of the history of information has necessarily been brief, and somewhat simplistic. Economic, social, technical and academic developments have gone alongside the growth of knowledge and the technologies and systems which have tried to control the resulting increases in information, records and documents. These developments have never been as orderly as they may seem, as each inﬂuences, and is inﬂuenced by, the others. We can, nonetheless, learn lessons from the information past, and use them to understand the information present and to imagine the information future. • • • • Figure 2.11  Paul Otlet in his home oﬃce, 1937 (public domain, via Wikimedia Commons) Figure 2.12  Henri La Fontaine (photographie Geruzet Freres, Bruxelles) (public domain, via Wikimedia Commons) Understanding the history of information and documents is not only intrinsically interesting, but is helpful in understanding the present and in seeing analogies with past problems and issues. There are several diﬀerent approaches and perspectives in the study of the history of information and documents. The developments which have, each in turn, drastically changed the information environment have been language, writing, printing, mass communications and networked digital information. Morán-Reyes (2015, 587) Introduction Topics at the core of the information sciences, such as the nature of knowledge and what we can know, how meaning and truth are ascertained, and how things can be distinguished, named, categorised, and classiﬁed, have been the concern of philosophy for many centuries. Yet information science has no agreed philosophy of its own; rather, a wide variety of philosophies and philosophers have been pressed into service to analyse its concerns. In this chapter we will look at some ways in which philosophy and information science overlap and interact, and how philosophical ideas may directly aﬀect the theory and practice of the information disciplines. This is an extensive, and in some aspects technical, topic, and only a selective and informal overview will be given, with references to the literature for those wishing to take it further. Philosophy and its relevance to information science There are usually held to be three main branches of philosophy: ontology and metaphysics – what is it to ‘be’, and what kinds of things can exist; epistemology – what is it to ‘know’, what can we know, and how can we be sure of our knowledge; and ethics – how can actions be ‘right’, and how should we act. All of these have relevance to the information sciences; see Furner (2017a) for more detailed discussion. Metaphysics (the study of what can exist) and ontology (the study of fundamental categories and kinds of things) address the existence and nature of entities such as information, documents, relevance, aboutness and many more. Epistemology questions what is meant by knowledge, with very practical consequences for knowledge management. Ethics questions what is the right use of information, and touches on issues such as censorship and privacy. This is treated in detail in Chapter 15, and will not be repeated here. For accessible short introductions to philosophy itself, see Craig (2020), Grayling (2020) and Williamson (2020); for ontology and metaphysics, see Ney (2014) and Rea (2020); and for epistemology, see Audi (2011), Pritchard (2018) and Nagel (2014). Furner (2010) gives a review of the nature of philosophy and its relation to the information disciplines, reminding us that there are two main 
===
--- Chunk 90 ---
2014). Furner (2010) gives a review of the nature of philosophy and its relation to the information disciplines, reminding us that there are two main aspects: analysing the nature of the information disciplines from a philosophical viewpoint, and analysing the nature of entities which are important for the subject. The ﬁrst has led to consideration of the value for the information sciences of general philosophical positions such as realism, positivism and constructionism. The second has led, in particular, to analyses of the nature of data, information and knowledge. Hardiman (2014) gives a wide-ranging review of philosophical positions, showing their relevance to archives and records management. There has been limited examination of the inﬂuence of philosophical positions on information science, despite the fact that they may have a signiﬁcant, if implicit, inﬂuence on practice. A realist perspective, for example, asserting that an objective external world exists, and we can understand it to an extent, underlies the systems paradigm in information science, and research methods such as experiment and quantitative surveys. A constructivist or constructionist perspective, asserting that reality is, at least to a degree, subjective, and created by individuals and groups, underlies the cognitive paradigm, and a preference for holistic and qualitative research, focusing on individuals’ knowledge and experience. See Hjørland (2004; 2005) for realist and positivist perspectives in i
===
--- Chunk 91 ---
ic and qualitative research, focusing on individuals’ knowledge and experience. See Hjørland (2004; 2005) for realist and positivist perspectives in information science, and Talja, Tuominen and Savolainen (2005) for constructivist/constructionist  perspectives.  Other  philosophical positions examined from an information science perspective are pragmatism and neo-pragmatism (Sundin and Johannisson, 2005; Buschman, 2017), and empiricism (Hjørland, 2005; 2011). There has been no consensus that the information disciplines need a foundational philosophy. For example, Zwaldo (1997), noting that, in their respective literatures, librarians rarely discussed philosophy and philosophers never discussed library science, suggested that it was unnecessary, and rather self-defeating, to seek for a single philosophy, or indeed any philosophy of LIS. For a rejoinder, see Radford and Budd (1997), who argue that a lack of philosophical discussion in the theory and practice of LIS does not mean that philosophy was absent; rather, that philosophical positions, typically rather simplistic, have been, and are, assumed and taken for granted. The idea that the information disciplines have not been interested in philosophical issues is far from the truth; as Fallis and Whitcomb (2009, 176) write, with numerous examples, ‘quite a lot of applied epistemology has been done by information scientists’. Many commentators have argued that it would be to the advantage of the information disciplines to ﬁnd a

Many commentators have argued that it would be to the advantage of the information disciplines to ﬁnd a more secure theoretical foundation; see Bawden and Robinson (2018) for a review. Most notably, Luciano Floridi (2002) argued that LIS needs a foundational philosophy and that the discipline’s identity crisis, originating in the 1930s, has been due to a search for such a foundation. LIS and philosophy, in Floridi’s argument, are closely associated, because of the topics in which they are interested and because of the level and scope of their research. There have been criticisms of the rather superﬁcial way in which some of those who advocate for the value of philosophy in information science have applied it. Floridi (2002, 47) writes that information researchers ‘have been lured by a variety of friendly but pre-established philosophies instead of ﬁghting for their own place in the philosophical ﬁeld’. Zwaldo (1997) likens it to borrowing a book, which is never ours, and which we will soon return and replace with another. Vickery (1997, 458) expressed this tendency as ‘examining the ideas of a … philosopher, extracting principles and oﬀering them as presuppositions upon which information science may be based’, while Frohmann (1992, 366) noted eloquently that ‘high-ﬂying LIS researchers swoop indiscriminately down upon the theoretical terrain, colonising Popperian worlds, or cannibalizing hermeneutics, phenomenology, general syste

There have, however, been three strands of thought which have developed a deep relation between philosophy and the information disciplines, with the opportunity for information science to inﬂuence and add to the philosophy, rather than just drawing from it. We can categorise these as philosophies of information, philosophies of knowledge and critical theory as related to documents and media, and we now consider each in turn. Philosophies of information Most philosophies of information are ontological or metaphysical, that is to say they focus on analysing what information is. This aspect is discussed in detail in Chapter 5, and only the general philosophical issues are covered here; for an overview from a variety of perspectives, see Floridi (2016), and for a shorter review, see Compton (2015). The aĴempt to build a philosophy around information and data, rather than knowledge, which has been a concern of philosophers since the earliest times, began with Shannon’s mathematical theory of communication. This was the ﬁrst successful aĴempt to give a rigorous quantitative theory of information, at the cost of neglecting the meaning of an information-bearing messa

--- Chunk 94 ---

Several theorists aĴempted to extend Shannon’s information theory to include the meaning of, and knowledge in, the communicated information, the most notable being the American philosopher Fred Dretske (1932– 2013), with his concept that knowledge is information-produced belief (Dretske, 1981). Floridi (2019a) reviews these aĴempts, concluding that none has been fully successful. Karl Popper The Austrian-born philosopher Karl Popper (1902–94), who spent most of his career at the London School of Economics, developed his ‘Three Worlds’ ontology, in part as a response to the limitations of the problematic traditional philosophical justiﬁed, true belief view of knowledge: World 1 is the physical world, World 2 is the subjective mental world and World 3 consists of objective, communicable knowledge, ‘knowledge without a knowing subject’, which Popper denoted rather vaguely as ‘the contents of books and libraries’, which includes errors and grows and develops in an evolutionary way (Popper, 1992; 1979; NoĴurno, 2002). Popper’s idea, and particularly his World 3, were heralded by Brookes (1980) to be a philosophical foundation for information science, and the task of information science to be the exploration and organisation of World 3. However, its impact has been limited. Although it has been popular as a pedagogical model, and

Although it has been popular as a pedagogical model, and used on occasions for analysing the information environment (see, for example, Bawden, 2002 and Gnoli, 2018), it has generated liĴle in the way of either detailed conceptual insight or practical guidance. Popper’s conception did, however, inﬂuence Luciano Floridi’s development of his philosophy of information (PI) (Gorichanaz et al., 2020, 593 and 608–9). Luciano Floridi Floridi’s PI has been developed since the 1990s and is currently the most thorough and sophisticated approach of its kind; for detailed treatment, see Floridi (2011; 2013; 2019b), and for accessible overviews, see Floridi (2010; 2014a). Rather than being the philosophy of a restricted subject area, it is an all-encompassing philosophy for the information age: ‘philosophy of our time, for our time’ (Floridi, 2019b, xii). It is rooted in an ontology which sees reality as ultimately informational, a form of realism termed Informational Structural Realism (ISR). Data is deﬁned as any diﬀerence or lack of uniformity, and information as well-formed, meaningful, truthful data, as will be discussed fully in Chapter 5. No  other information philosophy foundation has aĴempted such a broad scope. Six concepts within PI are of particular relevance to the information sciences. The fourth revolution, following the earlier revolutions of Copernicus, Darwin and Freud, is the shiĞ which places information and communication technologies at the heart of our society. Following prehistory, in which there was no recorded information, and history, in which recorded information is important, we are now at the stage of hyperhistory, in which our society is entirely dependent on information and communication technologies (ICTs). This is characterised by the infosphere, an information environment blending physical and digital, in which we live onlife, again seamlessly blending physical and digital. Communication and interaction in the infosphere is determined by informational frictions: whatever impedes the free ﬂow of information. The transition to onlife happens only once in the history of humanity. Floridi (2002, 2004) put forward the idea that not merely was PI a suitable foundation for LIS, but that LIS should be viewed as applied PI, and hence research and reﬂective practice in LIS could contribute to the development of philosophy. This idea has been debated since then, and, although by no means universally agreed, the idea is gaining support; for reviews and commentaries, see Dinneen and Brauner (2015), Fyﬀe (2015), Van der Veer Martens (2017), Bawden and Robinson (2018) and Gorichanaz et al. (2020). In summary, we can give a number of reasons why PI may be a suitable philosophical foundation for the information sciences. The deﬁnition of information within PI is more appropriate than that in numerous other theories of information (Dinneen and Brauner, 2015). Although PI’s deﬁnition of information includes ‘truthful’, this does not ignore the fact that ‘libraries are full of “knowledge”’ (Floridi, 2004, 662); in the PI perspective, LIS deals with semantic content recorded in documents.  Semantic  content  includes  information  (true), misinformation (false) and disinformation (deliberately false). Information science is not concerned with the truth of information per se, but with the quality of semantic content. PI gives special importance, and ethical value, to documents because of their status as rich informational entities; although because every entity is assigned some moral (informational) value to begin with, this does not imply that they will continue to have the same value aĞer any thought has been applied: ‘the point at stake is not some daĞ idea about the intrinsic value of Shakespeare versus Dan Brown’ (Floridi, 2008, 193). The information sciences can also contribute to PI as well as take from it; a response to the criticisms about their taking from a variety of ‘foreign’ philosophies: ‘By contributing to the development of PI, LIS can carry on the task of developing its own theoretical foundation from within’ (Floridi, 2002, 48); ‘LIS may just be as important to PI as PI is to LIS in terms of deepening our mutual understanding  of  information  ontologies,  the  dynamics  of informational domains, and the variety of evolving relationships among information organisms and information objects’ (Van der Veer Martens, 2015, 348). Although Floridi’s is the best-known philosophy of information and with the greatest reach, there have been other approaches. These are typically focused on the nature of information and have not, as yet at least, developed any interactions with the sciences of recorded information and documentation. Examples, very much in the analytical philosophical tradition, are the mathematical/logical theory of information developed by Burgin and Feistel (2017) and the metaphilosophy, combining philosophies of science and of information, of Wu and Brenner (2017). Though all these approaches are centred on the concept of information, they also typically include data; for perspectives on the philosophy of data per se, see Furner (2017b) and Leonelli (2016). Philosophies of knowledge Knowledge has been a subject for philosophical enquiry for very many  years  (Nagel,  2014;  Pritchard,  2018). This is problematic for information science, since it requires someone to be actively believing something, that what they are believing is true and that their belief be justiﬁed, typically by the senses – the believer saw or heard something. Michael Polanyi A distinct approach to knowledge is that of Michael Polanyi (1891– 1976), Hungarian-born but who spent most of his career in Britain. Originally a physical chemist, who later contributed to philosophy and social science, he developed an epistemology based on tacit knowledge or personal knowledge (Polanyi, 1962; 1966). Things are known which cannot be expressed fully in words, diagrams, formulae or any means of objective communication. This is summed up in his dictum that ‘we may know more than we can tell’. Tacit knowledge is oĞen regarded as a ‘knowing how’ rather than ‘knowing that’, and Polanyi argued that all knowledge is either tacit, or is rooted in tacit knowledge. The concept has been developed by others; for example, to distinguish between knowledge which is tacit because no one has gone to the eﬀort of making it explicit and things our bodies can do that we cannot describe even in principle, and between individual and social tacit knowledge (Collins, 2010). Its signiﬁcance for the information sciences is the impetus it gave to the development of knowledge management, to be covered in Chapter 14. Social epistemology One signiﬁcant philosophical movement based on knowledge was, remarkably, originated by librarians, Margaret Egan (1905–59) and Jesse Shera (1903–82) (Egan and Shera, 1952; Furner, 2004; Fyﬀe
===
--- Chunk 102 ---
ed on knowledge was, remarkably, originated by librarians, Margaret Egan (1905–59) and Jesse Shera (1903–82) (Egan and Shera, 1952; Furner, 2004; Fyﬀe, 2015). Although Egan and Shera were by no means the ﬁrst to reﬂect on the social nature of knowledge, they were the ﬁrst to use a speciﬁc term, social epistemology, to denote it. This is the only example so far of the information sciences contributing a new concept to philosophy. Social epistemology has at its root the collaborative study and communication of knowledge, in order to discover truth and create new knowledge, and how knowledge can be possessed by societies and by groups; it stands in contrast to traditional epistemology, which focuses on the knowledge of individual persons. This is not fully congruent with the interests of the information disciplines, which are mainly concerned with sources and records of knowledge, rather than knowledge per se. Nonetheless, Shera (1970, 108) asserted that social epistemology ‘can give librarianship its intellectual foundation for which we have been searching for so long’, while Fyﬀe (2015) suggested that LIS has been treated as a branch of social epistemology since the mid-20th century. The nature of social epistemology has changed since its inception; see, for example, Zandonade (2004), Fallis (2006), Fuller (2012) and Dragos (2019). Its focus has always been on knowledge in society, the communication of ideas throughout the whole social fabric, and the ways in which this is aﬀe

This is a broad concept, covering a variety of approaches and foci. For reviews of the current state of social epistemology, see Goldman and O’Connor (2021) and Fricker et al. (2019). Egan and Shera held that a library’s purpose is to be the centre for a community’s knowledge creation and communication, and that libraries and similar institutions have a central role in social epistemology. More recent formulations do not give information institutions such a central place. Nonetheless, there remains a strong relation between social epistemology and the information sciences, whose nature is still a subject for debate. Floridi (2002) argued that social epistemology cannot be a basis for LIS, since it has as its basis the study of knowledge in order to discover truth, while LIS has to deal with a much wider range of sources than those which provide ‘true knowledge’, and its remit is not knowledge itself, but the documents and records which convey knowledge. The two are certainly related, but both are in need of a common foundation, which Floridi identiﬁes as PI. Fyﬀe (2015) supports this viewpoint; Furner (2015) makes a similar point: that ‘knowledge studies’, which social epistemology would equate to, would be far wider than LIS could reasonably encompass. Critical theory and media theory Critical theory is a broad term, including structuralist, post- structuralist  and  post-modernist  theory,  phenomenology, hermeneutics and media and communication theory. Its style of philosophy is typically qualitative, interpretivist and literary, rather than formal, analytical and logical. It is generally associated with continental European philosophers, such as Adorno, Barthes, Baudrillard, Benjamin, Bourdieu, Deleuze, Derrida, Foucault, Gadamer, GuaĴari, Habermas, Heidegger and Lacan, and also with the Toronto school of communication theory, epitomised by McLuhan and Innis (Bronner, 2017; Bohman, 2019). Summary Despite continuing and increasing interest in the intersection of philosophy and the sciences of information, there is no agreement on any single philosophy, or philosophical approach, as a foundation for information science. It may be that there never will be such in a diverse and multidisciplinary ﬁeld. Nonetheless, the search for satisfactory foundations for the discipline is a vital task which will bring beneﬁts to practice as much as to academia. We currently have a variety of philosophies competing with, and to a degree complementing, each other. It seems that Floridi’s PI oﬀers much as the most generally appropriate foundation. • • • There is no single, generally accepted philosophical or theoretical foundation for the information sciences; rather a variety of alternatives have been suggested. Floridi’s PI gives the promise of a viable foundational basis. Further development in foundational theory and philosophy of the information sciences is important both for the academic subjects and for the practical disciplines.
