Claude Shannon (quoted in Soni, 2019) Introduction In this chapter we consider paradigms and turns, approaches to the study of the information disciplines and the practice of the information professions, which are generally regarded as more speciﬁc and contextual than the philosophies discussed in the previous chapter. We then consider the role of theory in information science. A theory is regarded as more speciﬁc and contextualised than a paradigm, although types of theory are closely associated with particular paradigms. However, the terms are not used consistently, and the philosophy–paradigm–theory hierarchy is not strictly observed in writings on information science. Paradigms and turns The Oxford English dictionary (December 2020) deﬁnes a paradigm, in the sense in which the term is used here, as ‘a conceptual or methodological model underlying the theories and practices of a science or discipline at a particular time; hence a generally accepted world view’. The term, brought into common use by the philosopher of science Thomas Kuhn (1922–96) in his work on scientiﬁc revolutions, describes a collection of beliefs about the subject maĴer of a subject, and a set of agreements a
===
--- Chunk 121 ---
Kuhn (1922–96) in his work on scientiﬁc revolutions, describes a collection of beliefs about the subject maĴer of a subject, and a set of agreements about how the subject should be studied. Acceptance of a paradigm is therefore mainly applicable to academic study and research, but it also inﬂuences practice, since it encapsulates a view of what a subject is like on the whole. It is important to realise that the emergence of a new paradigm does not mean the cessation of work based in older paradigms; the process is more one of addition, and perhaps gradual replacement. Information science has certainly seen several paradigms operating at the same time. This is somewhat diﬀerent to Kuhn’s original concept, by which there would usually be a single paradigm for a science, and a new paradigm would replace the old quite rapidly. A turn, in this context, implies a fairly rapid change of direction within a ﬁeld of study, aﬀecting the topics thought to be relevant and important and the appropriate ways of studying them. Nolin (2007, 2) characterises a turn as ‘some sort of cognitive interruption with a research tradition’, and Hartel (2019, 2) as ‘a recognizable intellectual project in which a group of scholars enthusiastically embrace a new set of theoretical, methodological, or substantive commitments [and] typically critique the status quo and focus aĴention on a diﬀerent research agenda or frontier’. A turn can be seen as roughly equivalent to the adoption of a new paradigm, and w

A turn can be seen as roughly equivalent to the adoption of a new paradigm, and we will treat paradigms and turns as synonymous in this chapter. They have also been referred in the information science literature as perspectives, viewpoints and traditions, and these are also subsumed here. There have been numerous named paradigms and turns in the information sciences. They include the system paradigm, the user paradigm, the behavioural paradigm, the information paradigm, the object paradigm, the bibliometric paradigm, the cognitive paradigm, the communication paradigm, the physical paradigm and the socio- cognitive paradigm. Some of these have an overlap, and others have not been inﬂuential. For discussion of some of these, and analysis of the idea of paradigms in information science, see Ellis (1992), Hjørland (2002; 2018) and Tang et al. (2021). Similarly, there have been numerous named turns. Cronin (2008) notes the user turn and the sociological turn, and also the linguistic turn, of wider scope but impacting on the information disciplines. Nolin and Åström (2010) identify the cognitive turn, the informational turn, the user-centred turn, the epistemological turn and the pragmatic turn. They note that these oĞen have wider scope than just the information sciences; the cognitive turn, for example, originated in psychology. We will outline four of the more inﬂuential paradigms/terms, in order to make the nature of information paradigms clearer: systems, cognitive, socio-cognitive and neo-documentary. The systems paradigm This is also termed the physical paradigm. Recognisable from the 1950s onwards, it is the original paradigm of the information sciences, used as the basis for the evaluation and improvement for information systems and services. A realist perspective, following the methods of the natural sciences, it emphasised quantitative and experimental methods for evaluating the performance of systems, particularly retrieval systems; see, for example, Sparck Jones (1981) and Robertson (2008). Quantitative user surveys, bibliometric analyses and performance metrics for information services also ﬁt within this paradigm. It is sometimes referred to as the Cranﬁeld paradigm, aĞer the well-known Cranﬁeld information retrieval experiments, which were the ﬁrst major studies carried out in this way, with test queries, test collections and metrics for comparison; in the case of Cranﬁeld, comparing alternative indexing and classiﬁcation systems. This experimental style of research is still popular in studies of retrieval algorithms and system interfaces (see Chapter 18) (Harman and Voorhees, 2006; Voorhees et al., 2020) and is a good illustration of the way in which paradigms continue, even if complemented, and to an extent over-shadowed, by new paradigms. The cognitive paradigm Starting in the 1970s and gaining impact in the 1980s, the cognitive paradigm, was a move away from the systems paradigm and towards a focus on the internal thought world of the individual information user. Based on Popper’s philosophy, it was particularly inﬂuenced by the ‘fundamental equation of information science’ proposed by Brookes (1980), in the form: K (S) + ΔI = K (S + ΔS) A knowledge structure, K (S) is changed into an altered knowledge structure K (S + ΔS) by an input of information, ΔI. ΔS is an indicator of the eﬀect of the modiﬁcation. The same information may have diﬀerent eﬀects on diﬀerent knowledge structures. It is a description of the information communication process as it aﬀects one individual’s knowledge, and hence is regarded as a foundation of the cognitive paradigm in information science, although it does not function as a true equation (Bawden, 2011). A number of theories and models were advanced, based on cognitive aspects of information use, oĞen considering mental mod

rue equation (Bawden, 2011). A number of theories and models were advanced, based on cognitive aspects of information use, oĞen considering mental models of users, and applied in information retrieval and information behaviour contexts (Ingwersen, 1999). The best-known example, the idea of an Anomalous State of Knowledge (ASK) (Belkin, Oddy and Brooks, 1982), assumes that a user recognises some anomaly or inadequacy in their knowledge of some issue, which they translate ﬁrst into an information need and then into queries to some kind of information system. The answers go some way to resolving the anomaly in their knowledge, but may generate more information needs. This kind of analysis led to ideas for retrieval systems built on diﬀerent principles to those generally available, typically with a much greater degree of interaction. Nolin (2007, 5), admiĴedly writing before some of the more recent turns, considered that ‘without doubt, the most inﬂuential turn in the history of information science has been the cognitive turn’, and its inﬂuence is still signiﬁcant. The socio-cognitive paradigm The socio-cognitive paradigm originated in the 1990s and is based on the idea that information behaviour and practices are embedded in a speciﬁc context: social, professional, educational, or disciplinary (Hjørland, 1995; 2002). It focuses on the construction and use of knowledge within communities, and in that sense is strongly related to social epistemology. It is strongly related to Birg

It is strongly related to Birger Hjørland’s domain analysis (discussed in Chapter 7), which oﬀers a framework for research, for disciplinary development and for professional practice. Although it focuses on the group and the community, it does not neglect the individual: rather, it allows ‘an interplay between  domain  structures  and  individual  knowledge,  an interaction between the individual and the social level’ (Hjørland, 1995, 409). Although it deals with knowledge construction, Hjørland identiﬁes it as a basically realist approach: ‘trying to ﬁnd the basis for information science in factors that are external to the individualistic-subjective perceptions of the users as opposed to . . . the behavioural and cognitive paradigms’ (Hjørland, 1995, 400). It refers back to the pioneers of the documentation movement, Otlet and Briet in particular, and was inspired by Michael Buckland’s concept of information-as-thing (Skare, Lund and Vårheim, 2007; Buckland, 1991). This perspective has developed around the new document theory of authors such as Buckland, Skare, Latham and Gorichanaz (Lund, 2011; Lund, Gorichanaz and Latham, 2016). Theories Theories are usually taken to be more speciﬁc than paradigms, addressing one topic or one aspect of a subject. We ﬁrst consider what we mean by theory, then examine the types of theory there can be, evaluate the role of theory in the information sciences and ﬁnally look at the relevance of theory to practitioners. For fuller discussion of theory in general see Pinﬁeld et al. (2020, chapter 3), and for a detailed analysis of theory in the humanities and social sciences, the kind of theory most relevant to the information sciences, see Corvellec (2013). What is theory? ‘Theory’ is a much-used term in science, philosophy and everyday life language. It is therefore strange that it is relatively seldom examined. (Hjørland, 2015, 113) The term ‘theory’ is indeed much used, and in diﬀerent ways. Perhaps the best and simplest explanation of the term is that of the philosopher Theodore Schatzki (2001), who suggests that a theory is simply a general and abstract account of something. Comparison of dictionary deﬁnitions suggests that ‘theory’ has three generally agreed connotations (Pinﬁeld et al., 2020, chapter 3): something which provi
===
--- Chunk 128 ---
rison of dictionary deﬁnitions suggests that ‘theory’ has three generally agreed connotations (Pinﬁeld et al., 2020, chapter 3): something which provides an abstraction of reality into general principles • • something that explains, or aids understanding something that acts as a guide to practice. All three meanings can be found in the theories of information science. The ‘understanding’ aspect is of particular importance: ‘Understanding is what theory is about: those other aĴributes of theory, prediction and application, are side-eﬀects only, secondary to the main purpose’ (Robertson, 2000, 1). The meaning of ‘theory’ varies across diﬀerent disciplines, and types of discipline, and not in a simplistic way; see Pinﬁeld et al. (2020, chapter 3) for an analysis. It is oĞen thought that the physical and biological sciences use rigorous quantitative ‘laws’ and ‘theories’, while the social and human sciences rely on ‘models’ and ‘frameworks’, but maĴers are not so straightforward. Qualitative and classiﬁcatory models are widely used even in the natural sciences, while the social sciences make use of quantitative and formal theories. In the humanities and social sciences, theory may also mean critical theory or literary theory or art theory – loosely deﬁned qualitative, hermeneutic forms of theory building, which would not be recognised as theory at all in the sciences. This idea that no single idea of theory is adequate for information science was emphasised in the well-known study of use of theory in the discipline by PeĴigrew and McKechnie (2001), whose analysis of over a thousand information science articles found that explicit theories were mentioned in only one third of the articles, a majority • • • • being theories brought in from other disciplines. Where theories from within information science itself were present, these were typically from a wide range of rather speciﬁc theories, such as models of information seeking, rather than broader theoretical perspectives. They noted that ‘there was no singular deﬁnition that would encompass all the varied uses of the term in the articles . . . For example, articles about information retrieval diﬀered vastly in their use of the term from those that focused on information behavior, history, or information policy’ (PeĴigrew and McKechnie, 2001, 65). Types of theory Several typologies or categorisations have been devised to clarify the various forms of theory presented. Two are widely known, and relevant to information science: those due to Reynolds and to Gregor respectively. For the social sciences generally, the sociologist Paul Reynolds identiﬁed four forms of theory (Reynolds, 1971): a set of laws

o Gregor respectively. For the social sciences generally, the sociologist Paul Reynolds identiﬁed four forms of theory (Reynolds, 1971): a set of laws, i.e., well-supported empirical generalisations an interrelated set of deﬁnitions, axioms and propositions descriptions of causal processes vague concepts, untested hypotheses, prescriptions for good behaviour. Shirley Gregor, an information systems scholar, proposed ﬁve types of theory for that discipline (Gregor, 2006). This typology has gained wide use beyond the information systems context. Its ﬁve categories are: • • • • • Type 1 – theory for analysing, typically initial descriptive aĴempts at theory Type 2 – theory for explaining Type 3 – theory for predicting Type 4 – theory for both explaining and predicting, typically described as ‘grand theories’ or meta-theories Type 5 – theory for design and action. Both these typologies are quite broad and hospitable, in that they allow the inclusion of theoretical entities which may be termed diﬀerently: frameworks, models and so on. Both have been used to analyse the creation and use of theory in the information sciences. Reynolds’ ﬁrst category (laws, meaning well-supported empirical generalisations) is unlikely to be of value for information science. More appropriate are the second, encompassing models for conceptual understanding and, particularly, the third, encompassing most of the process models for information retrieval, information behaviour, and information literacy. Gregor’s typology (2006) has been more quoted than any other in an information research context. All of Gregor’s ﬁve types of theory may be found in the literature, although types 1 and 2 predominate (Sonnenwald, 2016b). We can also categorise theories as to their scope, from a large-scale ‘grand theory’, ‘Theory of Everything’ or metatheory, to very local small-theories, explaining speciﬁc and limited points. A kind of theory of particular interest to information science is the ‘mid-range’ or ‘middle-range’ theory, deﬁned by the sociologist Robert Merton as ‘theories that lie between the minor but necessary working hypotheses that evolve in abundance during day-to-day research and the all-exclusive systematic eﬀorts to develop a uniﬁed theory that will explain all the observed uniformities of social behaviour, social organization and social change’ (Merton, 1968, 51). The descriptions of the creation of theory in information science in the collection edited by Sonnenwald (2016a) serve to reinforce this point. Theory in the information sciences One of the concerns that has long been expressed about information science as a discipline is that it lacks a theory base of its own, and indeed makes relatively liĴle use of theory per se. For example, Lor (2014, 30) states that ‘although some use is made of theory from other ﬁelds such as psychology, sociology or management, LIS has produced very liĴle theory of any signiﬁcance’. Even when theory is used in information science, it may go under another name. For example, Thelwall (2016) notes that, although his webometric studies may be ﬁĴed within Gregor’s typology, he did not consider that he was creating theory, and that, although he rarely cit
===
--- Chunk 133 ---
lthough his webometric studies may be ﬁĴed within Gregor’s typology, he did not consider that he was creating theory, and that, although he rarely cited explicitly named theories, he oĞen used ‘theoretical insights’. Similarly, Sugimoto (2016, 1) writes that ‘one diﬃculty in identifying theories of informetrics and scholarly communication is the diversity of terminology around theories’. She notes that contributors to a volume on theory in that aspect of the information sciences used ‘theories’,  ‘models’,  ‘taxonomies’,  ‘typologies’,  ‘frameworks’, ‘indices’, ‘hypotheses’ and ‘principles’, sometimes synonymously. And, to complete the set of problems, theoretical contributions do not necessarily build upon one another. As Hjørland (2017, 1797) puts it: ‘The overall situation in information science today is a chaos of theoretical contributions, each paying no or much too liĴle interest in the existing ones.’ Overviews of theory in the area of information  behaviour,  a  particularly  fruitful  area  within information science for the development of models and theories, are given by Bates (2005) and other authors in Fisher, Erdelez and McKechnie (2005), by Case and Given (2016, chapter 8) and by Wilson (2020a). With the exception of Shannon’s mathematical information theory and its derivatives (discussed in Chapter 5), models have typically been the way into theory building in information science. Hjørland (2015) has emphasised the importance of concepts in LIS theory building, and Savolainen (2019) has analysed in detail the kind of models used in information behaviour research. Use of metatheory, and of more formal or general approaches, has been limited. We now give some examples of theory creation and use within the information sciences under four headings: use of metatheory; developing models de nova; elaborating and extending existing models; and bringing in ‘pre-prepared’ theory from other disciplines. Fuller discussion, and more examples, are given by Pinﬁeld et al. (2020, chapter 3). Using metatheory Metatheory, the analysis of theory itself, and the application of broad general theories to particular topics, has been liĴle used in information science. Since Bates noted its lack of application in 2005, there have been only a few proponents and examples of these approaches. Hjørland has argued consistently that information science theories should be developed, and existing theories analysed, on the basis of metatheory (Hjørland, 1998; 2011a), speciﬁcally using broad theories of knowledge and of science. He has given examples of the application of metatheory to, for example, browsing (Hjørland, 2011a), indexing and retrieval (Hjørland, 2011b), and informetrics (Hjørland, 2016). Vakkari and Kuokkanen (1997) applie

Vakkari and Kuokkanen (1997) applied a sociological metatheory approach due to Wagner and Berger (1985) to an example of theory growth in information-seeking research. • • • This was a ‘reconstruction’, showing how the actual theory development via models could be interpreted in light of the metatheory. We may also consider the applications, albeit limited as yet, of Floridi’s PI within information science as metatheory. Developing theory de novo This approach aims at the creation of qualitative theory, oĞen termed a model or a framework, by identiﬁcation of concepts and their relationships. This is done using one of a variety of methods for developing theory from qualitative data without a prior guiding framework. These include the various ﬂavours of grounded theory, or methods such as thematic analysis. It is certainly the most common means by which new theory is created in the information sciences. Examples are: grounded theory used to derive a model of concepts and relations for the search process in a multilingual retrieval system (Vassilakaki and Johnson, 2015) grounded theory used in a qualitative study of the information practices of welfare workers, developing a series of conceptual models (French and Williamson, 2016) thematic analysis used to generate a model for evidence-based practice in librarianship (Gillespie, 2014). Elaborating existing models This approach involves theory building by the elaboration and incremental improvement of conceptual models, rather than by continually creating new models from scratch, without aiming for an over-ambitious, all-embracing model or theory. Robertson has • • • argued speciﬁcally for this kind of theory building: ‘I believe that the models we have at present can indeed be extended, by theoretical argument as well as by [pragmatic considerations], to cover more ground than they do at present and to be more useful as tools. But when I read a paper (as one does occasionally) which seems to make a claim to represent a Grand Theory, then I shall continue to take it with a pinch of salt’ (Robertson, 2000, 10). The most evident example of this has been a variety of extensions to Tom Wilson’s original information behaviour model, by Wilson himself and by others, as discussed in Chapter 12. Wilson (2016) has argued that the incremental extension and improvement of his series of conceptual models of information behaviour now amount to a general theory of that topic, although the term ‘theory’ had never been used by Wilson himself. Other examples of model extension and combination include: the combination of models for information seeking and for communication to create a new model, of broader scope (Robson and Robinson, 2013) successive improve

Bringing in theory from other disciplines • • • • It has oĞen been noted, sometimes as a criticism, that the information disciplines tend to adopt theory from other disciplines, rather than to create their own. As Dillon (2016, 230) puts it, ‘the information sciences have no theoretical core, but derive theoretical structures from outside disciplines . . . by its very nature, information science is an interdisciplinary ﬁeld and therefore it must draw theory from outside. This is certainly plausible, but my concern is that if we only derive our theoretical analyses from outside, it is even more diﬃcult to demonstrate the process of theory building . . . in the information sciences’. The ﬁnal method for introducing theory in information science is therefore to bring in a ‘pre-prepared’ theory from another discipline and apply it in the information context with liĴle or no adaption. Imported theory may sometimes not be readily understandable by an audience from the information disciplines, because it is based in unfamiliar concepts and perspectives. Examples of this problem, identiﬁed in a study of theory of open access issues, are the use of quantum game theory and of aspects of critical theory (Pinﬁeld et al., 2020, chapter 3). While it is generally true to say that information science has been an importer rather than an exporter of theory, there are some indications that this may be changing. Wilson (2020b) has demonstrated how other disciplines are making use of concepts of information behaviour developed within information science, while Willson (2019) gives the example of information behaviour studies contributing to the development of transition theory, originally developed in nursing studies and increasingly widely applied in the social sciences generally. In summary, we can say that these four general methods encapsulate the main ways in which theory has been developed within information science. The most common method has been the generation of new models by elaboration of existing models; least common has been use of any form of metatheory. Theory and the practitioner Concerns have been expressed over the years about the limited use of theory by practitioners in the information professions (Pinﬁeld et al., 2020, chapter 4); the same is said of many other professions, at least outside technology and medicine, such as education. There is a parallel, and indeed an overlap, with the supposed non-use of research results by information practitioners, discussed in Chapter 18. Floridi (2004) reminds us that there are three levels at which theory may be applied, for information science as for other disciplines: the level of day-to-day routine practice; the level of the delineation of the discipline and its knowledge base, as given in academic courses; and the foundational, and necessarily abstract, level. Theory most clearly operates at the last of these, though it may certainly inform the ﬁrst two. It is not necessarily a concern that theory is not routinely invoked by practitioners, as it may have served to form their professional knowledge. It may also, together with  res
===
--- Chunk 140 ---
ern that theory is not routinely invoked by practitioners, as it may have served to form their professional knowledge. It may also, together with  research  results,  inform  evidence-based  practice (Koufogiannakis and BreĴle, 2016). It is certainly the case that theory may be unconsciously used by practitioners: anyone using the management terminology of ‘quick wins’ or ‘low-hanging fruit’, for example, is using, consciously or otherwise, the language of theories of change. Furthermore, the non-use of theory by practitioners may be exaggerated. A detailed study of the theory/practice relation in the context of open access (Pinﬁeld et al., 2020) showed that open access practitioners, including publishers and librarians, did indeed create and use theory; conversely, researchers in the area were not necessarily consistent and conﬁdent users of theory. VanScoy, Thomson and Hartel (2020) give an example of how theory may be used directly in practice, applying the serious leisure perspective to programming in public libraries. Summary Paradigms and theories in the information sciences are numerous, ever increasing and applied inconsistently. Even when theory is • • • • used, in research or practice, it may not be called ‘theory’, and its creators and users may not regard it as such. A variety of paradigms or turns have been identiﬁed in information science, generally adding to those already there rather than replacing them. Theory in information science is likely to be ‘mid-range

Theory in information science is likely to be ‘mid-range’, and to be Reynolds’ 2 or 3 (conceptual understanding and conceptual process models), and Gregor’s 1 or 2 (description and explanation) or possibly 5 (action research). It largely comprises either conceptual frameworks for understanding or process models. It will most usually be created by incremental extension of existing models; less commonly by creating a model de novo or by bringing in a pre-packaged theory from another discipline. Paradigms are the general way in which a subject is regarded, in research and in practice. Turns are the introduction of a new paradigm, which generally adds to, rather than replaces, existing paradigms. There are many individual theories in information science, typically, qualitative conceptual models and frameworks. It is central to information science, but it is also important in many other disciplines, in the physical sciences, in the biological sciences, in computing and communication technology and in the social sciences. It is reasonable to ask whether the concept of information is • • • • in some sense ‘the same’ in all of these, or if it is just a coincidence that the same English word is used for diﬀerent things. The word has

• • • • in some sense ‘the same’ in all of these, or if it is just a coincidence that the same English word is used for diﬀerent things. The word has had a number of diﬀerent meanings over the years. Its entry in the Oxford English Dictionary (March 2021 edition) gives its current meanings as the imparting of knowledge, or the giving of form or character to something. As the quotation from Shannon, the originator of information theory, reminds us, we should not expect to ﬁnd a single, simple idea of information which will do in all circumstances. One reason for this complexity is that information may be discussed and analysed at a number of diﬀerent levels. For example, Liebenau and Backhouse (1990) show that any communication of information can be understood simultaneously at four levels: empiric: the physical transmission syntactic: the language or coding used semantic: the meaning of the message pragmatic: the signiﬁcance of the message to a recipient in a particular context. Information in computing and communications: Shannon theory Shannon and Wiener and I Have found it confusing to try To measure sagacity And channel capacity By ∑ pi log pi Anonymous, Behavioural Science, 1962, 7(July), 395 Until the mid-20th century, information was regarded as the communication of meaningful facts or knowledge, without any aĴempt being made to provide any more formal deﬁnition. The ﬁrst formal quantitative deﬁnition of information was provided by Claude Shannon (1916–2001) in his Mathematical Theory of Communication  (Shannon  and  Weaver,  1949).  Shannon,  a mathematician working for the Bell Laboratories, was a polymath, who made contributions to the design of digital computers, such that electronic circuits could implement Boolean algebra, and to robotics (Shannon, 1993; Gleick, 2011; Nahin, 2017; Soni and Goodman, 2017). Shannon was concerned with the eﬃciency of transmission of information in communication by telegraph and telephone, and hence n
===
--- Chunk 153 ---
ni and Goodman, 2017). Shannon was concerned with the eﬃciency of transmission of information in communication by telegraph and telephone, and hence not at all concerned with the meaning of the messages sent. His work built on that of his colleagues, Harry Nyquist (1889–1976), who in 1924 showed how to estimate the amount of information which could be transmiĴed in a channel of given bandwidth, and Ralph Hartley (1889–1970), who in 1928 established a quantitative measure of information so as to compare the transmission capacities of diﬀerent systems. Shannon’s theory was a purely statistical formalism, relating the information content of a message to the probability of occurrence of its symbols, regardless of its meaning. Indeed, he termed it a theory of communication, rather than on information. High information content in Shannon theory is related to low probability combinations of symbols, such that information is equated to surprise, lack of predictability and randomness. This has caused problems for those who have tried to apply Shannon theory to meaningful information. Nonetheless Shannon’s formalism is universally accepted as the basis for any theory of information. Commons) Shannon’s formalism was introduced in an article in 1948, later republished in book form (Shannon and Weaver, 1949). Warren Weaver (1894–1978), a distinguished mathematician, scientiﬁc administrator and proponent of the public understanding of science, contributed an essay – philosophical, non-mathematical, wide ranging and considerably easier to read than Shannon’s analysis – which has arguably had greater inﬂuence in spreading the ideas of information theory than Shannon’s own writing. Shannon deﬁned the fundamental problem of communication as the accurate reproduction at one point of a message selected from another point. Meaning is ignored: ‘these semantic aspects of communication are irrelevant to the engineering problem’ (Shannon and Weaver, 1949, 3). What maĴers is that the actual message in each case is one which is selected from the set of possible messages, and, if the number of possible messages is ﬁnite, then the information associated with any message is a function of the number of possible messages. Shannon derived his well-known formula for H, the measure of information: H = – K ∑ pi log pi where pi is the probability of each symbol and K is a constant deﬁning the units. (The minus sign is included to make the quantity of information, H, positive; necessarily a probability will always be less than 1, and the log of such a number is always negative.) Shannon pointed out that formulae of the general form H = – ∑ pi log pi appear very oĞen in information

--- Chunk 155 ---
the log of such a number is always negative.) Shannon pointed out that formulae of the general form H = – ∑ pi log pi appear very oĞen in information theory as measures of information, choice and uncertainty; the three concepts seem almost synonymous for his purposes. Shannon’s was not the only aĴempt to derive a mathematical theory of information based on ideas of probability and uncertainty. The British statistician R. A. Fisher (1892–1962) derived such a measure, as did the American mathematician Norbert Wiener (1894– 1964), the originator of cybernetics. The laĴer’s mathematical formalism was the same as Shannon’s but, confusingly, he treated information as the negative of physical entropy, associating it with structure and order, whereas Shannon equated information with entropy. Shannon’s information is, in eﬀect, the opposite of Wiener’s, which has caused confusion ever since for those who seek to understand the meaning of the mathematics (Qvortrup, 1993; Bawden and Robinson, 2015a). The relations between information, order, structure, and complexity are subtle, and far from fully understood (Bawden and Robinson, 2015b). Shannon theory gives the only convincing quantitative measure of information yet derived, and a great deal of work has been done to try to apply it in a variety of disciplines, from the sciences through the social sciences to the humanities (Floridi, 2010; Gleick, 2011; Bawden and Robinson, 2015a; 2015b). Numerous aĴempts have been made to extend it to 
===
--- Chunk 156 ---
e social sciences to the humanities (Floridi, 2010; Gleick, 2011; Bawden and Robinson, 2015a; 2015b). Numerous aĴempts have been made to extend it to deal with meaningful semantic information, and to develop logico-mathematical models for information ﬂow, by authors such as Bar-Hillel, Dretske, Barwise and Seligman, and Devlin. None has been fully successful; for a review, see Floridi (2019). Nonetheless, Shannon theory is the basis of all current formal conceptions of information. Information in the physical world In the physical world, information has been introduced in the last few decades as an explicit quantity in physical theories, a physical concept like energy or maĴer (Davies and Gregersen, 2010; Bawden and Robinson, 2013; Bawden & Robinson, 2020; Durham and Rickles, 2017; Bawden, 2019). This was dramatically stated by Nobel- winning physicist Frank Wilczek (2015, 17) in a prediction about physics in 100 years: ‘Fundamental action principles, and thus the laws of physics, will be interpreted as statements about information and its transformations.’ In computing and communications technology, information is processed by physical devices, so that it seems natural to think of information in this domain as a physical quantity. This was clearly established by Rolf Landauer, a computer scientist at IBM, who coined the phrase ‘Information is physical’; that is to say, information must always be instantiated in some physical system (Landauer, 1991). Landauer made calculation
===
--- Chunk 157 ---
‘Information is physical’; that is to say, information must always be instantiated in some physical system (Landauer, 1991). Landauer made calculations of the equivalence between energy and the processing of information in digital computers, emphasising the nature of information as a physical quantity. At the heart of this issue is the relation between information and entropy, roughly a measure of the disorder in physical systems; the mathematical formalism of physical entropy is essentially the same as Shannon’s information content. The idea of information as the opposite of entropy was popularised, with the label of ‘negentropy’, by Leon Brillouin (1956), who ﬁrst advocated the wide use of information theory in science. The greater the entropy of the system, the more information it contains. This may seem paradoxical for those who intuitively associate information with organisation and understanding, but think of the fact that it takes many more words to describe in detail a disordered system than an ordered, simpler one;  the  extra  words  needed  are  due  to  the  extra entropy/information in the system. The relation between information and entropy is subtle, and still not fully understood; for discussion and a literature review, see Bawden and Robinson (2015a), Parrondo, Horowitz and Sagawa (2015) and Hemmo and Shenker (2016). There are other ways in which information is entering the physical sciences. Formulations of quantum mechanics are being rewriĴen in information
===
--- Chunk 158 ---
016). There are other ways in which information is entering the physical sciences. Formulations of quantum mechanics are being rewriĴen in information terms (D’Ariano, Chiribella and PerinoĴi, 2019). Some theoreticians regard information as the most fundamental aspect of the physical universe from which everything else is built, following American physicist John Wheeler’s dictum ‘It from Bit’ (Barrow, Davies and Harper, 2004; Durham and Rickles, 2017). And there is the question of whether information about the state of the physical world can ever be destroyed, or whether it is always conserved. This is Stephen Hawking’s famous ‘black hole information paradox’. Hawking initially believed that information was irrevocably destroyed when maĴer fell into a black hole; the maĴer is not yet fully solved, but it seems likely that information can re-emerge from a black hole. The informational approach to physics is increasing in inﬂuence, although there are those who argue that neither the Shannon formalism nor the ideas of negentropy are able to provide a satisfactory explanation of physical phenomena; see, for example, Anta (2021). Information in the biological world A similar idea to Wiener’s conception of information as negative entropy was proposed by the German physicist Erwin Schrödinger, one of the pioneers of quantum mechanics, who suggested that living organisms feed upon negative entropy (Schrödinger, 1944; Moberg, 2020). Since then information has become a central concept in the biological sciences, with the ability to process and transmit information being taken as a part of the deﬁnition of life; see Davies (2019) for an accessible overview. There are a number of speciﬁc instances for applying information concepts in biology (Robinson and Bawden, 2013; Bawden and Robinson, 2020). The encoding of genetic information in DNA is perhaps most obvious (Yockey, 2011). The communication of information between living cells, plants and animals, and the idea that non-human species may use external memory devices, such as spiders’ webs, have been studied for many years (Stegmann, 2018; Karban, 2015). More recent are the ideas of code biology, the analysis of informational codes in living systems at various levels from the genetic code to codes of culture (Barbieri, 2015), and various integrated  information  theories,  frameworks  for  explaining consciousness as associated with the integration of information through complex processing (Tononi et al., 2016; Brogaard, Chomanski and Gatzia, 2021). Eliot, Choruses from the rock) In the social world, information is generally regarded in line with the dictionary deﬁnitions mentioned above, as associated with meaning and with the communication of facts and knowledge. In line with the philosophical view, discussed in Chapter 3, that knowledge must be true, it is usual to regard information as something that is truthful, i.e. correct, and to distinguish it from misinformation  (incorrect  information)  and  disinformation (deliberately incorrect information). We may also distinguish malinformation, information which is true, but communicated from bad motives. All these varieties of information are subsumed under the heading of semantic content, and it is semantic content which makes up the recorded information with which information science deals. For more detailed analysis of the varieties of information, see Floridi (2010, chapter 4), Fallis (2016) and Søe (2019; 2021). Another quality of information in the social realm is the extent to which it is relevant to its potential users. The provision of relevant information is a central task for all information services, and the proportion of information provided which is relevant is an important metric for judging the success of such services. Saracevic (2007, 1915) suggests that relevance is ‘a, if not even the, key notion in information science in general’. However, the concept of relevance is complex and contested, and a variety of slightly diﬀerent related concepts have been proposed, such as utility, usefulness, topicality, pertinence and resonance. For example, while one document may be judged relevant, another ten similar documents, while equally relevant, may be seen as being of decreasing interest and usefulness. Again, a document may be relevant in terms of subject, but if it is old, or in a language the user cannot read, or wriĴen for professional experts while the user is a lay person, it may be of limited usefulness. For reviews of the concept of relevance, see Saracevic (2007; 2016) and Ruthven (2020). A further quality of information is that it may be regarded as embodied, that is to say that human bodies may be sources and repositories of information. Such a view has implications for how information behaviour and practices are understood; see, for example, Olsson and Lloyd (2017) and Leug (2020). In  the  social  world,  information  implies  meaning,  and communication between people. There are various conceptions of this kind of information, even within the information sciences; see Capurro and Hjørland (2003), Bates (2017) and Mingers and Standing (2018) for overviews. Buckland (1991; 2017, chapter 2) distinguishes three uses of the term ‘information’: information-as-thing, where the information is associated with a document, i.e. a digital or physical entity; information-as-process, where the information is that which changes a person’s knowledge state, in the process of their becoming informed; and information-as-knowledge, where the information is equated with the knowledge which it imparts. Information-as-thing  regards  information  as  physical  and objective, or at least as being ‘contained within’ physical documents, and essentially equivalent to them. The other two meanings treat information as abstract and intangible. Buckland gives arguments in favour of the information-as-thing approach, as being very directly relevant to information science, inasmuch as it deals primarily with information in the form of documents. Information-as-process underlies theories of information behaviour with a focus on the experience of individuals, while information-as-knowledge invokes the ideas that information and knowledge are closely related, without specifying an exact relation. One well-known model places information on a spectrum with data and knowledge, and sometimes other entities, implying that they are ‘the same sort of thing’, and one may be transformed into another. This model is commonly represented as a pyramid, with the lower layers containing a large amount of material, which is ‘reﬁned’ into a smaller amount of material at higher levels. The reﬁning is done by value-added processes within information systems, such as compilation,  comparison,  evaluation,  contextualisation,  and summarisation (Taylor, 1986). Although this model, oĞen referred to as the DIKW hierarchy, has been criticised for its over-simplicity, it has remained inﬂuential (Rowley, 2011; Frické, 2019). The original presentation of this model by Ackoﬀ (1989) had ﬁve layers: data, information, knowledge, understanding, and wisdom (Figure 5.3). Understanding was rapidly dropped from the model, though it has been suggested that it would be desirable for it to be reinstated (Bawden and Robinson, 2016). An additional layer is sometimes added between data and information: capta are data of interest which are collected and stored. Mind the gap: uniﬁed theories of information There have been aĴempts over the years to provide general theories of information, able to explain the concept in all domains. We will discuss three which have speciﬁc relevance to LIS, those due to Stonier, Bates and Floridi, mentioning others brieﬂy. Tom Stonier (1927–99), a scholar of science and society, proposed a conception of information integrated across the physical, biological and mental worlds (Stonier, 1990; Stonier, 1992; Stonier, 1997). In this conception, information is a physical entity analogous to maĴer and to energy, being the capacity to create and maintain organisation. This organising function of information is expressed in the biological world and then in human intelligence, and in meaning, ﬁnally expressed in recorded information. Although it has been suggested that a framework for LIS could be developed based on Stonier’s theory of information (Morán-Reyes, 2015), there has been liĴle • • • • • explicit development of his ideas, and his work is regarded as an early example of a uniﬁed gap-bridging theory of information. Marcia Bates, a library science academic, has presented an all- encompassing model, which she characterises as ‘evolutionary’ (Bates, 2005; 2006). It distinguished a number of ‘information-like’ entities: Information 1 – the paĴern of organisation of maĴer and energy Information 2 – some paĴern of organisation of maĴer and energy given meaning by a living being Data 1 – that portion of the entire information environment available to a sensing organism that is taken in, or processed, by that organism Data 2 – information selected or generated by human beings for social purposes Knowledge – information given meaning and integrated with other contents of understanding. An ambitious aĴempt at integrating information in all its contexts, this remains somewhat vague and has not been further developed. Luciano Floridi (2010; 2011) has presented a General Deﬁnition of Information (GDI) as part of his Philosophy of Information (PI), deﬁning it as ‘well-formed, meaningful and truthful data’. Data is understood here as simply a lack of uniformity, a noticeable diﬀerence or distinction in something. To count as information, individual data elements must be compiled into a collection which must be well formed (put together correctly according to relevant syntax), meaningful (complying with relevant semantics) and truthful, as distinct from misinformation

--- Chunk 167 ---

Taken together, information, misinformation and disinformation amount to semantic content. Floridi’s analysis also includes biological information in detail; noting that it is complex and multifaceted, he treats, for example, genetic and neural information separately. Meaningful information and knowledge are part of the same conceptual family; information is converted to knowledge by being interrelated; knowledge is true information set in context. Meaningful information must also be relevant in order to qualify as knowledge, and this aspect may be formally modelled, as also the distinction between ‘knowing’, ‘believing’, and ‘being informed’. In this way, Floridi avoids the problems of the traditional philosophical deﬁnition of knowledge as ‘justiﬁed true belief’, which is too focused on the individual knower to be helpful in analysing information issues. Floridi emphasises that PI is not intended to provide a single, uniﬁed theory of information in all domains but, rather, to provide a formal framework for linking and relating the various aspects and manifestations of information, and hence for integrating, though not in a reductionist way, all information-centred disciplines (Floridi, 2016b). There are other general, or uniﬁed, theories of information, looking at the meaning of concepts of information in diﬀerent domains. They are generally mathematical and logical in nature, and have not yet been applied in LIS; see Burgin and HoĤirchner (2017b) and Bawden and Robinson (2020) for reviews. We will give a brief mention of four. Burgin has developed a mathematical General Theory of Information over several decades, incorporating the insights of Shannon, Bar-Hillel, Dretske and others, and aiming to explain relations between the meanings of the word ‘information’. Wu and Brenner have devised a metaphilosophy with information at its centre (Brenner, 2015; Wu and Brenner, 2017). This examines the role of information, with both its physical and non-physical components, in complex processes across various domains, using a non-standard logic, Logic in Reality (LIR), for its analyses. Michael Buckland (2017) Introduction Documents, as carriers of information, play a central role in the information disciplines and professions, and the documentation movement of the ﬁrst half of the 20th century was one of the predecessors of information science. However, although documents carry information and data, they are not synonymous with either. The complex relation between these concepts, and the signiﬁcance of that relation for the information disciplines, has been discussed for many years, gaining new impetus in recent years. For diverse and detailed perspectives on the concept of document, and its relationship to information and data, see Hjørland (2000), Ørom (2007), Kosciejew and Richard (2015), Furner (2016) and Schöpfel et al. (2020). Document theory The English word ‘document’ comes from the Latin docere, to teach or to inform, with ‘-ment’ implying the means. The Oxford English Dictionary deﬁnes a document as ‘something wriĴen, inscribed, etc., which furnishes evidence or information upon any subject’, and this is how documents are generally understood. It might therefore be thought that the meaning of ‘document’ is straightforward and that the only issues that can arise relate to the diﬀerences between printed and electronic documents. This is far from the case. It can be argued that if a ‘document’ is some physical thing which records thoughts or ideas – information – then we should include paintings, sculpture, and perhaps even any artefact, as documents. But then, what about geological specimens in museums, carefully labelled and collocated with similar minerals; might we not go to look at them to ﬁnd out about the mineral as an alternative to reading about it in a book? An antelope in the wild may be just an antelope; but in a zoo, placed where it can be studied, in surroundings indicative of its natural habitat, does it not convey information? And is an information-bearing ‘thing’ not a document? If a photograph of the lunar surface is a document, why not the real thing seen t
===
--- Chunk 181 ---
y information? And is an information-bearing ‘thing’ not a document? If a photograph of the lunar surface is a document, why not the real thing seen through a telescope? And so on. These issues were addressed by European documentalists in the ﬁrst half of the 20th century, particularly Paul Otlet (1868–1944), Henri La Fontaine (1854–1943), Frits Donker Duyvis (1894–1961) and Suzanne Briet (1894–1989), whose 1951 text sums up the ideas of documentation in this period. For appreciations of their work, see Wright (2014), Maack (2004) and Lancaster-Jones (1961); their classic texts are also still worth rereading (Otlet, 1934; Briet, 1951). The work of these early documentalists was in response to the greatly increased volume of published scholarly information, particularly in science and technology, from the middle of the 19th century, and to the consequent need for beĴer ways to control it. It built on the earlier study of bibliography, which, since the 18th century, had studied the selection, organisation and dissemination of printed works. The documentalists regarded bibliography as an aspect of a wider subject of documentation, which also encompassed authorship, printing and publishing and library services. They raised for the ﬁrst time the questions of what were the limits of what a document is and what were the processes of documentation, coming to the view that any object should be regarded as a document if it provided information and evidence. More recently, a number of s

More recently, a number of scholars, particularly those associated with the Document Academy and with the Tromso Institute for Documentation Studies, have espoused the centrality of the document idea for information science, looking backwards to its origins in the documentation movement and forwards to the newer ideas of document theory. See, for example, Skare, Lund and Vårheim (2007), Document Academy (n.d.), Lund and Buckland (2008), Lund, Gorichanaz and Latham (2016) and Buckland (2018). Michael Buckland brought the issues to aĴention in his inﬂuential article on ‘What is a document?’ (Buckland, 1997). These cannot be deﬁned by form, medium or location in the way that physical documents can, being  less  ‘solid’  and  permanent;  hence  the  pragmatic ‘documentation’ approach, deﬁning a document by function, is particularly appropriate. Modern document theory, sometimes termed neo-document theory, examines the concept of ‘document’, and how it can be used in conjunction with other concepts to beĴer understand the • • communication of information and knowledge in an infosphere where many documents take digital form (Lund, 2010; Lund, 2011; Lund and Skare, 2017; Document Academy, n.d.; Buckland, 2014; Buckland, 2017). Alongside the nature and aĴributes of documents, document theory studies the processes of documentation, by which documents are created, organised and used. These are essentially the components of the informat
===
--- Chunk 185 ---
heory studies the processes of documentation, by which documents are created, organised and used. These are essentially the components of the information communication chain (Robinson, 2009). Documents may take very many diverse forms, but there is a common distinction between two main forms: documents by intention: deliberately created as a document, such as books and photographs documents by aĴribution: objects not created as documents, but which become documents later, such as plant specimens in a herbarium. Buckland makes a threefold distinction between: items created as documents; those made into or presented as documents; and those which are regarded as documents by someone, whether or not they were created with a documentary intention. Under this last, semiotic viewpoint, any object may be a document. Although most documents will be recognised as such by everyone as able to convey information and meaning across space and/or time, some objects may also be regarded as a document by a person at a particular time for a particular purpose. This means that many things may be documents, so document theory focuses on a set of aĴributes which documents, of whatever nature, possess, at least to some extent. Indexicality: a document must be about something, or point to something (like an index ﬁnger, hence the name). It has an ‘aboutness’, and may act as a symbol. Documentality: the special power of a document, by which it fulﬁls a social function in a particular context, at a ti
===
--- Chunk 186 ---
tness’, and may act as a symbol. Documentality: the special power of a document, by which it fulﬁls a social function in a particular context, at a time and place. It has an agency such that it can aﬀect its users and bring change in the world. Because of this power, people will generally need training so as to eﬀectively create and use documents. Complementarity: from the principle of complementarity in physics, which dictates that objects have properties that cannot be observed at the same time. A document has three forms of aĴribute: material, its physical or technical make-up; informational, relating to the mental, cognitive activity of its creators and users; and social, its economic, political or cultural signiﬁcance and connotations. Fixity: documents must stay largely stable over time to fulﬁl their function. Books can last for hundreds of years, essentially unaltered; digital documents are more mutable, while remaining useful, and hence neo-document theory recognises the associated notion of ﬂuidity. Productivity: new documents can be created from an original. This was regarded by the original document theorists as a hierarchical process, with a primary document leading to second and tertiary documents. An example would be an article leading to an entry in an abstracting and indexing tool or in a bibliography; or a geological specimen generating photographs, descriptive notes, etc. Neo-document theory also allows for non-hierarchical, or rhizomic, productivity, witho

The processes of documentation, in document theory, include: authoring  or  otherwise  creating;  selection  and  collection; organisation, arrangement, classiﬁcation and indexing; copying, reproduction and dissemination; preservation, conservation and digitisation; and destruction. These are, of course, the processes of the communication chain of recorded information, the basis for the operation of libraries, archives and other document institutions. However, the practical value of document theory is not limited to documentation in such institutions, nor is it limited to the kinds of documents with which they are typically concerned. Documentary processes are also important in the everyday life of individuals, both in recording the past and in planning for the future (McKenzie and Davies, 2021). Regarding other kinds of entities as documents is also valuable. For example, treating landscapes as documents allowed them to be used as evidence in court cases relating to land and water rights (Grenersen, 2012; Grenersen, Kemi and Nilsen, 2016), while considering museum objects as documents will help curators to beĴer understand and improve the experience of museum visitors (Latham, 2012). Categorising and organising documents Documentation, as noted above, has developed from the earlier study of bibliography, which, since the 18th century, had studied the • • description, selection for particular purposes, organisation and dissemination of printed work (Buckland, 2018). This led also to systems for resource description and classiﬁcation (discussed in Chapter 8). We can make some points here about documents as information resources. Even if we restrict ourselves to the usual viewpoint of the information sciences, regarding documents as being discrete entities deliberately created for the purpose of conveying information, we still ﬁnd some diﬃculties. In particular, we may have a problem deciding when two documents are ‘the same’. If I have a copy of a textbook and you have a copy of the same edition of the same book, then these are clearly diﬀerent objects. But in a library catalogue they will be treated as two examples of the same document. What if the book is translated, word for word, as precisely as possible, into another language: is it the same document, or diﬀerent? At what point do an author’s ideas, on their way to becoming a published book, become a ‘document’? These are quite diﬃcult issues conceptually and pose real practical problems for resource description, in particular for library cataloguing codes. They led to the development of the Functional Requirements for Bibliographic Records (FRBR) conceptual model and its successor, the Library Reference Model (LRM) (Žumer, 2018). These models are based on the distinction of four levels: work: the intellectual or artistic content of a distinct creation expression: a distinct combination of signs conveying intellectual or artistic content • • manifestation: a set of all carriers that are assumed to share the same characteristics as to intellectual or artistic content and aspects of physical form. That set is deﬁned by both the overall content and the production plan for its carrier or carriers, e.g. a speciﬁc edition of Shakespeare’s Hamlet item: an object carrying signs intended to convey intellectual or artistic content; ‘a single exemplar of a manifestation’. This might be made clearer by a speciﬁc example. A work is a distinct creative output, say Shakespeare’s Hamlet. An expression is the realisation of a work – the English text of Hamlet. A manifestation is the physical embodiment of an expression – a speciﬁc edition of Hamlet in English. And an item is a single example of a manifestation – a particular copy of that edition of Hamlet. There has been scope for disagreement on how these four levels should be understood. A simple categorisation of documents by resource level has been a useful, if simplistic, organising principle in the information disciplines. The levels are: zeroth: raw information before it enters the communication chain, for example the output from laboratory instruments, search interface/API (Application Programming Interface) output primary: the ‘original information’, e.g. journal articles, blog posts, tweets secondary: value-added information, from some organisation of primary material, e.g. textbooks, reviews, abstracts tertiary: materials pointing to, and aiding the use of, primary and secondary materials, e.g., bibliographies, directories quaternary: giving access to resource listings at a higher level, essentially ‘lists of lists’ • quintenary: lists of lists of lists. The two highest levels have proliferated in the web environment, whereas in the days of print a few quaternary ‘bibliographies of bibliographies’ were all that could be found. Categorisations of this sort are necessarily subjective, according to how the resource is used and viewed by its user; a bibliography of medical articles, for example, would normally be taken as a tertiary resource, but to a future historian of healthcare information it would be a primary document. Collections Collections, in the sense of those of interest to the information sciences, and documents go naturally together. As we have seen, one of the things which makes a document a document is that it is in an organised collection of related documents; and it is diﬃcult to envisage a collection of information without documents. We discuss the management of collections in Chapter 14, and focus here on the concept of collection. The Oxford English Dictionary deﬁnes collection as ‘a number of objects collected or gathered together, viewed as a whole; a group of things collected and arranged’. The collection, an organised set of information-bearing items chosen for a particular purpose in a particular context or environment, and usually unique to that • • situation, is fundamental to the information sciences. The library is the archetypical form of information collection: as Corrall (2012, 3) puts it, ‘the whole notion of a library is fundamentally associated with the idea of a collection, to the extent that the words “library” and “collection” are almost synonymous’. A useful distinction, though not an absolute one, is between two forms of collection: collections of ideas, embodied in documents collections of objects, which may provoke ideas in the viewer. The former is typiﬁed by the library, the laĴer by the gallery. The move towards a digital information environment has implications for the nature of the collection itself, as well as for the practicalities of managing it. Some collections are truly digital, and these fully digital collections may be assembled very rapidly, in a way in which physical collections cannot be. Conversely, very few collections now avoid any digital dimension. Managing ‘hybrid’ or ‘complex’ collections presents particular problems of maintaining consistency of approach and presenting the collection in a uniﬁed way. The move to digital collections generally means a move from ‘ownership’ and ‘location’ to ‘access’, as has been recognised for many years. The collection takes on a dynamic and impermanent nature, with varied and unpredictable lifecycles, and to some degree no longer under local control. Any digital resource, perceived as a single entity by its users, may in fact be a composite or aggregate of distributed documents: a collection, composed of such entities, is even more an aggregate. This means that such a collection can no longer be thought of as a set of physical items in a particular location, or even as a collection of • • • • digital items on a particular computer, but, rather, as a means of selecting documents from the universe of knowledge. Such a collection may be deﬁned as ‘a set of criteria for selecting resources from the broader information space’, with collection membership deﬁned ‘through criteria rather than containment’ (Lagoze and Fielding, 1998). The number of entities recognised as documents is increasing, both because of the recognition of the range of entities with documentary properties and because of new forms of digital documents being created. Birger Hjørland (2017, 452) Introduction The nature of information and knowledge, and the ways in which information services are provided, diﬀer considerably in diﬀerent contexts. This is an important theoretical and practical issue for the information sciences. In this chapter we consider what is meant by an information context or domain, and how domains may be ch
===
--- Chunk 203 ---
practical issue for the information sciences. In this chapter we consider what is meant by an information context or domain, and how domains may be characterised or understood, with a note on the importance of terminology in deﬁning and representing domains. We then examine domain analysis, the approach developed for this topic. Some brief examples of particular domains are given to show the distinctions which may be made between them, and their eﬀects in practice. Finally, we consider the changing nature of information work in speciﬁc domains. Information domains The contexts of information communication and use may be described in various ways: by geographic area, e.g. Europe; by type of institution, e.g. universities; or by the demographics of the information users, e.g. children and young people. The most helpful distinction, particularly for understanding information resources and information practices, is the information domain, which oĞen aligns with an academic discipline, e.g. mathematics or history; a professional or vocational activity, e.g. healthcare or ﬁnance; or a leisure interest, e.g. book collecting; or with a more loosely deﬁned area, e.g. everyday information. Hjørland (2010, 1650) suggests that a domain may be a scientiﬁc discipline or a scholarly ﬁeld. It may also be a discourse community connected to a political party, a religion, a trade, or a hobby. Domains are deﬁned and explained by three dimensions: ontological, epistemological and sociological. Th
===
--- Chunk 204 ---
itical party, a religion, a trade, or a hobby. Domains are deﬁned and explained by three dimensions: ontological, epistemological and sociological. The ontological dimension deﬁnes the domain by its main object of interest: botany by plants, history by the past, theology by the divine, etc.; this is the most usual way of deﬁning a domain. The epistemological dimension relates to the kind of knowledge in the domain, or perhaps diﬀerent kinds of knowledge associated with diﬀerent paradigms or ways of understanding. The sociological dimension relates to the kind of people and groups involved in the domain. It is clear that there are distinct diﬀerences in the way information is regarded and used in diﬀerent domains, aﬀecting information literacy, searching behaviour and information-sharing behaviour, among other things; see, for example, Pinto and Sales (2015), Tamine and Chouquet (2017), Fry et al. (2016), Madden et al. (2018), Russell- Rose, Chamberlain and Azzopardi (2018), Gregory et al. (2019), and Dreisiebner and Schlögl (2019). Hence the need for an awareness of domain and for approaches like domain analysis. A framework to give a clear idea of what a domain is, and how domains diﬀer one from another, will be helpful in understanding their information aspects. Categorising the domain with which one is dealing in this way helps to show what its ‘informational nature’ may be, and also helps to identify similarities and analogies with other domains which may be matched by si

There are several models and frameworks for understanding subjects and domains. Three of these have been found useful for the information sciences: those of Hirst, Becher and Whitley, discussed below. Domain analysis has also been used in conjunction with the social theories of Pierre Bourdieu (Morado Nascimento and Marteleto, 2008). Other understandings of ‘domain’ are noted by Hjørland (2017) and, under the heading of ‘disciplinarity’, by Sugimoto and Weingart (2015). The educational philosopher Paul Hirst (1946–2003) argued that, since disciplines are closely associated with their knowledge base, we can understand a discipline by understanding its ‘form of knowledge’ (Hirst, 1974; Walsh, 1993). There are seven main domains or forms of knowledge, deﬁned by the fundamental nature of the knowledge and concepts with which they deal: mathematics; physical sciences; human sciences; literature and the ﬁne arts; morality; religion; and philosophy. Where a discipline equates to one of these forms, it is what would be regarded as a ‘pure’ academic subject. Hirst also recognises ‘practical disciplines’, based on one of the forms but oriented toward solving practical problems. Engineering, for example would be a practical discipline based on the form of the physical scienc
===
--- Chunk 206 ---
orms but oriented toward solving practical problems. Engineering, for example would be a practical discipline based on the form of the physical sciences. Some academic subjects, however, do not align neatly with any form. Rather, they are focused on a topic or subject of interest, using any of the forms which are useful in studying and understanding it. Hirst refers to these as ﬁelds of study; they are typically, though not necessarily, multidisciplinary. Examples are peace studies, women’s studies and media studies; it was suggested in Chapter 1 that the information disciplines might also be of this nature. Tony Becher (1930–2009), a British higher education researcher, analysed the social and cognitive nature of academic disciplines along two rather traditional dimensions: pure/applied and hard/soĞ (Becher and Trowler, 2001). Clearly, these have strong implications for information practices (Fry, 2006); for example, contrasting disciplines whose knowledge structures are hard/pure (e.g. physics) with soĞ/pure (e.g. anthropology) or hard/applied (e.g. mechanical engineering). Richard Whitley, a sociologist from Manchester Business School, analysed sciences as systems for the production of diﬀerent kinds of knowledge by focusing on their internal structure, and identiﬁed seven diﬀerent kinds of scientiﬁc disciplines (Whitley, 2000). Examples are ‘professional adhocracies’ (e.g. biomedical sciences) and ‘conceptually integrated bureaucracies’ (e.g. physics). In his model, disci

In his model, disciplines are distinguished primarily by the degree of mutual dependence between researchers in creating new knowledge and the degree of task uncertainty in agreeing on research problems, methods and validity of knowledge acquired. Whitley’s model has been used by Fry (2006) and Roos and Hedlund (2016) to contrast the diﬀerences in information practices between diﬀerent disciplines. Domain terminologies Terminology, the structured naming of things, is one of the most basic  and  familiar  tools  for  organising  information  and communicating it accurately and unambiguously. Many domains, particularly in scientiﬁc, medical and technical areas, have their own specialised terminologies, which deﬁne and shape the domain and are vital to the communication of information within it. All domains have their own terminology; the terminology of everyday information, for example, is the dictionary; the standard dictionary of the language, and perhaps dictionaries of regional accents and of slang terms. An understanding of the terminology of a domain is a necessity for eﬀective information provision. Terminology resources encompass a number of overlapping categories: general dictionaries, which may be multilingual; dictionaries and glossaries for speciﬁc subjects; special-purpose dictionaries (e.g. rhyming, quotations, crossword clues); dictio

For the nature and history of some terminology tools, see Hitchens (2005), Hüllen (2004), Muggleston (2011), Tackabery (2005) and Stirling (2007). There are also special and detailed terminologies within the sciences for chemical structures and reactions, for living things, and for many aspects of biomedicine and healthcare. The notations of subjects such as mathematics, chemistry, music, and dance may also • • • • be regarded as forms of terminology, or at least as things which must be understood to make sense of terminology. Domain analysis Providing a theoretical basis for the study of information domains is the concept of domain analysis, derived by the Danish academic Birger Hjørland (2002; 2010; 2017). It is an approach within the socio- cognitive paradigm of information science (discussed in Chapter 4). As Hartel (2019, 5) summarises it, ‘domain analysis refutes the notion of universal information phenomena, and focuses upon informational paĴerns withi
===
--- Chunk 209 ---
s Hartel (2019, 5) summarises it, ‘domain analysis refutes the notion of universal information phenomena, and focuses upon informational paĴerns within social worlds. [It] directs the [information worker] towards mastery of their subject by producing literature guides, special classiﬁcations, and user studies, and to a strategic understanding of the history, culture, epidemiology, and institutional dynamics of their ﬁelds’. Domain analysis is a realist approach in philosophical terms; it seeks a basis for information science in factors external to the individual which are objective rather than subjective, and which may be located in the expertise and practices of subject specialists. Hjørland sees domain analysis as central to the work of the information scientist and as comprising eleven distinct ways in which information science may approach a domain. These approaches are: the production of literature guides and subject gateways the production of special classiﬁcations and thesauri researching indexing and retrieval in specialist subjects empirical user studies • • • • • • • bibliometric studies historical studies studies of documents and ‘genres’ epistemological and critical studies studies of terminology and special languages, and discourse analysis studies of structures and organisations in the communication of information studies in cognition, computing and artiﬁcial intelligence. Some alternative ways have been suggested, including discourse analysis, database semantic
===
--- Chunk 210 ---
studies in cognition, computing and artiﬁcial intelligence. Some alternative ways have been suggested, including discourse analysis, database semantics, and archival provenance (Hjørland, 2017). For an example, see Robinson (2010) for an analysis of the healthcare domain, which has a particularly rich and diverse set of resources and users, using all eleven aspects. Domain analysis is an approach for both research and practice, and provides a bridge between the two. An information professional working in a particular subject area need not carry out such domain analysis studies, though they might well do so, but they would certainly need to be aware of the results of such studies. For example, a healthcare information specialist would need to be aware of special terminologies used in collections of healthcare information (for example, the International Classiﬁcation of Diseases), though they need not themselves have carried out comparative studies. Similarly, a law librarian should be aware of what is known about the information behaviour of lawyers, law students, etc., though they might not carry out such studies themselves. Chemistry Chemistry is the study of substances, their properties and reactions, is, in Hirst’s terms, an academic discipline, with the form of knowledge of physical science, although its theories are oĞen conceptual or semi-qualitative. It is the basis of numerous practical disciplines. It has no popular or public dimension as an activity in its own right, but there is a strong interest in chemically related information, for example to do with the environment or with foods. Chemistry is traditionally divided into three branches: organic, dealing with carbon compounds; inorganic, dealing with all other elements and compounds; and physical, the application of the concepts and methods of physics to chemical problems. There are many subﬁelds and crossover disciplines, such as biochemistry, polymer chemistry, medicinal chemistry, forensic chemistry, and environmental  chemistry.  This  natural  subdivision  strongly inﬂuences information resources. Chemistry is important scientiﬁcally, socially and economically; is fundamental to the life sciences and to many engineering and technology areas; and underlies the chemical and pharmaceutical industries. Its information base is extensive. It is a ‘lending science’, hence the prevalence of resources in ‘chemistry for . . .’. The subject has oĞen led the development of information pro

ve. It is a ‘lending science’, hence the prevalence of resources in ‘chemistry for . . .’. The subject has oĞen led the development of information products and services: learned journals, textbooks and monographs, and abstracting and indexing services in the 19th century; and applications of bibliometrics, mechanised documentation, online databases, and use of the web in the 20th century (WilleĴ, 2008). Major resources, in addition to textbooks, monographs and journals, include bibliographic databases and property databanks. The best-known examples are the information sources of the Chemical Abstracts Service, part of the American Chemical Society, founded in 1907, and the Beilstein data compilations, dating from 1881. Older chemical information is oĞen of value. This links chemical information with the related subject of chemoinformatics. These resources, organised by structure and reaction type, are unique to chemistry and deﬁne it as an information domain (Solla, Currano and Roth, 2013). It is an academic subject, but without a practical discipline directly associated with it. Professional historians tend to be teachers, researchers, museum and archive professionals, or authors/presenters of popular history. There is a great public interest in the subject, as aĴested by the many books, magazines, TV and radio programmes and web resources devoted to it.
