Users of history information therefore span the spectrum from a relatively small group of academics and professionals to the much larger number of the interested general public. There has always been debate as to what kind of a subject it is; this has signiﬁcance for what kind of information resources will be regarded as most important. Those who see it as located within the social sciences will look for general trends and explanations of events from social data compilations, seeking to establish general historical ‘laws’. Those who locate it in the humanities, seeing history as the interpretation of unique events, will focus more on individual accounts. The discipline is traditionally divided into sub-disciplines: social history, economic history, political history, military history and so on. Another common division is history by country or region: English history, European history, etc., and a third by time period. This gives a natural structuring to the discipline’s information resources. Most, if not all, other subjects have a historical dimension, and several of these have formed interdisciplinary subjects in their own right, e.g. history of science, history of medicine and history of art. Serious leisure Serious leisure is an area which, though not academic or professional, may certainly be regarded as an information domain. Since about 2010 there ha
===
--- Chunk 218 ---
e Serious leisure is an area which, though not academic or professional, may certainly be regarded as an information domain. Since about 2010 there has been an increased interest in the information practices and information resources associated with serious leisure. Before that, the focus of information for the general public was on education, employment and (to a lesser extent) citizenship. However, it has been realised that the information resources and behaviours for leisure pursuits – where the emphasis is on play, pleasure and enjoyment, rather than on solving problems and carrying out tasks – are just as sophisticated and signiﬁcant as those for work and study. The idea of ‘serious leisure’ was devised by the Canada-based sociologist Robert Stebbins (2009; 2020). One of the main contentions • • • • is that those involved develop a very deep and rich knowledge of their leisure topic and develop sophisticated practices in creating, organising, sharing and using information. The study of the information dimension of serious leisure was pioneered by Jenna Hartel (2010) and has generated a considerable literature of its own. There are various categorisations of serious leisure activities. A typical one divides the area into four (oĞen overlapping) aspects: hobbyist (e.g. collecting things, craĞs) volunteer amateur (e.g. music or athletics) fandom (sports, music, cult media . . .). All of these aspects have been studied from the information point of view, typically using ethn

--- Chunk 219 ---
r athletics) fandom (sports, music, cult media . . .). All of these aspects have been studied from the information point of view, typically using ethnographic study methods (although a wide variety of methods have been applied), and applying a number of information behaviour models, including the everyday life information models of Savolainen and of Hektor, and the small- world model of Chatman. They have found extensive, sophisticated and sometimes idiosyncratic information resources and practices, including creating, sharing, organising, tagging and archiving (Hartel, Cox and Griggin, 2016; Case and Given, 2016, 330–3; de Kosnik, 2016; Mansourian, 2020). These are now becoming of increasing interest to library and information services, most obviously with an interest in providing access to materials produced by serious leisure protagonists, such as fanworks (Price and Robinson, 2017), and in programming and providing facilities such as makerspaces (VanScoy, Thomson and Hartel, 2020). There is also the question of whether some of the methods devised in the serious leisure domain, such as tagging methods, may be more generally applicable. Other domains Other domains have informational features of interest; we brieﬂy mention four here. Mathematics Mathematics is a ubiquitous subject, studied by every person during their formal education, and applied in some ways by most people in their everyday life. It has a uniquely wide set of users, from professional mathematicians and stu
===
--- Chunk 220 ---
ucation, and applied in some ways by most people in their everyday life. It has a uniquely wide set of users, from professional mathematicians and students of all levels, through workers in the many occupations which use mathematics, to the enthusiasts for recreational mathematics. It therefore has a particularly wide range of types of resources. The information practices of those using mathematical information lie between those of scientiﬁc research and of applied science and engineering, reﬂecting the nature of mathematics as both a discipline in its own right and a tool for application in many other contexts, with the relatively slow and incremental process of mathematical research having a particular inﬂuence on information behaviour (Sapa, Krakowska and Janiak, 2014; Barsky, 2012; Gordon et al., 2020). Mathematical knowledge is one of Paul Hirst’s unique forms of knowledge, and the subject has a uniquely abstract knowledge base, with a variety of classiﬁcations (Fraser, 2020) and an extensive and sophisticated language with a variety of notations developed over hundreds of years (Mazur, 2014). For this reason, it has an unusually wide range of ‘logic and language’ resources, including guides to how to read and write mathematics, as well as how to understand its terminology and notation. Law Law is an example of a subject which might be thought to form a homogeneous academic and professional domain, but which is very diverse geographically, including in informational term
===
--- Chunk 221 ---
ich might be thought to form a homogeneous academic and professional domain, but which is very diverse geographically, including in informational terms. Not merely are laws diﬀerent in diﬀerent countries, but in those jurisdictions, typically in Anglophone countries, which have a common law system, legislation is interpreted and nuanced by judicial decisions in a way that does not happen in systems of civil law, as in many continental European countries. The consequence is that in countries such as the UK and the USA there is a wide range of legal resources providing information on case reports, precedents and citations to cases, which has no equivalent elsewhere. Terminology may pose problems, with legal use of words and phrases diﬀering from the usual dictionary deﬁnition. In the UK there is much use of Latin terms and obscure abbreviations, with texts and resources known by the proper names of their original authors or editors. Art, design and fashion These comprise a domain which has perhaps the widest range of document forms, and correspondingly diverse collections, including images of all kinds, architectural models, materials and fashion pieces (Glassman and Dyki, 2017; Peirson-Smith and Peirson-Smith, 2020). Information practices are focused on assisting inspiration and creativity, and include a need for printed materials as well as digital, and a preference for browsing and informal access. Pharmaceuticals Pharmaceuticals, although rooted in the academic disciplines of pharmacology, medicinal chemistry and pharmacy, is a domain closely involved with one of the most information-intensive industries and with the equally information-intensive clinical use of medicines. Because of this background, and because of its economic and social importance, this area has perhaps the widest range of resources of any domain, from chemistry and biology to pharmaceutical technologies to medicine, from pure science to commercial and patent information, and from highly specialised resources to those aimed at the general public (Bawden and Robinson, 2011). Domain-specialist information work One of the main origins of information science is domain-speciﬁc information work, in special libraries, information services and documentation centres. The traditional roles of the subject librarian and the subject-specialist information oﬃcer have changed, particularly as users are now well able to do much of their own searching online, doing away to an extent with the intermediary role. Nonetheless, subject-specialist roles remain of considerable importance, particularly in areas such as law and medicine. What kind of subject knowledge, if any, is needed for such roles is a very long-standing question. It is generally agreed that a domain- specialist information professional does not need the same degree of subject knowle
===
--- Chunk 223 ---
very long-standing question. It is generally agreed that a domain- specialist information professional does not need the same degree of subject knowledge as their users: medical librarians are not usually qualiﬁed doctors or nurses. What is needed is some subject • • • • • • • • • knowledge, plus knowledge of subject-speciﬁc sources, user needs, etc.: the subject background necessary to allow insight into needs and domain-speciﬁc sources, and to enable the interpretation and evaluation of information. This is oĞen described as an understanding of the logic and language of a subject area; an appreciation that, for example, Phyllostachys aurea is a plant rather than a Greek philosopher (Morris-Knower, 2001). How such domain understanding is best gained, and whether information skills or subject knowledge are more important, are questions which recur frequently. Moreau (2019) gives a detailed account of how a librarian new to the health science area gained such understanding, and the surveys of Sterner (2020) and Koos and Scheinfeld (2020) show that, while a subject background is valuable to science and health librarians, subject expertise can be acquired in a variety of ways. The concept of domain, and the approach of domain analysis, allows us to understand and deal with these diﬀerences, in both research and practice. The linking of domain analysis with the communication chain of recorded information • • • • provides a unique character for information science (Robinson, 2009). The subject-specialist role, dealing with information within a particular domain, is of importance, particularly in areas such as law, business, healthcare and the sciences. Domain analysis is a framework for studying information communication within subject areas and user groups, and for the provision of information services to such groups. It is a socio-cognitive approach, based on examining the nature of knowledge within social groups and implications for information provision. Jorge Luis Borges, The Analytical Language of John Wilkins Introduction The organisation of information, and of documents which convey information, is one of the fundamental aspects of information science. In many respects, this amounts to classifying and name giving: as essential in our science as Linnaeus proclaimed it to be in his, though for rather diﬀerent reasons. These reasons are the needs to describe the nature of a document (its title, creator, date of creation, physical form, publishing details, etc.), fully and accurately, through cataloguing and metadata cre
===
--- Chunk 235 ---
a document (its title, creator, date of creation, physical form, publishing details, etc.), fully and accurately, through cataloguing and metadata creation, and to denote its subject, what it is about, through classifying, indexing and summarising. The subject may be referred to as either information organisation (IO) or knowledge organisation (KO). OĞen these terms are treated as synonymous. KO strictly refers to the organising and structure of knowledge itself, a rather abstract and philosophical activity, while IO is usually taken as the seeking of pragmatic solutions to the organisation of information-bearing documents, physical or digital, so that they can be accessed and retrieved. Hjørland (2012) notes that the terms are typically used in diﬀerent contexts, but that the underlying theoretical principles are identical; he suggests that KO is the more appropriate term, because it relates to the social context of information rather than to information theory and computing. We will use the term IO throughout this chapter, for consistency with the title of the book and other chapters. One of the main aspects of the subject is the way in which long- standing concepts and techniques are being adapted to the modern digital environment. Some fundamentals of the topic, particular aspects of the theory of classiﬁcation, go back many centuries, and some of the main tools used today have their origins in the 19th century. They were developed as part of the aĴempt to provide bibliog
===
--- Chunk 236 ---
 centuries, and some of the main tools used today have their origins in the 19th century. They were developed as part of the aĴempt to provide bibliographic control of printed materials; to record, identify and make accessible all the intellectual output of humanity, as expressed in recorded knowledge. They, and newer equivalents, are now being used to provide access to the rapidly expanding stock of digital material. The processes of IO, themselves part of the wider set of processes of documentation, have always been intellectual activities, carried out by expert people. However, automated, or at least machine-aided, systems for metadata creation, including automatic classiﬁcation and automated indexing, are making a signiﬁcant impact. IO is an extensive and complex subject in its own right, but fortunately it is covered by a wide range of textbooks, articles and web resources. Wide coverage of the whole topic is given by Gnoli (2020a), Joudrey and Taylor (2017) and Glushko (2013); also valuable are the articles in the growing online encyclopedia of knowledge organisation created by the International Society for Knowledge Organization (ISKO) We will outline the main topics and issues, pointing to where more detailed treatments can be found. We will look ﬁrst at some of the fundamental issues of information organisation, before examining the main tools, issues and processes: metadata, resource description, classiﬁcation, taxonomy and ontology, and alphabetic vocabularies. Fundamentals of information organisation The questions raised by IO have been asked since the earliest days of philosophy. Is there a single ‘natural’ classiﬁcation of everything in the world? On what basis do we assign things to categories? How do our mental concepts relate to physical things? How distinct can two things be and still be given the same name? And so on. There is a great deal of theory underlying all organisations of information and knowledge, whether classiﬁcation schemes for documents or scientiﬁc taxonomies, of plants, animals, rocks, stars, etc. For detailed treatment of the theory of IO, see Svenonious (2000), Hjørland (2016a; 2021) and Gnoli (2020a); only an outline is given here. IO has been approached from a number of perspectives. Following Gnoli (2020a), we can identify ﬁve dimensions in which IO has been developed, in theory and in practice. • • • • Phenomenon: rooted in ontology, this leads to organisation by the phenomena of reality, the things that exist in the world, rather than by how we think of them. Such considerations have led to the development of classiﬁcation schemes such as Brown and Integrative Levels. IO systems built on this basis include all subjects which may be envisaged, whether or not any documents mention them; the opposite of the principle of literary warrant, noted below. Perspectiv
===
--- Chunk 238 ---
subjects which may be envisaged, whether or not any documents mention them; the opposite of the principle of literary warrant, noted below. Perspective: rooted in epistemology this leads to organisation by how our knowledge is structured, typically by academic discipline, and leads to discipline-based classiﬁcation such as Dewey. It may lead to IO being inﬂuenced by philosophical perspectives such as realism or pragmatism. Document: a focus on information-bearing documents as the units to be organised leads to metadata formats for diﬀerent kinds of documents and to the inclusion of document- or publication-type indicators in classiﬁcation schemes, thesauri, etc. It may also lead to IO tools being developed on the basis of literary warrant, such that only subjects and topics which appear in existing documents should be included in a vocabulary (Barité, 2018). Collection: IO is oĞen applied to a collection of some kinds of document, its purpose being to structure the collection to make it understandable and usable. Although the principles of IO remain the same, the details will diﬀer with the kind of collection. Hjørland (2016a), for example, notes the ways that IO is applied in libraries, archives, museums, bibliographic databases and the internet. • • • • • User: IO systems need to respect the needs, preferences and capabilities of their users. For example, many classiﬁcations and taxonomies have between ﬁve and ten main headings, reﬂecting the number of entities people can h

 of their users. For example, many classiﬁcations and taxonomies have between ﬁve and ten main headings, reﬂecting the number of entities people can hold in mind at one time (Bawden and Robinson, 2016). A user-centred focus is also seen when small or specialised libraries use a local scheme for arranging physical materials, in preference to a general classiﬁcation scheme. Hjørland (2017) proposes that there are four basic approaches to classiﬁcation, which are applicable to all IO: rationalism, based on the logical application of rules based on clearly stated fundamental principles empiricism, based on assessment of similarity according to neutral comparison of all available criteria, without any assessment of which criteria are important historicism, based on analysis of development over time, bringing together entities which have a common ancestry, or which are related in the development of theory pragmatism, based on a critical and subjective analysis of the purpose of the organisation to bring out relationships meaningful for that purpose. Examples of all these approaches may be seen in practical IO systems. Several fundamental ideas within IO can be identiﬁed, which will recur as diﬀerent aspects are considered. We can summarise them under three headings: concepts and categories; hierarchy and facets; and controlled vocabulary. Concepts and categories A concept is a basic unit of knowledge, an idea, a building block of thought. The exact nature of concepts, and in partic
===
--- Chunk 240 ---
ary. Concepts and categories A concept is a basic unit of knowledge, an idea, a building block of thought. The exact nature of concepts, and in particular the relation between a concept as a representation of external reality, as an internal subject of individual thought and as a culturally agreed concept, has been the subject of much debate; see, for example, Van Loocke (1999), Hjørland (2017) and Margolis and Laurence (2021). Concepts are of signiﬁcance to IO in two main ways. Analysis of the conceptual nature of any document determines its aboutness, by which it may be classiﬁed or indexed (Holley and Joudrey, 2021). And the tools of IO, such as classiﬁcation schemes and thesauri, are constructed of concepts, albeit necessarily expressed as words or notations. Concepts are divided into categories, groups of generally similar concepts, which may be overlapping (a concept may be in more than one category) or mutually exclusive (a concept ﬁts into one and only one category). The idea of categories and how they are formed, which is at the heart of much IO (Hjørland, 2017; Glushko et al., 2013), goes back to the philosophers of classical Greece, and to Aristotle in particular, and has again been the subject of much philosophical debate (Thomasson, 2019). Hierarchy and facets Division into categories is typically by hierarchy, again an idea going back to classical Greece (Bergman, 2021). It is usually taken that • • • hierarchies may be formed in three ways, with classes divided

--- Chunk 241 ---
n an idea going back to classical Greece (Bergman, 2021). It is usually taken that • • • hierarchies may be formed in three ways, with classes divided into subclasses: by type or kind, e.g. PLANTS > FLOWERING PLANTS > ROSES by part of a whole, e.g. HUMAN BODY > ARM > ELBOW by instance or example, e.g. OCEANS > ATLANTIC. Although there are examples of non-hierarchical structures in IO (see, for example, Robinson and Maguire, 2010), hierarchy is generally fundamental. Hierarchy gives a way of organising any knowledge structure or collection of information, but it is rigid and one dimensional and does not allow any ways of showing other relationships between the concepts. To deal with this, the idea of facet and of facet analysis was originated. Facets are non-hierarchical aspects or characteristics of a subject area, used to form classes, and facet analysis involves dividing the concepts within a subject domain into consistent sections, based on facets (La Barre, 2010; Hjørland, 2013; Hudon, 2020). The concept of facet analysis was originated by the Indian librarian and documentalist S. R. Ranganathan (1892–1972), who proposed a set of ﬁve ‘fundamental facets’, applicable to any subject: personality, maĴer, energy, space and time (PMEST). Extensions to this, and alternative sets of fundamental facets, have been proposed subsequently, but facets are usually derived to suit each case. Controlled vocabulary A controlled vocabulary, another foundational concept within KO, is a set of agreed and standardised terms to be used for some IO purpose,  including  indexing,  retrieval  and  classiﬁcatory arrangements (Joudrey and Taylor, 2017, chapter 10; Smith, 2021). They vary from the very simple, such as keyword lists and synonym rings, to which others are more complex, including inter-term relations and explanations of terms, such as subject-heading lists, classiﬁcations, taxonomies, and thesauri. They control the variability and redundancy of natural language. An argument about whether controlled or uncontrolled vocabularies are ‘best’ has continued for many years. The obvious answer is that a combination of both is desirable: a controlled vocabulary for consistency and for its term relations, with uncontrolled terms for precision and for new terms which have not been included in the controlled vocabulary. KOSs are usually described as either alphabetic, with the terms arranged in alphabetical order according to the language of the vocabulary, or systematic, with the terms arranged according to the system of a classiﬁcation or taxonomy. Some simple KOSs are restricted to one form; for example, a list of terms without any inter- term relations can only be presented either alphabetically or in an arbitrary order. KOSs with some complexity in term information can generally be viewed in diﬀerent ways; for example, classiﬁcations like Dewey have alphabetic indexes, and taxonomies and thesauri can be interconverted. Metadata The Oxford English Dictionary deﬁnes metadata as ‘data whose purpose is to describe and give information about other data’. In the context of IO, it is generally understood as data which describes the nature and subject of a document; short, structured and standardised records, which can act as surrogates for the original document for search and display. It may be encountered in ﬁles of metadata, the classic example being a library catalogue where each record gives the metadata for a book or other item in the document itself, or it may be encoded within digital documents, for example embedded in HTML or XML coding. Metadata is crucial to IO, giving the information necessary for organising,  managing,  searching  and  accessing  documents. Metadata creators seek to provide answers to questions such as these for a document: ‘what is this?’, ‘how does it diﬀer from similar things?’, ‘how can it best be described?’, ‘how can it best be made retrievable?’, and ‘how can it clearly be shown how, and by whom, it can be used?’ For relatively short introductions to metadata, see Pomerantz (2015), Gartner (2016) and Hider (2018), and for more detailed treatment see Haynes (2018), Joudrey and Taylor (2017) and Zeng and Qin (2016), the last giving many examples of metadata formats and schemas. The creation and use of metadata have been regarded as intellectual processes carried out by expert people. Increasingly, however, metadata, even of the kinds of relevance to IO, is being created and applied by machine. There are some metadata standards intended primarily for automated use, such as the ONIX (Online Information Exchange) family of standards, used to transmit bibliographic and licensing data about new publications from publishers to purchasing institutions. There have been two separate approaches to metadata. One is the longstanding bibliographic approach, library related and typiﬁed by the MAchine Readable Cataloguing (MARC) standard; the other is the internet and digital resource approach, typiﬁed by Dublin Core. The two approaches are becoming integrated in more recent metadata standards and schemas. Bibliographic metadata has traditionally been thought of as having two components: descriptive and subject. These were traditionally instantiated in diﬀerent physical forms; for example, the distinct ‘author/title catalogue’ and ‘subject catalogue’, in libraries using drawers of catalogue cards, but both are now usually subsumed within one metadata format, and described as descriptive metadata. Descriptive metadata answers questions such as ‘what is this called?’, ‘who wrote it?’, ‘how old is it?’, ‘how big is it?’, ‘what kind of thing is it?’, and ‘where is it?’ The subject elements answer the question ‘what is it about?’ The details of description will vary according to the physical nature of the item: e.g. ‘how big is it?’ will be answered in terms of pages and centimetres for a book, and megabytes for a digital resource. Classiﬁcation and categorisation Classiﬁcations and categorisations (and also taxonomies and ontologies, considered in the next section) are forms of IO which aim to show the relationships between concepts, generally although not always hierarchical relationships, by bringing together terms representing concepts’ similar meanings. They are therefore referred to as concept-based or systematic KOSs: constructed of concepts, according to a ‘system’. Cla
===
--- Chunk 257 ---

Classiﬁcation is oĞen thought of as a system for arranging collections of printed materials by subject, but it is also useful for visualising and browsing digital materials. In all contexts, a classiﬁcation can oﬀer a map of a subject or collection, showing the interrelation of all its parts. Dealing with concepts and classes as opposed to terms and phrases, classiﬁcations show the relations between concepts more clearly and explicitly than alphabetic vocabularies, to which they are complementary. There is a considerable body of classiﬁcation theory, and principles of classiﬁcation also provide the rationale for the more complex alphabetic vocabularies, such as thesauri. We will ﬁrst consider general principles of classiﬁcation and then look at examples of some important schemes. Dividing the world into distinct aspects appears to be a deep- rooted human impulse. See Bowker and Star (2000) and Hjørland (2017) for wide-ranging discussions of classiﬁcation in general, including but not limited to IO schemes. Much classiﬁcation theory comes not from information science but from other disciplines, especially from philosophy and from the taxonomic sciences, biology in particular. The information sciences have been relatively late on the scene, with all the main classiﬁcation schemes in current use being developed in the late 19th and ea
===
--- Chunk 258 ---
mation sciences have been relatively late on the scene, with all the main classiﬁcation schemes in current use being developed in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and theoretical examination of classiﬁcation for IO purposes beginning only in the 20th century. The philosophical roots of classiﬁcation lie in Aristotle’s hierarchical division of the world according to the aĴributes of its entities, with non-overlapping categories created by applying one criterion of division at a time, and alternatively on WiĴgenstein’s ideas of overlapping categories based on ‘family resemblances’ with multiple similarities. The two approaches, which are as applicable to scientiﬁc taxonomy as to classiﬁcation of knowledge and documents, are termed monothetic and polythetic, respectively (Leazer, Montoya and Furner, 2020). Because classiﬁcations, in the IO sense, are created on the basis of concepts and their meaning, they are necessarily subjective, since the many ways concepts can be categorised and ordered all have validity. There is no claim, as there is with some ontologies and scientiﬁc taxonomies, that they represent a truth about the world. It follows that there cannot be such a thing as a ‘correct’ classiﬁcation; though this does not mean that classiﬁcations cannot be judged as being more or less consistent, complete or useful. George Perec (1936–82), the French novelist and essayist, noted a list of ways in which a library might be arranged: alphabetically; by continent or count
===
--- Chunk 259 ---
ge Perec (1936–82), the French novelist and essayist, noted a list of ways in which a library might be arranged: alphabetically; by continent or country; by colour; by date of purchase; by date of publication; by format; by genre; by literary period; by language; according to our reading priorities; according to the binding of the materials; and by series. His gloomy conclusion was that, although all are valid to an extent, none is ‘satisfactory in itself’ (Perec, 2020, 60–9). The same, alas, is true of any classiﬁcation; none can be perfect for all purposes. (We thank Vanda Broughton for reminding us of Perec’s ideas.) An issue faced by all IO classiﬁcation is that subjects, and documents, rarely deal with just one concept but, rather, with multiple concepts in combination, so that we cannot say that a document deals with just one topic and hence has one unique place in a classiﬁcation scheme. For example, should a document dealing with scientiﬁc research in Victorian London be classiﬁed with materials on science, on the Victorian period, or on London? There is no evident solution; the best that can be achieved is to specify a consistent ordering of the aspects, so-called citation order, and ideally to have a system allowing access by any aspect. Since they are static, they are problematic for rapidly changing subject ﬁelds, since any new topic must be included by a revision of the scheme. An analytico-synthetic classiﬁcation allows notations to be combined to create new topics and typically has sets of commonly combined concepts such as place and time. However, such classiﬁcations also typically have many pre-combined complex classes. Several classiﬁcations originally created as purely enumerative are now of this form, with a synthetic, number-building capability for complex topics. Figure 8.5  Number building in UDC (Vanda Broughton) Fully faceted classiﬁcations take this principle of combination more radically. Terminology is grouped into related concepts by facet analysis, from which the classiﬁcation for any item can be constructed, so that codes can be created for new topics by combination, with a minimum of predeﬁned combinations. Faceted classiﬁcation, along with facet analysis, was devised by Ranganathan in his Colon Classiﬁcation, named for the punctuation mark which characterises its notation. Many faceted classiﬁcation schemes in speciﬁc subject areas, particularly in science, technology and social sciences, were created during the 1950s and 1960s for classifying specialised or technical material, particularly in systems using techniques  of  mechanised  documentation  and,  later,  early applications of computers. The concept was researched and promoted, in particular, by the UK-based Classiﬁcation Research Group from 1948 (McIlwaine and Broughton, 2000; Broughton, 2017a; Miksa, 2017). Faceted classiﬁcation lost popularity, however, because of its perceived complexity and diﬃculty of use, and fully faceted schemes are liĴle used in practice, although schemes such as the Integrative Levels Classiﬁcation and the second edition of the Bliss Classi

y faceted schemes are liĴle used in practice, although schemes such as the Integrative Levels Classiﬁcation and the second edition of the Bliss Classiﬁcation continue to be developed. For an assessment of a variety of issues of faceted classiﬁcation in a digital environment see the chapters in Slavic and Gnoli (2017), in particular Broughton (2017a). General schemes of classiͅcation Space does not permit a detailed account of any schemes, but we will brieﬂy mention some of the more signiﬁcant general schemes, to illustrate the breadth of classiﬁcation types, with a note of where to ﬁnd further information. Other schemes are described by articles in the ISKO Encyclopedia of Knowledge Organization, including national • • • and regional schemes from China, Japan, Korea, and Russia, and special schemes for various subjects. The Dewey Decimal Classiﬁcation (Broughton, 2015, chapter 17) is the most widely used classiﬁcation, applied in hundreds of thousands of libraries worldwide, as well as in digital collections. Devised by the American librarian Melville Dewey and ﬁrst published in 1876, it is now in its 23rd edition. Originally a purely enumerative scheme, with its well-known ten major disciplinary classes, divided and subdivided by ten to allow its convenient decimal notation, its structure reﬂects the 19th-century Western world and the ‘liberal arts’ seĴing in which it was created, and its theoretical basis is limited. It is an example of an IO tool whose success is due to it
===
--- Chunk 265 ---
and the ‘liberal arts’ seĴing in which it was created, and its theoretical basis is limited. It is an example of an IO tool whose success is due to its reach, convenience and good support from its parent organisation. The Universal Decimal Classiﬁcation (Broughton, 2015, chapters 18 and 19) was created in 1905 by the documentalists Paul Otlet and Henri La Fontaine, as an extension of Dewey’s scheme, to allow retrieval of documents rather than just shelf arrangement of books. The ﬁrst scheme with an analytico-synthetic nature, it was more ﬂexible in dealing with detailed and complex topics than previous schemes. Subsequent editions have introduced more faceted elements (Slavic and Davis, 2017). The Library of Congress Classiﬁcation (Chan, Intner and Weihs, 2016) was devised by that library, and begun in 1901. It remains the purest example of a large enumerative scheme which has limited synthetic capabilities and provides very detailed, • • • • sometimes idiosyncratic, subject listings, based upon enumeration within 21 major disciplinary classes. The Colon Classiﬁcation (Satĳa, 2017) is a fully faceted disciplinary classiﬁcation, the ﬁrst of its kind, published by Ranganathan in 1933, developed through two major revisions and numerous editions. Organised by the PMEST facet analysis principle, it is intended for use with any kinds of documents in a library context. It has had liĴle application in practice, even in the Indian subcontinent, but has been very inﬂuential on the deve

The ﬁrst edition of the Bliss Bibliographic Classiﬁcation was published in the 1930s by Henry Evelyn Bliss (1870–1955), one of the early theorists of IO. An enumerative disciplinary scheme, though with a synthetic number-building capability, it was regarded as the most scholarly and philosophically sound of the enumerative schemes. A second edition of this scheme, still under development, is fully faceted and is regarded as particularly theoretically sound (Broughton, 2018). The Brown Subject Classiﬁcation (Beghtol, 2004), developed by British librarian James Duﬀ Brown (1862–1914) and published in 1906, is an early example of a phenomenon classiﬁcation, with an analytico-synthetic nature. Although no longer used in practice, it has a place in classiﬁcation history and has been an inspiration for current developments. The Integrative Levels Classiﬁcation (Gnoli, 2020b) is a fully faceted phenomenon classiﬁcation based on the idea of levels of reality in general systems theories and applicable to any kind of • document. It is being developed primarily to instantiate ideas of classiﬁcation theory, though it has been applied to a number of small bibliographic databases. The Basic Concept Classiﬁcation (Szostak, 2020) is a fully faceted phenomenon classiﬁcation under development, designed to connect users to

The Basic Concept Classiﬁcation (Szostak, 2020) is a fully faceted phenomenon classiﬁcation under development, designed to connect users to any document, object or idea and to provide a general classiﬁcation of particular value for interdisciplinary issues. It is constructed so far as possible from basic concepts, i.e. those concepts which are so fundamental that they are understood in the same way in all contexts and societies. So far, we have described formal classiﬁcations, published and intended to be widely applied. There are, of course, very many simpler classiﬁcations and categorisations in use in contexts including personal collections, bookshops, small libraries and leisure and fan communities; some of these are gaining wide visibility through their use on social media. Taxonomy and ontology Taxonomy The word taxonomy comes from the Greek taxis, meaning an order or arrangement. It has most commonly been used to mean a scientiﬁc classiﬁcation of some aspect of the natural world, the best-known being biological ‘tree of life’ taxonomies. These classiﬁcations are purely hierarchical and, like the ontologies mentioned later, are intended to be realistic, to represent an aspect of the world as it really is. When such taxonomies are amended it is supposed to be done on the basis of objective facts, not subjective opinion or convenience. They are usually associated with a systematic nomenclature for naming the entities in the taxonomy. In the information sciences
===
--- Chunk 268 ---
pinion or convenience. They are usually associated with a systematic nomenclature for naming the entities in the taxonomy. In the information sciences a taxonomy is regarded as a classiﬁcation devised for a particular environment or a particular set of information; it does not necessarily cover a subject area comprehensively, as a library classiﬁcation would. Taxonomies usually reﬂect the local conditions closely, are adapted to the local ‘culture’ and may be modiﬁed and extended more frequently than other information organisation tools. See Hedden (2016) for a thorough discussion of this kind of taxonomy. Taxonomies are usually intellectually constructed, but may be automatically generated and maintained; for a review of methods for automatic taxonomy generation, see Irfan et al. (2019). They are a popular tool for organising digital information resources and supporting browsing and searching, and may be linked to a thesaurus as a way of viewing the taxonomy terms alphabetically. Taxonomies may diﬀer from the norms of classiﬁcation, for example by allowing the same concept to appear more than once, at diﬀerent levels, if this is helpful to the user’s browsing. They may be a high-level description of subject maĴer; for example, a ‘corporate taxonomy’ is a way of expressing the interests of an organisation so as to, for example, organise in-house data. Alternatively, taxonomies may include many speciﬁc examples – names of places, people or departments, for example, as well as 
===
--- Chunk 269 ---
organise in-house data. Alternatively, taxonomies may include many speciﬁc examples – names of places, people or departments, for example, as well as general concept headings – and may have more similarity with a thesaurus than a library classiﬁcation. They may also include much descriptive information about the concepts and items, acting as a kind of glossary. Taxonomies are typically used to give access to diverse forms of materials – databases, documents, e-mails, people – and hence can support knowledge-management programmes. Ontology Ontology, coming from the Greek ontos, ‘that which exists’, has been used and still is used within philosophy to mean the study of what kinds of things can exist and how they can be described. It is sometimes used to describe, informally, a general set of things of concern; the ontology of an area in this sense would be the major concepts within it. In the information sciences the term is now used to mean a formal description of a domain of knowledge, in terms of the entities within it and their relationships, which may be processed directly by computer for deduction, question answering, etc. For the changing meaning of the word, see Almeida (2013) and Machado, Almeida and Souza (2020); for ontology use in the biological sciences see Hoehndorf, Schoﬁeld and Gkoutos (2015) and Zheng et al. Alphabetic vocabularies There are several kinds of alphabetic controlled vocabularies in which the terms – words or phrases – are arranged in alphabetical order. There are no well-deﬁned distinctions between them; in general, the distinction lies in how much information is provided about each term, including term deﬁniti
===
--- Chunk 272 ---
no well-deﬁned distinctions between them; in general, the distinction lies in how much information is provided about each term, including term deﬁnitions and interrelations. Keyword lists are the simplest form of alphabetic controlled vocabulary. OĞen they consist of nothing more than a list of ‘approved terms’; sometimes they include synonyms. They are a simple and cheap form of terminology to develop and use, but are very limited in their usefulness and applicable only to small ﬁles and simple searches. Subject headings are lists of terms – oĞen quite lengthy to represent complex concepts – which are used for indexing for retrieval, and sometimes for browsing. They will generally include synonyms, and sometimes hierarchical and ‘SEE ALSO’ relations. The Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) is the most widely known and widely used terminology of this sort (Broughton, 2017b). A very large vocabulary, ﬁrst published in 1914, its 42nd edition was published in 2020. It has over 250,000 terms, covering all subject areas, with approximately 4,000 added each year. USE/USE FOR, BROADER TERM/NARROWER TERM and RELATED TERM relations are included. The large number of terms reﬂects the need for this kind of vocabulary to provide detailed description for precision in retrieval. This is partly achieved by including many proper names of people, places, living things, vehicles, diseases, etc., partly by creating pre-coordinated terms including more than one concept and partly by subd
===
--- Chunk 273 ---
f people, places, living things, vehicles, diseases, etc., partly by creating pre-coordinated terms including more than one concept and partly by subdividing headings by topical subdivisions (aspects of a topic, listed for each heading), by geographical subdivisions (where it is allowed for a heading) and by free-ﬂoating subdivisions, including subjects, form and time period. Thesauri in the information sciences should not be confused with reference works such as Roget’s Thesaurus. Both are concerned with precision in terminology. Roget-style thesauri provide alternatives for a given term, since, as Roget himself put it, ‘specious phraseology’ spreads ‘prejudice and error’ (Kendall, 2008, 8). Retrieval thesauri generally control the vocabulary used in indexing and/or retrieval. Such thesauri are deﬁned by international standards (ISO, 2011; ISO, 2013), although not all vocabularies called thesauri observe their prescriptions. For detailed coverage of thesauri, albeit dated in detail, see Aitchison, Gilchrist and Bawden (2000) and Broughton (2006); for a more recent review see Dextre Clarke (2019); and for commentary on their continuing relevance see Shiri (2012), Hjørland (2016b), Bawden (2016) and Dextre Clarke (2016). The ISO 25964 standard deﬁnes a thesaurus as a ‘controlled and structured vocabulary in which concepts are represented by terms, organised so that relationships between the concepts are made explicit, and preferred terms are accompanied by lead-in entries for 
===
--- Chunk 274 ---
resented by terms, organised so that relationships between the concepts are made explicit, and preferred terms are accompanied by lead-in entries for synonyms or quasi-synonyms’. The standard recommends, for consistency, that thesaurus terms should be nouns or noun phrases, but other parts of speech can be found in many thesauri. The usual set of thesaurus inter-term relationships is equivalence, hierarchy and associative. The equivalence relation (USE/USE FOR) denotes terms which are synonyms or quasi-synonyms. The allowance for quasi-synonyms, terms which do not mean exactly the same but which are suﬃciently similar to be regarded as synonymous for the purposes of the thesaurus, shows that the guiding principle for this kind of vocabulary is pragmatic convenience, rather than ontological realism. The requirement for selection of one term as preferred, rather than just collecting synonyms, reﬂects the origin of the thesaurus in the age of printed indexes, when it was necessary to have a single entry point for a concept: there can be only one preferred term for a concept, but any number of non-preferred terms or none. Preferred terms have a full thesaurus entry; non-preferred terms usually just a single-line USE relation, pointing to the preferred term. The hierarchy relation (BROADER TERM/NARROWER TERM) is used when one term falls entirely within the scope of the other. It establishes the structure of a thesaurus and allows it to be inter- converted with a taxonomy. The stan
===
--- Chunk 275 ---
lls entirely within the scope of the other. It establishes the structure of a thesaurus and allows it to be inter- converted with a taxonomy. The standard recognises three forms of hierarchy: generic (e.g. METALS – IRON), part–whole (e.g. HANDS – FINGERS) and instance (e.g. OCEANS – ATLANTIC). A term generally has one broader term (none for terms at the top of the hierarchy); some thesauri are multi-hierarchy and allow more than one broader term. A term may have any number of narrower terms; none for terms at the boĴom of the hierarchy. The relation is symmetrical (except in some special circumstances, such as some multilingual thesauri): if A is the broader term of B, then B must necessarily be a narrower term of A. The associative relation (RELATED TERM, or SEE ALSO) denotes relations which are neither equivalence nor hierarchy, but point to additional terms which might be of use to indexers or searchers. The standard gives examples such as terms with overlapping meaning (e.g. SHIPS – BOATS), activities and places where they are carried out (e.g. NURSING – HOSPITALS) and disciplines and their object of study (e.g. ASTRONOMY – STARS). Inclusion of this relation is typically pragmatic, according to perceived user needs. The relation is not necessarily symmetrical: if A is a related term to B, then B may or may not be a related term of A. Thesauri in areas with a strong hierarchical structure, typically in science and medicine, are likely to have fewer associative terms than t

Thesauri in areas with a strong hierarchical structure, typically in science and medicine, are likely to have fewer associative terms than those in areas of humanities, social subjects and everyday life. A further relation used in some thesauri is ‘Top Term’ or ‘Heading Parent’, identifying the hierarchy in which the term occurs. A few thesauri have used other forms of inter-term relation but, in general, equivalence, hierarchy and associative are regarded as suﬃcient for retrieval. ISO25964 also recommends scope notes, giving deﬁnitions or explanations of terms, and/or prescribing their use in indexing and retrieval, although these need not be present for all terms. An example of a thesaurus term showing all these relations is shown in Figure 8.6 on the next page. Thesauri were originally designed to be used by both indexer and searcher, to ensure that both were using the same term for the same concept. In the digital environment, thesauri may still be used in this way, or may be used only for indexing or only for searching by, for example, assisting automatic indexing; automatically expanding searches by adding additional terms; and suggesting alternative terms to a searcher. See Shiri (2012) and Dextre Clarke (2019) for examples. It may also including abstracting or summarising. Classifying implies the addition of one or more classiﬁcation codes from whatever classiﬁcation scheme is in use. The ethos of most classiﬁcation schemes is that one unique code should be assigned, although in digital environments there is no reason why more than one code should not be added. Indexing is usually taken to mean the assignment of a number of terms from an alphabetic vocabulary; if no controlled vocabulary is used, the process is called free term indexing or tagging. If the tagging is carried out by individual users, rather than indexers, who share metadata production, it may be known as social tagging and the resultant set of terms as a folksonomy (Raﬀerty, 2018; Price and Robinson, 2021). Indexing is usually assumed to be applicable to text documents, but it may be necessary to index other forms of material, such as images, datasets and maps. The process of indexing is governed by international standards (ISO, 1985; ISO, 1996). For overviews of the principles and practice of indexing, see Lancaster (2003), Hjørland (2018) and Duncan (2021). The indexing of any particular document, according to the ISO 5963 standard is a three-stage process: understanding of the content – the 
===
--- Chunk 278 ---
ncan (2021). The indexing of any particular document, according to the ISO 5963 standard is a three-stage process: understanding of the content – the indexer decides what the document is ‘about’; analysis of the content – the indexer decides which concepts are to be indexed, and to what depth; translation of concepts into indexing terms – the indexer chooses the most appropriate terms from the vocabulary being used. There are two main criteria for how indexing is carried out: exhaustivity, the extent to which all possible concepts are included; and depth, the degree of speciﬁcity with which concepts are described. An abstract or summary of a document may also be a part of subject metadata, acting as a surrogate for the document for retrieval or display, and is a long-established part of IO (Borko and Bernier, 1975; Lancaster, 2003; Chowdhury, 2017, chapter 8). According to the relevant international standard (ISO, 1976), an abstract is ‘an abbreviated, accurate representation of the contents of a document, without added interpretation or criticism and without distinction as to who wrote the abstract’. Abstracting has a long history; summaries of articles have been used as means of keeping up with the scientiﬁc, medical and professional literature in particular, for many years. Borko and Bernier (1975) suggest that its origins can be traced back to classical times, with the ﬁrst recognisable abstracting journals, and sections for abstracts in general journals, dating from the 
===
--- Chunk 279 ---
n be traced back to classical times, with the ﬁrst recognisable abstracting journals, and sections for abstracts in general journals, dating from the 17th century, their use expanding greatly in the 19th century, together with the creation of subject-specialist abstracting and indexing services. Abstracts may vary in a number of respects, and so may be categorised diﬀerently. A fundamental diﬀerence is whether they are informative, intended to give suﬃcient information to be a replacement for the original, or indicative, giving just enough information for a reader to decide whether the item is of interest. They are increasingly likely to be structured (Jamar, Šauperl and Bawden, 2014; Hartley and Cabanac, 2017) or graphical (Stahl- Timmins, Black and Simpson, 2019). Systems for automatic, or at least machine-aided, classiﬁcation, categorisation and indexing are of increasing importance, with a variety of statistical and machine-learning approaches being applied • • • • (Golub, 2019). Automatic abstracting has been a goal for many years, since the ﬁrst research on the topic, carried out by H. P. Luhn in the late 1950s. Much eﬀort has been expended since then on the design of systems, using a variety of approaches to automatic abstracting and summarising, including sentence extraction, text mining and machine learning (Chowdhury, 2017, chapter 8). Summary Intellectual tools for IO have changed surprisingly slowly; some of those used today, more than a century aĞer they were ﬁrst introduced, would be recognisable to Melville Dewey and to Anthony Panizzi. The dramatic changes in the technical means by which documents are created and disseminated has not been fully matched by the means by which they are managed. The inﬂuence of automated means for metadata creation, particularly those based on AI, is increasing, and may have dramatic eﬀects in the coming years. IO remains at the heart of information science, its importance enhanced in new information environments. New forms of descriptive metadata have emerged to deal with new forms of document, while subject description remains relatively little altered. Long-established theories and concepts remain important, despite technical advances. The full eﬀect of automated IO systems is yet to be realised. Key readings Broughton, V. David Stuart (2020, xvi) Introduction Technology, from the Greek techné, meaning art, skill or craĞ, is usually taken to mean the understanding of how to use tools, in the broadest sense of the word. The term information technology was ﬁrst used in the 1950s to describe the application of mechanised documentation and then-new digital computers, and became widely used in the 1980s to describe the wider-spread use of digital technology (Zorkoczy, 1982). Information technology is usually associated with computers and networks. But, in a wider sense stemming from the original meaning of the word, the technologies of information include all the tools and machines which have been used to assist the creation and dissemination of information throughout history, as discussed in Chapter 2; from ink and paper, through printing to microforms, document reproduction and photocopying, and mechanised documentation technologies such as card indexes, punched cards, edge-notched cards, and optical coincidence cards. Krajewski (2011) examines the idea of card index ﬁles as a ‘universal paper machine’, in a sense the forerunner of the computer, between the 16th and 20th centuries. Our focus here is on digital technologies, echoing the view expressed by Gilster (1997) that all information today is digital, has been digital or may be

focus here is on digital technologies, echoing the view expressed by Gilster (1997) that all information today is digital, has been digital or may be digital. This chapter covers the basics of digital technologies and the handling of data; the following chapter deals with information systems. Digital technologies We will describe these aspects only in outline; see Ince (2011) and Dasgupta (2016) for more detailed but accessible accounts, and Primiero (2020) for a more advanced summary; for accounts of the historical development of the computer, see Ceruzzi (2012) and Haigh and Ceruzzi (2021). Any digital device represents data in the form of binary digits or bits. PaĴerns of bits, bit strings with bits conventionally represented by 0 and 1, may represent data or instructions. A collection of eight bits is known as a byte. Quantities of data are represented as multiples of bytes, for example: a kilobyte, deﬁned as 210 bytes, i.e. 1024 bytes. Any character or symbol may be represented by a bit string, but this requires an agreed coding. The most widely used code since the beginning of the computer age was the American National Standards  Institute’s  ASCII  (American  Standard  Code  for Information Interchange) 7-bit code, but it is limited to the Latin alphabet, Arabic numerals and a few other symbols. It has been supplanted by Unicode, which can handle a wider variety of symbols and scripts. It can do this by using a 32-bit code; the more bits in the code, the more diﬀerent 
===
--- Chunk 294 ---
Unicode, which can handle a wider variety of symbols and scripts. It can do this by using a 32-bit code; the more bits in the code, the more diﬀerent symbols can be coded. Codes provide arbitrary representations of characters; for example, the ASCII code for the leĴer L is the bit string 1001100. The idea that a general-purpose computing machine might be possible stems from the theoretical studies of the British mathematician Alan Turing (1912–54), whose concept of the Turing machine, developed in the 1930s, showed that a single machine limited to a few simple operations (read, write, delete, compare) could undertake any task if appropriately programmed. The basic architecture for a practical digital computer was set out by John von Neumann (1903–57), the Hungarian-American mathematician, in the 1940s (Figure 9.1). His design, which gave the ﬁrst formal description of a single-memory stored-program computer, is shown in Figure 9.2. Figure 9.1  John von Neumann (Alan Richards photographer. From the Shelby White and Leon Levy Archives Center, Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton, NJ, USA) Figure 9.2  Von Neumann computer architecture (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA) This architecture is general purpose, in the sense that it can run a variety of programs. This distinguishes it from special-purpose digital computers which carry out only one task, as in digital cameras, kitchen appliances, cars, etc. A von Neumann machine loads and runs programs as necessary, to accomplish very di

only one task, as in digital cameras, kitchen appliances, cars, etc. A von Neumann machine loads and runs programs as necessary, to accomplish very diﬀerent tasks. The heart of the computer, the processor, oĞen referred to as the central processing unit (CPU), carries out a set of very basic arithmetical and logical operations with instructions and data pulled in from the memory, also referred to as main or working memory. This sequence is referred to as the fetch–execute cycle. Two components of the processor are sometimes distinguished: an arithmetic and logic unit, which carries out the operations, and a control unit, which governs the operations of the cycle. While programs and data are being used they are kept in the memory. While not being used they are stored long-term in ﬁle storage. Items in memory are accessible much more rapidly than items in ﬁle storage, but memory is more expensive, so computers have much more ﬁle storage than memory. Data comes into the computer through its input devices and is sent into the outside world through the output devices. The components are linked together through circuits usually denoted as a bus, sometimes referred to more speciﬁcally as a data bus or address bus. All of these components have undergone considerable change since the ﬁrst computers were designed. Processor design has gone through three main technological stages. The ﬁrst generation of computers used valves as processor components, and the second generation used transi
===
--- Chunk 296 ---
e through three main technological stages. The ﬁrst generation of computers used valves as processor components, and the second generation used transistors. Computers of the third generation, including all present-day computers, use circuits on ‘silicon chips’, by very-large-scale integration (VLSI), which allows millions of components to be placed on a single computer chip, thus increasing processing speed. The storage elements of the computer’s memory comprise regular arrays of silicon-based units, each holding a bit of data, and created using the same VLSI methods as processors. Earlier generations of computers used core storage, with data held on tiny, magnetised elements arranged in a three-dimensional laĴice. File storage, holding data and programs that are not needed immediately, has always used magnetic media, which can hold large volumes of data cheaply, provided that quick access is not required. Earlier generations of computers used a variety of tapes, drums and disks; current computers use hard  disks, rapidly  spinning magnetisable disks with moveable arms with read/write heads, to read data from, or write data to, any area of the disk. Regardless of the technology, each area holds one bit of information, according to its magnetic state. Networks Virtually all computers are connected via some form of network to others, to enable communication and information access and sharing. Since the 1990s the internet and the World Wide Web have become ubiquitous, such that it has become diﬃcult to think about digital technologies without these at centre stage. The growth of networked computing has been driven by three factors: communications technology, soĞware and standards. In terms of technology, older forms of wired network, originating in the twisted copper-pair cables used for telegraph systems from the mid- 19th century, have been succeeded by ﬁbre-optic cables and various forms  of  wireless  transmission.  These  allow  much  faster transmission speeds and greater information-carrying capacity; such systems are described loosely as broadband. SoĞware systems have improved the eﬃciency and reliability of transmission greatly: an important example is packet switching, by which messages may be split up and their constituents sent by the fastest available route, being recombined before delivery. The internet, originating in 1960s networks built for defence research in the USA, is a worldwide network of networks, integrated by common standards: the internet control protocols, commonly known as TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol). The World Wide Web, oĞen spoken of as if it were synonymous with the internet, is in fact a major internet application. A system for allowing access to interlinked hypertext documents stored on networked computers, it originated in the work of Sir Tim Berners- Lee at CERN, the European nuclear research establishment. Berners- Lee introduced the idea in 1989 in an internal memorandum with the modest title ‘Information management: a proposal’. The web is based on client–server architecture: a web browser, the client, on the user’s computer accesses the website on the remote server computer, through the internet, and downloads the required web page. This relies on a number of standards. For example, web pages must be created using a mark-up language, typically HTML, sometimes referred to as the lingua franca of the internet, and be identiﬁed by a Uniform Resource Identiﬁer, commonly referred to as a Uniform Resource Locator or URL; a Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) enables communication between client and server. The internet and web, despite their great reach and inﬂuence, are by no means the only signiﬁcant computer networks. Many private, local and regional networks exist, generally using the standards of the internet and web for compatibility. Software SoĞware, in its various forms, provides the instructions for digital computers to carry out their tasks and can be categorised into systems soĞware (ﬁrmware and operating systems) and application soĞware; for short overviews, see Ince (2011), White and Downs (2015) and Dasgupta (2016). Firmware, such as BIOS (Basic Input Output System), EFI (Extensible Firmware Interface) and UEFI (Uniﬁed Extensible Firmware Interface), comes pre-installed on all computers and is activated when the computer is powered up, to initialise the hardware and start the operating system. The operating system, speciﬁc to a particular type of computer, controls the hardware, allocates system resources, such as memory, and runs applications. Users interact with the operating system to manage ﬁles, use input and output devices, and run applications. Examples of operating systems are Windows, Unix and several variants of Unix, including Linux and Mac OS. Users interact with the opera

Users interact with the operating system via a program termed a shell because it forms an outer layer around an operating system; examples of shells are Bash, zsh and Powershell. Most users will rely on a graphical user interface to the shell for convenience. An alternative form of interface uses a command line, with the user typing instructions (such interfaces are commonly referred to as shells, although strictly the shell is the program to which they are the interface). This type of interface oﬀers a more direct control over computer operations than with a graphical interface, but requires the user to understand the set of commands and the syntax, and to have some understanding of the workings of the operating system. Applications soĞware, discrete programs for carrying out speciﬁc tasks, for a speciﬁc purpose, may either be installed on individual computers, as, for example, word processors, spreadsheets, and web browsers typically are, or may be accessed on the web. The laĴer is usual for search engines, library management systems, and social media platforms. At the risk of over-simpliﬁcation, we can say there are four kinds of soĞware language: low-level and high-level programming languages, scripting languages and mark-up languages. Low-level programming languages, also referred to as assembly languages or machine code, encode instructions at the very detailed level of processor operations; these languages are therefore necessarily speciﬁc to a particular type of computer. This kind of programming is complex and diﬃcult, but results in very eﬃcient operation; it is reserved for situations where reliably fast processing is essential. High-level programming languages express instructions in terms closer to user intentions, and are converted by other soĞware systems, compilers and interpreters into processor instructions in machine code for a particular hardware. Programs are therefore much easier to write, understand and modify than those in machine code. Such languages can be used on diﬀerent types of computer. There have been many such languages, some general purpose and some aimed at a particular kind of application. The ﬁrst examples were developed in the 1950s, and two of the earliest are still in use: FORTRAN, still a language of choice for scientiﬁc and engineering applications, and COBOL, still used in many legacy systems for business applications. Currently popular languages are Java, C++, R and Python. Compilers convert a whole program into machine code, whereas interpreters convert one line at time. Programming languages are described as either compiled, for example C++, or interpreted, for example Python. Scripting languages are a particularly signiﬁcant form of high-level language, designed to support interaction, particularly with web resources; for example, to update a web page in response to a user’s input rather than reloading the page each time, or to create a mashup, an integration of data from several web sources. Examples are JavaScript, PHP and Perl. Mark-up languages are somewhat diﬀerent in nature, as they are designed to annotate text so as to denote either structural elements (‘this is an author name’), presentation (‘print this in italic’) or both. The ﬁrst such languages were designed for formaĴing documents for printing; an example is LaTeX. More recent examples control the format and structure of web resources; examples are HTML and XML. For small-scale soĞware development, perhaps for a piece of code to be used temporarily or just by one person, writing the code and testing that it works correctly is suﬃcient. For a major piece of soĞware, other stages will include design, testing and maintenance; these stages, together with the coding stages, make up system development or soĞware engineering. For accessible introductions to these topics, see Louridas (2020) and Montfort (2021). One inﬂuence on the way soĞware is created is the availability of libraries of subroutines, packages of code in a particular language to undertake speciﬁc tasks which can be included in programs by a single call. If a subroutine library (also called a code library) is available for a particular topic, it means that a coder can create a program very quickly and economically by a series of calls to subroutines, without having to write the code in detail; see Wintjen (2020) for detailed examples. There are an increasing number of subroutine libraries available for topics of relevance to the information disciplines. For example, the Python language has libraries of subroutines for text processing, for extracting data from URLs, for extracting data from mark-up languages such as HTML and XML and for processing 
===
--- Chunk 305 ---
of subroutines for text processing, for extracting data from URLs, for extracting data from mark-up languages such as HTML and XML and for processing data from Wikipedia. An innovation in the way soĞware is provided has come from the open source movement. Commercial soĞware is usually provided as a ‘black box’; the user has no access to the program code and therefore cannot modify the system at all, nor even know exactly how it works. With open source soĞware, the user is given the full source code – the original programs – which they are free to modify. This makes it easy to customise soĞware to meet local needs and preferences. It also allows users to collaborate in extending and improving the systems, correcting errors, etc. Most such soĞware is free, leading it to be known as FOSS (Free and Open Source SoĞware). Well-known examples of full FOSS systems relevant to library and information management are the Koha and FOLIO-ERM library management systems, the EPrints repository system, the Drupal content management system and the Open Journal Systems (OJS) e-journal publishing system; see, for example, Breeding (2017) and Choo and PrueĴ (2019). Many smaller-scale FOSS soĞware products are available; the GitHub repository is the most commonly used means for making these available (Beer, 2017). Github is commonly integrated with the Jupyter notebook environment, which combines simple word processing with the ability to create and run programs; this integration allows for testi
===
--- Chunk 306 ---
the Jupyter notebook environment, which combines simple word processing with the ability to create and run programs; this integration allows for testing, sharing and distribution of open source soĞware and is widely used for data- wrangling functionality, including library/information applications (Wintjen, 2020). There are a number of reasons why information professionals may wish to do their own coding, particularly now that relevant code libraries make it so much quicker and easier to do so. The main reasons would be to customise a procedure to a speciﬁc situation, to merge data from diﬀerent sources, to create tidy, consistent data or to link systems and data together in a particular context. Artiͅcial intelligence Artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) encompasses a complex array of concepts and processes, directed to making it possible for digital computers to do the kind of things that minds can do; see Boden (2016), Cantwell Smith (2019) and Mitchell (2019) for accessible overviews, Floridi (2019) for ideas of its future and Mitchell (2021) for caveats about how much we can expect from AI, especially with regard to endowing machines with common knowledge and common sense. It is ‘a growing resource of interactive, autonomous, self-learning agency, which enables computational artefacts to perform tasks that otherwise would require human intelligence to be carried out successfully’ (Taddeo and Floridi, 2018, 751). Although AI as such has been possible only since the middle of the 2
===
--- Chunk 307 ---
man intelligence to be carried out successfully’ (Taddeo and Floridi, 2018, 751). Although AI as such has been possible only since the middle of the 20th century, it has been preceded by several centuries of interest in mechanical automata, game-playing machines, calculating machines, automated reasoning and the like; see Pickover (2019) for an informal history. Although Ada Lovelace mused on a ‘calculus of the nervous system’, and the possibility of mechanical devices composing music, AI became a prospect only with the development of the digital computer. Alan Turing’s 1950 article ‘Computing Machinery and Intelligence’ was the ﬁrst serious philosophical investigation of the question ‘can machines think?’ In order to avoid the problem that a machine might be doing what might be regarded as thinking but in a very diﬀerent way from a human, Turing proposed that the question be replaced by the question as to whether machines could pass what is now known as the Turing Test. Turing proposed an ‘Imitation Game’, in which a judge would interact remotely with a human and a computer by typed questions and answers, and would decide which was the computer; if the judge could not reliably decide which was the computer, then the machine passed the test, as Turing believed that digital computers would be able to do. Turing’s article also proposed for the ﬁrst time how a machine might learn, and noted a series of objections to the idea of AI which are still raised today. The term ‘artiﬁcia
===
--- Chunk 308 ---
posed for the ﬁrst time how a machine might learn, and noted a series of objections to the idea of AI which are still raised today. The term ‘artiﬁcial intelligence’ is aĴributed to John McCarthy (1927–2011) and appears in a proposal for a workshop at Dartmouth College, in which ‘the artiﬁcial intelligence problem is taken to be that of making a machine behave in ways that would be called intelligent if a human were so behaving’ (McCarthy et al., 1955). The workshop, held in 1956, established the topic as a ﬁeld for realistic academic study (Nilsson, 2012). A fundamental insight was provided by another founder of AI, Marvin Minsky (1927–2016), who argued that intelligence was not the result of a single sophisticated agent or principle but, rather, the result of the interaction of many simple processes (Minsky, 1987). This suggested that AI might be achieved by the combination of relatively simple programs. The ﬁrst approaches to practical AI were centred on aĴempting to capture in a logic-based program the knowledge and reasoning processes of a human expert: a doctor diagnosing disease, or a chemist interpreting analytical data or planning the synthesis of new compounds. This symbolic approach to AI, now sometimes referred to as Good Old Fashioned AI (GOFAI), had some successes, but proved to be limited by the diﬃculty of entering the large amounts of knowledge, particularly general ‘common sense’ knowledge, required for even seemingly simple tasks. A newer generation, or ‘se
===
--- Chunk 309 ---
ng the large amounts of knowledge, particularly general ‘common sense’ knowledge, required for even seemingly simple tasks. A newer generation, or ‘second wave’, of AI systems relies on programs which enable machines to learn for themselves, given very large datasets and massive computing power. (Big Data is not necessarily a sine qua non for AI; Floridi (2019) notes that in some cases small datasets of high quality may be more valuable.) For example, in 2011, IBM’s Watson AI program beat a human champion at the game Jeopardy, which requires general knowledge questions, including puns, jokes and cultural references, to be solved quickly, without access to any external resources. Watson’s success was due to massive computing power using probabilistic reasoning, plus extensive resources, such as the whole of Wikipedia and many other reference works, held in computer memory. In 2017 the program AlphaZero was given only the rules of chess as a starting point, and trained its neural networks by playing against itself many millions of times. Within hours it was at a level to compete with the best chess programs. This ‘brute force’ approach has led to greater success, but at the cost that it may be impossible to understand how and why the system is working; as Turing foresaw, machines may be ‘thinking’ but they do it diﬀerently. In particular, we should not aĴribute any element of ‘understanding’ to an AI because it can equal, or beĴer, human performance at tasks which would require
===
--- Chunk 310 ---
ticular, we should not aĴribute any element of ‘understanding’ to an AI because it can equal, or beĴer, human performance at tasks which would require a human to understand a situation. At the core of most modern AI systems is machine learning, a way of programming computers to learn from experience, using large sets of data for training (Alpaydin, 2016). This comes in three forms: supervised learning, in which the algorithms are given large sets of labelled examples; unsupervised learning, in which the algorithms discover paĴerns de novo in sets of unlabelled data; and reinforcement learning, in which the system receives feedback as to whether the change it made was good or bad. This approach encompasses the neural net data structure, a complex linkage of many simple processing units and evolutionary or genetic algorithms, which allows programs to develop themselves to improve their performance. So- called deep learning uses a neural net with many layers by which machines train themselves to perform tasks (Kelleher, 2019). This can lead to very high performance, at the cost of creating models of such complexity that it may be diﬃcult to understand why the artiﬁcial agent is making its judgements. All machine-learning systems face such problems of explanation, and also problems of algorithmic bias if the original data is incorrect or biased in any way. Although somewhat displaced by machine learning and statistical algorithms, research continues on knowledge representation, u
