Methods for studying information behaviour We will consider information research methods in Chapter 18, but we should note here that a wide variety of research approaches and methods have been used to investigate information behaviour (Case and Given, 2016, part 4; Greifeneder, 2014). In summary, we can say that surveys of one kind or another have been the most common method, but methods have included questionnaires; telephone and web surveys; interviews, focus groups and Delphi studies; observation; diaries, logs, audio journals and photo diaries; HCI methods, such as eye-tracking; think-aloud; ethnography and phenomenography, critical success factors, critical incidents and vigneĴes; web log analysis; content and discourse analysis; conceptual and thematic analysis; systematic reviews and meta- synthesis of the literature. At the most detailed, and reductionist, level, neuroscience methods have been applied to investigate the brain function correlates of information behaviour (Sharot and Sunstein, 2020). In general terms, there has been a move away from largely quantitative survey methods, almost universal in the ﬁrst decades of ‘user studies’, and to greater use of in-depth qualitative techniques as interest has moved towards investigating information behaviour and practices in wider contexts. The focus has similarly chan
===
--- Chunk 399 ---
qualitative techniques as interest has moved towards investigating information behaviour and practices in wider contexts. The focus has similarly changed. Initial studies were generally carried out from a systems perspective, investigating which systems and services were used, by whom and to what extent, with limited consideration of the purpose or success of their use. Later studies considered the information behaviour of individuals from a cognitive viewpoint, while a primarily social viewpoint followed, including detailed consideration of information in the wider context of the life and work of groups and communities. Interest has also been focused on collaborative and sharing information behaviours (du Preez, 2018; Ford, 2015, chapter 5; Hertzum and Hansen, 2019), on liminal or transition behaviours as people change status and roles (Willson, 2019) and on broadening the concept of information behaviour to include ‘non-users’ and those who avoid or ignore information (Manheim, 2014; Case and Given, 2016, 117–19). There has been a recognition of the link between information behaviour and information literacy, even that they are ‘two sides of the same coin’ (Limberg and Sundin, 2006). An understanding of the former can provide guidance for promoting the laĴer. Information behaviour concepts Information behaviour itself has been a contested concept. Firstly, there is the grammatical objection that information cannot behave, so the correct term should be ‘information-related b
===
--- Chunk 400 ---
 a contested concept. Firstly, there is the grammatical objection that information cannot behave, so the correct term should be ‘information-related behaviour’. Though this is correct, the grammatically dubious term is ubiquitous, so we use it here. Secondly, and more substantially, ‘behaviour’ has connotations  of  the  discredited  psychological  concept  of behaviourism and could be taken to be limited to observable, objective actions, which would greatly limit the scope of the idea. However, in general usage, behaviour is here taken to include cognitive behaviour: needs, opinions, motives, knowledge and so on, and that is the sense in which we use the term. Thirdly, it has been suggested that the correct term should be ‘human information behaviour’ (HIB), as distinct from the information behaviour of animals, extra-terrestrials, machines, etc. This point is reasonable, since it is well established that many animal species have mechanisms for conveying rich information (Stegmann, 2013), and it has been suggested that the behaviour of complex algorithms should be studied by anthropological methods (Rahwan et al., 2019). The best deﬁnition would perhaps encompass the information behaviour of any inforgs, that is, any entities in the infosphere which can generate, gather and use information. That is the sense in which we will use the term, recognising that, to date, studies are largely limited to humans. Information behaviour, originally understood as limited to interaction w

Information behaviour, originally understood as limited to interaction with formal information sources and systems, is now deﬁned more broadly as, for example, ‘the many ways in which human beings interact with information, in particular the ways in which people seek and utilize information’ (Bates, 2010, 2381) and as ‘the totality of human behavior in relation to sources and channels of information, including both active and passive information seeking and information use. Thus, it includes face-to-face communication with others, as well as the passive reception of information as in, for example, watching TV advertisements, without any intention to act on the information given’ (Wilson, 2000, 49). Some commentators, for example Case (2006), have warned against too wide a broadening of scope, as otherwise there may nothing in the information sciences which could not be called information behaviour. Nonetheless, the continuing trend is a broadening of the scope of the concept and related ideas (Savolainen, 2007). Information practice is a term increasingly used alongside information behaviour. The diﬀerence is one of emphasis and perspective, the behaviour perspective coming from a psychological background, while the practice perspective comes from sociology (Savolainen, 2007; Wilson et al., 2009). The former reﬂects a cognitive viewpoint: what individual people think and know, what information needs

The laĴer reﬂects a socio-cognitive and constructivist viewpoint: how information activities are embedded in the wider social practices of the group, and particularly in the cultural factors aﬀecting information sharing, the repeated actions characteristic of a particular community (Orlikowski, 2002). Information practices will therefore be aligned with the ideas of domain analysis, also a socio- cognitive approach (Fry, 2006). The concept of information experience or document experience focuses on the subjective experience of an individual’s engagement with information, perhaps in the form of documents, with the aim of giving a holistic understanding of how individuals deal with information as part of their experience of the world (Bruce et al., 2014; Gorichanaz, 2019; Savolainen, 2020). Theories and models of information behaviour There has been a proliferation of theories and models in the information behaviour area, much more so than in any other aspect of information science. A compilation from the early 21st century listed 75 (Fisher, Erdelez and McKechnie, 2005), and more have been added since. Many have been adopted from other disciplines, such as psychology and sociology, but an increasing proportion have been devised within information science. Only a few have had wide usage, and aĴempts to combine them have been limited (Savolainen, 2016b). They are, in the terms discussed in Chapter 4, theories for description and explanation, mainly listing the concepts involved and showing their interrelations, oĞen in the form of simple conceptual diagrams of process ﬂow charts. Descriptive models Descriptive models list the factors and activities involved in the aspects of information behaviour being considered; they may be presented graphically or just as a list. The earliest of these was a diagrammatic representation of a very general information communication model, showing relations between users and information resources, mediated by technology and tools, due to Tom Wilson (1981). Wilson, a British information science professor who spent most of his career at Sheﬃeld University, has been an innovator in the study of information behaviour, developing a series of inﬂuential models (Bawden, 2006; Wilson, 2016), and was instrumental in establishing the series of ‘Information Seeking in Context’ (ISIC) international conferences. Ellis’s behavioural model is an inﬂuential example of this kind (Ellis, 1989; Ellis, Cox and Hall, 1993). The model does not deﬁne the interrelations between the features, nor the order in which they are carried out; that is determined for each situation. This is one of the most tested of all information behaviour models, having been used with studies of groups including scientists and engineers, lawyers, web users and social science researchers, and its features having been embedded in a model for slow information behaviour (Poirier and Robinson, 2014). Individual diﬀerences and information styles It has long been recognised that information users, even with the same subject interests and same education level, cannot be treated as a homogeneous mass. There are individual diﬀerences, shown in individual information styles (Line, 1998). However, there is no agreed method for determining such styles reliably. Several of the models and frameworks mentioned above focus on the individual information user, their actions, thoughts and motivations. An interesting extension of this is to try to determine, and label or categorise, an individual’s typical paĴern of information behaviour, which we might call their ‘information style’ (Bawden and Robinson, 2011). Much of the work in this area has analysed the relation between personality factors or thinking styles, and interaction with information systems, such as search engines or e- journals. There have been fewer examples of studies of individual diﬀerences of wider information behaviour; O’Brien, Dickinson and Askin (2017) give a review of research between 2000 and 2015. An early, and typical, example is a study of scientists working at an agricultural research organisation (Palmer, 1991). --- Chunk 415 ---
oups: non- seekers, for whom information access was not a priority; lone, wide rangers, preferring to work alone, reading and scanning widely and relying on serendipitous information discovery; unseĴled, self- conscious seekers, concerned about missing important information; conﬁdent collectors, amassing their own information collections, rather than routinely searching for information; and hunters, with regular information-gathering routines and a focus on currently relevant information. A more recent example examined the behaviour of hospital patients in respect of information about their treatment; grounded theory analysis of observation and interview data showed ﬁve groups: avoiders; receivers, who accepted information but did not actively seek it; askers, who sought information only from their care providers; seekers, who looked for information for various sources; and veriﬁers, who checked information from multiple sources (Costello and Veinot, 2019). Subjective categorisations of this kind may spark insights, and there are a number in the literature; however, they are rarely consistent, and their objective validity may be doubted. A more systematic approach is to try to determine information behaviour by some kind of survey and then to compare the results with personality as assessed by some psychometric test. An example is the work of Jannica Heinström (2003; 2005), who assessed three paĴerns of information behaviour – fast surﬁng, broad scanning and deep diving – whi
===
--- Chunk 416 ---
is the work of Jannica Heinström (2003; 2005), who assessed three paĴerns of information behaviour – fast surﬁng, broad scanning and deep diving – which were related to personality factors and learning style. For example, the fast surﬁng behaviour – associated with a rapid search for a few highly relevant documents, ideally supporting already formed viewpoints – was related to neuroticism, to cautiousness (low openness to experience) and to carelessness (low conscientiousness), as well as to a typically superﬁcial and non- strategic approach to study. These ideas led to identiﬁcation of ﬁve ‘information aĴitudes’, linked to personality traits, and resulting in typical paĴerns of information behaviour: invitational; exploring; purposeful; passive; and avoiding (Heinström, 2010). Summary Information behaviour has been systematically studied for over 50 years, using a wide variety of research methods, initially largely quantitative (typically surveys) but now largely qualitative (typically interviews and ethnographic observation). Initially, interest was focused on information retrieval, using formal library and • • • information systems, but interest has broadened to the wider information seeking or gathering, and to the inclusion of all aspects of dealing with information, including creation, sharing and avoidance. There are many, arguably too many, qualitative theories and conceptual models dealing with information behaviour, but few have been widely applied in research or pr
===
--- Chunk 417 ---
, arguably too many, qualitative theories and conceptual models dealing with information behaviour, but few have been widely applied in research or practice. A few general principles are understood. Choice of sources is determined largely by least eﬀort, familiarity and convenience, and the seeking process by the principle of satisﬁcing, geĴing what is good enough (Connaway, Dickey and Radford, 2011; Warwick et al., 2009; Prabha et al., 2007) and geĴing it ‘just-in-time’ (Miller et al., 2021) – arguably, following Zipf’s Principle of Least Eﬀort. Information behaviour has mainly been studied within groups deﬁned by occupation and academic subject, though there has recently been interest in ‘everyday life’ information behaviour, including ‘serious leisure’ information practices. Information behaviour is oĞen subtle and diﬃcult to interpret, and there is an interest in considering individuals’ information style. Information behaviour has been studied for many years, using an increasingly wide range of methods. There are numerous conceptual models and qualitative theories accounting for diﬀerent aspects and contexts of information behaviour, but few general principles. Information behaviour is determined primarily by domain and task, but is also aﬀected by individual diﬀerences. Key readings Case, D. O. and Given, L. M. Information chains and lifecycles The idea of a communication chain, or information chain, or information lifecycle of recorded information is fundamental for the information sciences, and it is also commonly invoked in explanations of information and digital literacies. Such a chain describes the processes of documentation from creation, through dissemination, organisation, storage and use to disposal. They have been applied to information and data, and to journal articles, books, archival records and other forms of document. Communicating information typically falls within ‘dissemination’ or similar steps, but is obviously dependent upon other stages. There have been many variants of chains and lifecycles used over the years to explain the nature of information dissemination in particular, and the changes in it brought about by technological and ot

cles used over the years to explain the nature of information dissemination in particular, and the changes in it brought about by technological and other factors (Duﬀ, 1997; Robinson, 2009; Cox and Tam, 2018; Wing, 2019; Yakel, Faniel and Maiorana, 2019). However, the general processes within the chain remain invariant; information resources must be created by someone, disseminated in some way, etc. The communication chain conceptual model, of which a typical example is shown in Figure 13.1, is therefore a simple but eﬀective way of categorising and understanding changes in the information landscape. Figure 13.1  The information communication chain Borgman (2019) suggests that, in the case of data, linear models imply a single sequence of stages from creation to use to end of usefulness, with the implication that the data can be recreated if needed subsequently, while cyclical models imply the possibility of reuse, and are more applicable for data that may be diﬃcult to recreate, and keep their value indeﬁnitely, such as astronomical observations. This laĴer implies the active processes of data stewardship and data curation (also referred to as digital curation), which may include elements such as migration between storage media (Oliver and Harvey, 2016; Higgins, 2018). This is a considerable contrast to the original, rather static and linear information chain of printed documents, which typically took the form of: • • • • • • Figure 13.2  The data curation lifecycle (Data Curation Centre, CC BY) creation (author) reviewing and editing (publisher) printing, warehousing, and distribution providing access (booksellers, libraries) conservation and preservation discarding or archiving. Each step in the chain necessarily followed its predecessor, and each was carried out by the appropriate professional group. This kind of simple chain has been considerably subverted by the digital transition. Some stages, such as printing, warehousing and distribution, have been essentially eliminated. Others may be carried out by the same people: an author of a professional or academic article can now prepare a manuscript, edit it into a suitable form and deposit it, with suitable metadata, in a repository such as arXiv or Humanities Commons. The whole chain is completed by one person, needing only the repository infrastructure to be in place, and access to digital authoring tools. Outside the academic/professional context, the same can be achieved by amateurs; the communication chain has become much more widely accessible. One consequence is that the information disciplines are now taking more of an interest in the creation stage of the chain, previously considered to be the province of the domain expert, the journalist, and the creative writer. As examples of information- centred studies of the creation stage, see Gorichanaz (2018), Lee, Ocepek and Makri (2021) and Multas and Hirvonen (2021). Cox and Tam (2018) have analysed and compared a number of lifecycle models for research data, information and knowledge, pointing out that they necessarily over-simplify a complex process and that other metaphors and models may be helpful in capturing the richness of the ways in which research data and information are created, processed, used, and reused. Other forms of document may have simpler lifecycles; organisational records, for example, are likely to have a relatively clear and predictable cycle. On the whole, despite their limitations, chains and cycles are helpful models for understanding the disruptive eﬀects of the digital transition as we move to new infrastructures for the infosphere. The new information infrastructures, and the documents whose communication they facilitate, are digital, mobile, pervasive, immersive, and social. We now outline some of them, distinguishing the communication of data, particularly research data, from the communication of knowledge through publishing in its broadest sense, including the communication of news. There are overlaps between these categories, for instance the relatively recent development of data journalism, whereby methods for analysing and visualising data are used to create news stories (Bounegru and Gray, 2021). This is an example of the way in which distinctions between the communication of types of information and of documents are breaking down in the digital environment. In turn, this is an aspect of what Floridi (2017) terms digital’s cleaving power, the ability to couple and recouple, to separate and recombine, information and documents in varied ways. Communicating data One of the major new roles for information science which has developed since 2000 has been the curation and stewardship of data and datasets. Data is discussed at several points in this book, and here we focus on issues in the communication of data. In the past, it was common for data not to be included in publications; at best it might be noted as being available from the authors on request. However, it is now regarded as good practice to make all data be made available at the time of publication, and this is increasingly required by funders of research and by regulatory bodies. This has required a change in publishing practices, particularly in the scientiﬁc literature. Data may most obviously be published in a traditional way, as a part of a document such as a journal article, or as ancillary data deposited with a document or deposited in a data repository operated by a publisher for all their journal titles. However, this is not always required and many published scientiﬁc studies do not present the data supporting their ﬁndings (Miyakawa, 2020). There are an increasing number of data journals, devoted to the publication and promotion of datasets (Candela et al., 2015; Kim, 2020). Alternatively, datasets may be deposited in an institutional repository or in a subject repository; the laĴer may be formally constituted and funded, or may be an informal community resource run by researchers themselves. In order that data may be communicated it must ﬁrst be collected or created, and then actively curated, in the ways encapsulated in data lifecycles noted earlier. Borgman (2019) makes the point that keeping digital data compilations accessible and usable over time requires active management, such as checking its continued validity, and migrating it as necessary between formats, soĞware versions, and storage media; the ‘benign neglect’ which allows paper documents to remain viable indeﬁnitely in appropriate storage conditions does

Metadata and data description standards are of obvious importance if datasets are to be combined and reused eﬀectively, but are oĞen lacking (Yakel, Faniel and Maiorana, 2019). An inﬂuential set of guidelines is the FAIR (Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse) guiding principles for scientiﬁc data stewardship and publication, but adherence to these is variable in scientiﬁc publications (Wilkinson et al., 2016; Wiley, 2020). There are particular issues in the way data and datasets are cited so that they can be subsequently accessed (Yoon et al., 2021). Communicating knowledge For several centuries, the dissemination of knowledge in the form of wriĴen documents has been the responsibility of the publishing industry. To an extent it still is, although the digital transition has made it possible for authors, and other actors in the communication chain such as libraries, to undertake activities which have heretofore been the sole remit of publishers. This has led to suggestions that a publishing industry, at least as it has been known, is no longer needed. However, publishing, although much changed, is still an important element of the information environment. For a forthright defence of the publisher’s role, particularly for academic publishing, see the blog post enumerating 96 things that publishe
===
--- Chunk 438 ---
ronment. For a forthright defence of the publisher’s role, particularly for academic publishing, see the blog post enumerating 96 things that publishers do (Anderson, 2016). It is conventional to regard publishing in distinct sectors: academic or scholarly, publishing materials for research, scholarship and tertiary education; educational, publishing materials for primary and secondary education; and trade, publishing all other materials. In some presentations, educational publishing is subsumed under trade; academic or scholarly publishing is always distinct. News, both newspapers and broadcast media, are generally treated separately. There is debate as to whether operators of social media platforms should be regarded as publishers. Hitherto they have not been viewed in this way, despite the fact that they are the main source of news and general information for many people; if they were treated as publishers, it would have consequences for the way their content is regulated. It is beyond our scope to deal with publishing and the publishing industry in any detail; rather, we will focus on aspects directly aﬀecting the changing information chain and the work of the information professional. For a comprehensive overview of all aspects and sectors of publishing, see Phillips and Bhaskar (2019), and for a scholarly analysis of economic pressures and technological changes to publishing and bookselling practices which have endured for centuries, see Thompson (2012). For overviews of the publishing of books, journals and magazines, see respectively Clark and Phillips (2019), Cope and Phillips (2014) and Das, Stam and Blake (2021). The communication of news has changed dramatically, with newspapers largely migrating to digital forms and broadcast media being supplemented, and to a degree supplanted, by niche digital sources and by social media. News is increasingly created with the aid of data, algorithms and social media. One casualty has been the newspaper libraries and archives which previously supported the fact-checking whose importance has since been rediscovered by the more responsible news media. This large topic is beyond our scope; for perspectives, see Brock (2013), Lamble (2016), Diakopoulos (2019) and Marconi (2020). We will focus on four aspects of the changes being brought about in publishing and information dissemination by digital technologies and economic and social factors: the changing nature of published documents; changing models of publishing; open access; and quality and ethical issues. The changing nature of published documents The nature of published documents has changed and continues to change in several respects. Most obviously there is a wider range of document types: to the traditional range of printed documents including books, journals and magazines, reports of various kinds
===
--- Chunk 440 ---

Most of these are informal and ephemeral, rather than formally published, overlapping with the older idea of informal grey literature. A proportion are more substantial and permanent documents, with identiﬁers such as DOIs, the digital equivalent of the traditional ISBN identiﬁer for single documents, and ISSN identiﬁer for serials, such as journals and magazines (Swoger, 2013). Furthermore, even straightforward digital equivalents of printed documents may come in multiple formats: web page, tablet such as Kindle or iPad variants and mobile versions for use on smartphones. Nor are the changes simple replacements of printed products by digital equivalents. There are only a few examples of such direct replacement: frequently updated reference tools, such as telephone directories and technical product brochures are such. Even for forms which are generally believed to have ‘gone digital’, such as academic journals, some still oﬀer a printed version. Also, many of the digital materials are a kind of meta to a main document; journal articles, for example, aĴract social media mentions of the kind captured in the Altmetric doughnut (Zheng et al., 2019; Holmberg et al., 2020). In the digital environment they may be updated and edited at will, so that the stability of a published document is a management choice rather than a technical necessity. The digital realm allows greatly enhanced extension of documents into the infosphere, building on the much more limited facilities of the world of print. Images in printed documents can now be augmented by embedded media, leading to fully multimedia documents. The references and footnotes of the printed document are now hyperlinked, so that new virtual documents can be created by combining material from various sources. Immersive experiences, previously provided by the suspension of belief produced by good writing, are now becoming available through augmented and virtual reality, and the unreality of the multisensory digital document (Robinson, 2015). With the removal of the costs and storage problems associated with printed journals, there is arguably no longer the same necessity for journal editors to restrict what is published by consideration of how ‘interesting’ or ‘original’ it is, or how closely it matches a journal’s subject orientation. Other suggestions have included publication before peer review, with articles subsequently reviewed, amended and feedback incorporated, and selected articles recommended for particular audiences; see, for example, Stern and O’Shea (2019). Such ideas have, as yet, been tried out only on a small scale; see, for example, Thelwall et al. (2020) and Tennant et al. (2021). Finally, the digital transition is amplifying the trend towards ‘bitesize’ rather than ‘long form’ reading; see, for example, Tenopir et al. (2015). The tendency, stemming from information overload even in the days of print, to rely on an abstract rather than an article, or a review rather than a book, is ampliﬁed by technologies which provide what are eﬀectively new document substitutes. An increasing proportion of web searches are completed without the user ever leaving the search engine, relying on the document ‘snippets’ provided in the results; for example, Google’s presentation of brief sections of a Wikipedia entry. Models of publishing Models of publishing are changing drastically – both the economic aspects and issues of how, and by whom, publishing is done. With documents in digital form, many of the former costs of publishing, printing, warehousing and transporting of printed items disappear. Even for printed books, digital soĞware and printing reduce costs, and remove the cost reductions of large print runs. Short print runs of niche titles, print-on-demand and self-publishing all become economically feasible. The traditional purchasing by libraries of individual journals has been largely replaced by journal ‘bundles’ or ‘Big Deals’, by which a publisher supplies a collection of journals; for a critical analysis, see Crawford (2014). This has not stopped continuing controversy over the increasing cost of journals, the so- called ‘journals crisis’, particularly when pricing is less transparent in the new environment and when many journals included in bundles may never be used (Mongeon et al., 2021). There has been a trend towards libraries aĴempting to reduce costs by ‘unbundling’ and returning to ordering individual titles (Ivanov, Johnson and Cassady, 2020). It should be said that the end of the academic journal has been predicted for some time, now that articles are typically found by using search engines on the web or on publishers’ journal bundles, rather than by seeking material in a particular journal. Nonetheless, it does mark a decoupling of article and journal, emphasising the increasing irrelevance of the journal issue and volume in the digital environment. It has been suggested that journals may cease to exist in the future, or may exist simply as collections of material of a particular kind. The popularity within some disciplines of the use of repositories, such as arXiv for the physical sciences, where articles may be deposited ahead of, or instead of, journal publication also suggests that journals might lose their importance. This does not seem to be the case, for the moment at least, and journals are retaining their place as a marker of quality and signiﬁcance of publication within disciplines and specialisms, albeit sometimes with enhanced functionality and new models of publication; see, for example, Herman et al. Open access Open access (OA) in its various forms has caused some disruption to publishing, though not as much (at least as yet) as was envisaged by its early proponents. Largely limited to academic journals, it has led to a mixed environment: subscription journals, typically purchased by libraries; hybrid journals for which a subscription is charged but authors may pay extra to have an article made OA; fully OA journals funded by author payments; and fully OA journals free to authors, produced by volunteer eﬀort and institutional support. There are other OA solutions: through the deposit of articles in institutional repositories, typically operated by university libraries, and in subject repositories, such as arXiv and Humanities Commons; through deposit in commercial repositories, such as Academia.edu and Researchgate; and through unethical, and arguably illegal, sites such as SciHub. For reviews of the complex and developing OA environment, see Suber (2012), Eve and Gray (2020) and Pinﬁeld et al. (2021). AĴempts have been made to systematise this complexity by denoting various forms of OA by various colour indicators, following the initial proposal of the Budapest Open Access Initiative (BOAI) in 2002: green: a version of an article in a subscription journal is self- archived in a repository • • • • gold: an article is pub
===
--- Chunk 446 ---
 Initiative (BOAI) in 2002: green: a version of an article in a subscription journal is self- archived in a repository • • • • gold: an article is published OA, in a fully OA or hybrid journal, with payment by authors or other parties bronze: articles may be read freely on a publisher’s web page, but may not be reused platinum or diamond: articles are free to use without payment by either subscriber or author black: articles are provided freely through unauthorised, and possibly illegal, copying. Though helpful to an extent, this colour designation is not applied consistently and does not cover all possibilities. The BOAI also made a distinction, still in use, between gratis OA, in which an article may be read freely by an individual, and libre OA, by which an article may be read freely and also reused in various ways, including by modifying and text mining. Another example of OA is an extension of self-publishing, which has been made much more feasible by digital media. This is community or crowdsourced publishing, to produce wiki resources of all kinds, of which Wikipedia is the best known and has had most impact. Usually without an association with any formal publisher, these sources vary greatly in their activity, quality and reach, but they provide an important form of published material unknown before use of the web became widespread. Quality and ethical issues These issues have always been a concern in publishing, with a desire to ensure, so far as possible, that what is published is correct and that plagiarism, wrong aĴribution, etc. are avoided. Publishers of all kinds have developed processes to deal with these problems, which are felt most acutely in the publication of scientiﬁc research and medical material. The digital transition, on the one hand, makes it easy to identify and to correct problems and on the other hand, introduces new versions of such problems. Two methods traditionally used by publishers to ensure that quality is maintained are peer review and the facility for retraction and correction. Peer review involves the reading and checking of submiĴed material by independent experts. For journal publication, it is usual for all articles to be peer reviewed before publication. For books, at least a synopsis and sample chapter would be peer reviewed, and in some cases the whole text of a book. Peer review may be blind, where authors and reviewers do not know each other’s identity, or open, where they do. Although universally applied, the process is not without its problems. On the one hand, there are examples of serious errors escaping detection by the reviewers and being published; on the other hand, there are examples of innovative and original work being denied publication by overly conservative reviewers. The digital environment allows new ways of peer reviewing, for example 
===
--- Chunk 448 ---
e and original work being denied publication by overly conservative reviewers. The digital environment allows new ways of peer reviewing, for example post-publication review, whereby the article is published and comments are made subsequently by reviewers for incorporation into a revised version. Digital tools can also assist reviewers by, for example, checking for plagiarism of previously published material. There is also a new need for ways of checking and validating computational research, which is becoming common in many disciplines (Willis and Stodden, 2020). For reviews of the peer review process and the ways it is changing, see Horbach and Hoﬀman (2018) and Tennant et al. (2021). The ease of publishing academic journals in digital form has led to the emergence of so-called predatory journals, which promise rapid OA publication for a fee, and with seemingly liĴle review or quality control. This is a controversial issue, since there are some rapid- publication OA journals with perfectly credible review and quality processes. It has also been suggested that it is wrong to label any journal as ‘predatory’, since they may oﬀer a valuable publication route for some authors, especially those from the developing world or who are not associated with an institution. Retraction of published papers found to be in serious error, and correction of those where less serious errors have been identiﬁed, has always been possible. Digital documents can easily be deleted or amended, making quality control easier but, at the same time, causing concern about the stability of the published record. Human aĴitudes have not caught up with technology in this respect; many authors still view a notiﬁcation of an error in a published document, and even more so a retraction, as so undesirable that they will seek to avoid it by whatever means they can. For analysis and discussion, see Vuong (2020) and Ajiferuke and Adekannbi (2020). The digital environment also enables publication fraud, by providing algorithmic means to generate fake datasets and images and even, to an extent, text; an example of large-scale fraudulent publication of this kind is given by Bilk (2020). These problems are likely to increase in the future, as AI makes production of credible fake publishable content much easier, through systems such as GPT- 3, which automatically produce text appearing to have been wriĴen by a person (Floridi and ChiriaĴi, 2020). So far, the ethical issues discussed have been to do with formal publication of books and journals. There are also considerable issues with less formal publication and with social media, largely to do with the detection and removal of false information, fake news and the like; for a perspective on the public role of social media companies and how they may be ethically regulated, see Floridi (2021). The content moderation of social media has itself been called into question as involving the use of low-paid workers, spending many hours each day dealing with the most unpleasant of materials (Roberts, 2019). Information places and spaces The digital transition has caused an existential crisis for the ‘information places’ of our society. This includes both those which existed to supply information-bearing documents – libraries, information centres, reading rooms, archives and record centres – and also, to a lesser extent, those which dealt with other forms of document – galleries, museums, etc. When documents beg

chives and record centres – and also, to a lesser extent, those which dealt with other forms of document – galleries, museums, etc. When documents began to exist to a considerable extent in digital form, there was not the same need for a physical place where such documents might be stored and accessed. What, then, was the future for the information places? The COVID-19 pandemic of 2020–21 focused minds on these issues, as many libraries and other information institutions had to close their physical spaces and pivot to a largely digital service. One early response was to speak of a hybrid library, involving two essentially separate parts, the physical and the digital. While this was a reasonable initial response, it was never going to be stable in the longer term and we can now see that it does not reﬂect, or accommodate, the onlife merging of the physical and the digital. Another, less sensible, early response was to reduce or even eliminate the physical space of information institutions, on the grounds that if information is digital there is no need for an information  place.  Related  to  this,  and  perhaps  more understandable, has been the move to merge information spaces with other activities of an institution. Some university libraries, for example, have merged their space with general IT provision, or with spaces for individual and group learning activities. Some local government authorities have merged their public library spaces with those oﬀering more general advice and transactions. While these responses may be understandable, and viable in the short term, they avoid the main question: what is the future for the information place, and where does it ﬁt into the onlife infrastructure? One of the eﬀects of digital’s cleaving power is to decouple location and presence; in the example given by Floridi (2017) one may be physically located in a coﬀee shop but interactively present in a social media site. Information institutions need to consider how to address both the location and the presence of their users, and to consider to what extent they should try to replicate the information experience of the situation when location and presence are synonymous. One valid response is that there will always be a need for some physical places to hold physical documents. Archives, library collections of old and rare books, museums and galleries will all continue to exist; and experience has shown that the printed book is retaining its appeal to a much greater extent than advocates of e- books originally believed. For this reason alone, there will be a need for the physical information place, with a physical collection, for the foreseeable future, however much it may be complemented by digital resources. The question is how to develop an onlife presence, so that the physical and digital naturally overlap rather than compete. It is highly unlikely that any single way to redesign information places and spaces will be eﬀective in meeting the needs of the new environment. Rather, as Shannon MaĴern (2014) points out, there needs to be an understanding of how developing physical, technical • and social infrastructures and architectures of information interact, and how they ﬁt into the information infrastructures of society. Of course, the discussion above relates to formal or oﬃcial information seĴings. There are many and varied unoﬃcial seĴings for information provision and exchange – sometimes termed information grounds – from bus queues to coﬀee shops and from doctors’ waiting rooms to oﬃce kitchens. These are also information spaces, albeit unplanned and unregulated, and the information activities which take place there are also likely to be aﬀected by the move to onlife. Summary The communication of information, in all the forms discussed here, is undergoing profound change. In some ways, this is not yet fully evident. While some changes have been clear and deﬁnite – the move of academic journals to digital formats and the disappearance of formerly ubiquitous 
===
--- Chunk 454 ---
ident. While some changes have been clear and deﬁnite – the move of academic journals to digital formats and the disappearance of formerly ubiquitous resources, such as the printed telephone directory – the rate of change elsewhere has been slow. Printed books are still very much with us, OA has not driven publishers out of business and many initiatives, such as the new forms of peer review, remain small scale and experimental. It would be a mistake, nonetheless, to minimise the magnitude of the change that is occurring as information communication takes on new forms in the emerging infosphere and new information infrastructures emerge. Information chains and lifecycles are useful, simple models for understanding the nature of information communication and the ways in which it is changing. • • • The move to onlife and the infosphere is changing the ways in which all forms of information and knowledge, data and news, are communicated. The nature of the new infrastructures that will be needed is not yet clear. New ethical problems, and new solutions, are emerging, especially in scientiͅc and medical publishing. William Cowper, The Winter Walk at Noon, Book 6 of The Task (1785) Introduction Information management and policy is a multifaceted concept and can be understood in diﬀerent ways. Sometimes it is understood as a wide and all-embracing concept including records management, knowledge management, library management and so on, and sometimes with a much narrower focus. It ranges in scope from personal through institutional to national and international. It may or may not be taken to include general management processes of budgeting, managing people, etc. There is a close relation with IT management, since the great majority of information management (IM) uses digital systems; and a similarly close relation with the legal and regulatory framework for proper information use, the area of information governance. Information management: fundamentals and models There are no widely accepted general models for information management (IM), although aĴempts have been made towards developing such models (Macevičiūtė and Thivant, 2019). There are a variety of conceptual models, generally taking the form of block or process diagrams, which have had considerable inﬂuence on practice. Some show the relation between data, information, knowledge and similar entities; for example, the data–information– knowledge–wisdom hierarchy, Popper’s concept of Worlds 2 (personal, subjective knowledge) and 3 (objective, communicable knowledge) and Floridi’s Philosophy of Information; others relate to the value of information. Fundamental to IM is the idea that information and data, and the documents in which they are carried, have a chain or lifecycle of clearly deﬁned stages. Use of such models is termed a process orientation, since it involves analysis of the various processes of the lifecycle. There are a variety of such models, and they will vary in detail according to their context and will change in detail with a changing information environment; the
===
--- Chunk 465 ---
variety of such models, and they will vary in detail according to their context and will change in detail with a changing information environment; they are examined further in Chapter 13. Information management also assumes that information may be regarded, to some extent, as a resource; hence the term information resource management, which emphasises this aspect. This assumes that information resources may be identiﬁed, counted and their cost, use (actual and potential) and value assessed. Information, considered as a resource, has some unusual and indeed paradoxical qualities. Information has multiple and unpredictable lifecycles, so that its use and value does not change with time in a regular manner; it is ‘diﬀusive’, tending to leak from any system of control, and the more it leaks the more there is; it is sharable, not exchangeable, it can be given away and retained at the same time; its value is subjective, depending upon its context and intended use by particular persons on particular occasions; and, rather than being a static entity, it is a dynamic force. For more discussion of these issues, see Eaton and Bawden (1991), Yates-Mercer and Bawden (2002) and Budd (2011). Although the objective value of information may be diﬃcult to determine, any approach to IM must make some aĴempt to do so, or there will be liĴle rationality behind management decisions. It is also assumed that it is possible to add value to information, by appropriate process. An inﬂuential model for 
===
--- Chunk 466 ---
lity behind management decisions. It is also assumed that it is possible to add value to information, by appropriate process. An inﬂuential model for understanding value- added processes in information lifecycles was introduced by Robert Taylor (1986); see Foster and Clough (2018) and Macevičiūtė and Thivant (2019) for recent adaptions. It provides a framework within which value-adding processes – such as classifying and relating, evaluating and interpreting, presenting options, and making choices – are carried out within information systems of all kinds. Information management is, to a large degree, a maĴer of enabling these processes to occur in an eﬃcient manner. Information management is usually regarded as an organisational issue, but there is a well-established concept of personal information management (PIM) (WhiĴaker, 2011; Hajibayova, 2019; Feng and Agosto, 2019). It is of relevance here because eﬀective organisational IM relies on a knowledge of the personal information practices of the individuals it serves, and can also support good PIM in its users. Data management Involving the management of structured datasets, this is usually taken to encompass database systems, data modelling, metadata, data quality and security issues and the maintenance of data warehouses, archives and repositories; see, for example, Gordon (2013). The management of large datasets has provided a new role for library and information specialists (Buckland, 2011; Cox et al., 2020) and has given rise to the new specialism of research data management  (RDM)  (Cox  and  Verbaan,  2018).  Before  this development, however, data management was seen as lying on the boundaries between LIS and computer science and information systems, and perhaps more naturally belonging to the laĴer. This led to a split, with documents and data typically being managed through diﬀerent processes and with diﬀerent systems. In some sectors, however, information services have a long involvement with data management, the pharmaceutical industry being an evident example (Bawden and Robinson, 2010). The split between data management and other forms of IM may be expected to diminish or disappear in the near future, particularly as technologies close the rather artiﬁcial gap between the handling of data and of information. The processes of data management, data curation and data stewardship, and the data lifecycle, are discussed in Chapter 13. Memory institutions’ information management Items in collections of museums, galleries, and other heritage institutions may be regarded as documents in their own right. The processes involved have usually been described as museum documentation, as exempliﬁed by the work of the UK Museum Documentation Association, founded in 1977. A particular issue is the need for specialised vocabularies for describing this kind of material. Archives and records management These aspects of IM are oĞen treated together, although their emphasis is rather diﬀerent. Records management deals with relatively modern documents created within an organisation for its own purposes and with their use, storage and disposal. Archival management deals with the selection and care of documents to be stored for a long period, typically for legal or historical purposes. For overviews, see Yeo (2018) and Shepherd (2017); for records management, see Franks (2018) and Oliver and Foscarini (2020) and for archive management see Millar (2017) and Hunter (2020). For reﬂection on the signiﬁcance and future of archives, see the volumes edited by Thomas et al. (2017) and by Brown (2018). Management of records and archives typically happens within an organisation, whether governmental, commercial, educational or non-proﬁt. At national level, national archives may be said to keep the national memory and may also act as a source of expertise for records and archive management. Documents are regarded as records when they are created or acquired by an organisation as part of a business process, so that their existence provides evidence of the fact that the process took place. Most records are created internally, b

Most records are created internally, but incoming messages and other documents, if they are used as part of a business process, are also records. They are distinguished from reference material, other documents which are used by the business but which do not qualify as records according to the above understanding. These are not kept with the records collection. Records management A record therefore has two main purposes. While it is active it supports the business process for which it was created or acquired; later it serves as a memory of the past with respect to that process. In some cases this laĴer function is so important that the record is kept indeﬁnitely; this is the function of archives. Records management is usually understood to be the systematic and consistent control of records throughout their lifetime, as speciﬁed in international standards (ISO 2016; 2020). More than most other kinds of document, records have a distinct and predictable lifecycle, encompassing the stages from creation or acquisition to circulation, use, storage and ﬁnal destruction or preservation. It is usual to categorise records in three stages over their lifetime: active records are those which are in use, needed for the purposes of the organisation; semi-active records are those which are no longer in use but which must be retained and kept accessible for a deﬁned period of time; 
===
--- Chunk 473 ---
he organisation; semi-active records are those which are no longer in use but which must be retained and kept accessible for a deﬁned period of time; inactive records are those which are no longer required, and need not be kept. When a record becomes inactive, the decision is made to destroy it or to preserve it. Those records which are preserved permanently – for historical, cultural or reference purposes – become archival records and are dealt with by the methods of archive management. The basic processes of records management are therefore: categorisation, organisation and indexing of records; storage of records appropriately, so that they are secure and can be retrieved when needed; providing access to records; retaining records for so long as they are needed and then destroying them or sending them for archival preservation. The processes of archive management are similar, except that the last of the four points becomes: retaining archival records indeﬁnitely or until archive policy with respect to particular records changes. Records rarely if ever occur singly, and the basic unit to be managed is the record series, a collection of records of similar nature. This may in turn be divided into ﬁles, usually the unit which is stored and retrieved, and within ﬁles are individual documents. An issue of particular importance in records and archives management is that of provenance; by whom was the record created or acquired, and in what context. This will determine how it is treated. The principle of original order states that records should be maintained in the order in which they were ﬁrst created and arranged. Archival management relies on the idea of fonds, or archive groups: the whole set of records, in whatever form or medium, created, collected or used by a person, family or organisation, which should be kept together. Both physical and digital records are generally arranged according to a ﬁle plan or ﬁle classiﬁcation, based on the functions and processes within the organisation which the records support and reﬂect. Accompanying the ﬁle plan is the retention schedule, which speciﬁes the lifecycle of each record series, in particular, how long it is to be kept at each stage and how it is ﬁnally to be disposed of, i.e. destroyed or archived. This is usually accompanied by a records retention authority, a formal policy document which speciﬁes the retention schedule and the reasons for it. Secure preservation of records is of obvious importance, since their loss can cause the failure of the business on which they rely. Knowledge management The idea of knowledge management (KM) originated in the 1980s and came into prominence in the 1990s as a widely promoted business concept, enabling the capturing and sharing of the ‘know how’ of individuals within an organisation; Koenig and Neveroski (2010) give an account of its origins. It is associated with organisational learning and knowledge mobilisation. Guidelines and requirements have been encapsulated in an international standard (ISO, 2018). It is, in essence, the management of ‘tacit knowledge’, the subjective knowledge in people’s heads which it may be diﬃcult to explain to others and which is oĞen not recorded in documents. This is sometimes categorised as personal, rather than propositional, knowledge: ‘knowing how’ rather than ‘knowing that’. It is the kind of knowledge gained by experience rather than by reading and formal ed
===
--- Chunk 476 ---
positional, knowledge: ‘knowing how’ rather than ‘knowing that’. It is the kind of knowledge gained by experience rather than by reading and formal education. It is what Popper would claim belongs to his ‘World 2’, although KM theorists usually prefer to refer back to Michael Polanyi’s (1962) theory of knowledge (mentioned in Chapter 3) encapsulated in his dictum ‘we may know more than we can tell’; see Day (2005) and Baumard (2010) for the signiﬁcance of Polanyi’s views for KM. The ‘bridging epistemologies’ idea of Cook and Brown (1999) has also been inﬂuential. There are usually three elements to a KM programme, though one oĞen predominates, according to context: content, the type of knowledge to be shared, and the way in which it is represented; technology, the means by which it is shared; culture, promoting the sharing of knowledge. Two main approaches have been adopted. One, seeing KM as an extension of conventional IM, focuses on creating ‘know-how databases’, to which members of an organisation contribute their knowledge. This shares many of the functions of IM, such as knowledge resource audits by analogy with the information audit. The second, considering that personal and tacit knowledge, by its nature, cannot be captured in this objective way, focuses on puĴing people in touch with one another and enabling discussion through tools such as indexes of expertise or corporate yellow pages. Popular methods are the community of practice, a group of practitioners who come together informally to share knowledge and experience, and formats for encouraging learning and knowledge exchange, such as knowledge cafés. KM has generated a large literature of its own; for recent texts, see Dalkir and Beaulieu (2018), Hislop, Bosua and Helms (2018), Massingham (2019) and Milton and Lambe (2019). For an integrated treatment of information and knowledge management, see Schopﬂin and Walsh (2019) and for examples of KM in a variety of organisations, see Collison, Corney and Eng (2019). This is, of course, largely focused on Western concepts of knowledge: the indigenous knowledge of the developing world may take very diﬀerent forms. Nonetheless, there has been concern for using ideas of KM to capture and preserve such knowledge and ensure that it is made, and remains, accessible; see Lwoga (2011) and Maina (2012). Business intelligence and environment scanning Rather than a form of IM, these are distinct activities which are oĞen associated with IM and KM (Macevičiūtė and Thivant, 2019). Business  intelligence  is  somewhat  broader  than  the competitor/competitive intelligence (CI) activity, from which it has grown. An information service may be asked to undertake this work, or its results may be integrated with an IM or KM service. Environmental scanning is the acquisition, organisation and dissemination of information about events, issues and trends in an organisation’s external environment, used to help plan the organisation’s future course of action. It may be closely related to knowledge management and other information functions (Holland, 2015). Collection management This involves the management of materials in a variety of collection institutions or memory institutions, including information centres, libraries, repositories, archives, record centres, museums and galleries. These collections will oĞen comprise digital or printed documents, but may also include items such as historical artefacts, art works, botanical, anatomical or geological specimens, etc.; such items will have documentation associated with them, as well as being documents in their own right. There is a continuing debate as to whether collections are the deﬁning and central feature of such institutions or whether equal or

n their own right. There is a continuing debate as to whether collections are the deﬁning and central feature of such institutions or whether equal or greater priority should be accorded to services, communication and knowledge creation; see, for example, Given and McTavish (2010) and Lankes (2016). Regardless of this, collection management remains central to information institutions. Collection management comprises ‘all the activities involved in building and managing . . . collections in all formats and genres, both locally held and remotely accessed’ (Johnson, 2018, 1). A distinction may be made between collection development, the building of a collection, and collection management, its ongoing maintenance. Four fundamental questions underlie all collection development and management processes: what purpose/s does the collection serve; for whom is the collection being maintained; what type of resources or items will be collected; and how best can the collection be organised? The processes of collection management will diﬀer in nature and emphasis according to the context, but usually include: selection, acquisition and processing of material so that it is integrated into the collection; preservation and provision of access; assessment of the quality and adequacy of the collection and evaluation of its use; and weeding and disposal. Changes in the environment have aﬀected collection management most in the areas of selection and acquisition. Selection is greatly aﬀected by the wider range of documents, media and formats available. This is not merely a maĴer of e-books and e-journals complementing or replacing their printed equivalents, but of entirely new document forms being eligible for collection; examples are art documentation (Engel and Wharton, 2017), and e-mail archives (Dinneen and Krtalić, 2020). It is also inﬂuenced by the ready availability of data from digital access systems, allowing patron- driven, demand-driven or data-driven selection, amounting to essentially the same thing, the semi-automated selection of materials in high demand (Blume, 2019). The social justice movement, a change in the ethical environment far wider than the information sector alone, has led to initiatives to decolonise the collection; this aﬀects not merely what is selected and weeded but how it is presented and described; see, for example, Blume and Roylance (2020). and Roylance (2020). The digital transition has moved the acquisitions process towards licensing for access rather than purchase for ownership. This has created a complex and specialised area of IM; see, for example, ‘Vendor relations, negotiations, and contracts’, chapter 5 of Johnson (2018). Other changes have included the controversial ‘big deal’ or ‘journal bundle’ subscription model and the similar use of ‘aggregators’ (Strieb and Blixtud, 2014), a greater interest in collaborative and co-operative collection development (Levenson and Nichols Hess, 2020), electronic legal deposit (Gooding and Terras, 2020) and the impact of OA resources, which have had an uncertain relation with institutional collections (Ball, Stone and Thompson, 2021). Information governance Information governance is an umbrella concept, of relatively recent origin, referring to the sets of policies, processes, standards and guidance on good practice which are applied within an organisation to ensure that all stages of the information lifecycle are managed correctly. They ensure that the organisation observes all relevant laws and regulations, avoids risk and uses its information in a way which is eﬀective, while being legally and ethically correct (Maclennan, 2014; Saﬀady, 2017; Smallwood, 2019). Information governance and IM are closely connected. The move to a digital information environment, with its consequences for beĴer use and, equally, more misuse of information, has pointed up the need for eﬀ
===
--- Chunk 482 ---
ove to a digital information environment, with its consequences for beĴer use and, equally, more misuse of information, has pointed up the need for eﬀective governance. Floridi (2018) denotes digital governance as involving policies, procedures and standards for the proper development, use and management of the infosphere; it is distinct from regulation and ethical behaviour, though it overlaps and complements both. The concept of information governance is interpreted diﬀerently according to the organisation’s context. Usually there is a focus on the legal framework for IM; legislation on maĴers like data protection, freedom of information, privacy, copyright, intellectual property and so on, together with any sector-speciﬁc regulations or issues aﬀecting the way information is managed. In health services, for example, information governance is particularly concerned with safeguarding information about patients and ensuring that it is used to best eﬀect in planning treatment. Correct dealing with information oĞen involves a formal assessment of the quality of procedures; the information governance concept largely subsumes concerns which were previously expressed as quality control and application of standards in IM; see Brooks (2019) for the role of records management principles in information governance and Haynes (2018) for the applications of metadata in IM and information governance. Information risk is a concept closely related to information governance, stemming from th
===
--- Chunk 483 ---
e applications of metadata in IM and information governance. Information risk is a concept closely related to information governance, stemming from the realisation that information problems can become serious business problems, can result in ﬁnancial penalties and other sanctions and can – in extreme cases – threaten the survival of a commercial organisation or the credibility and ability to function of a government department. These typically arise from the release of information which should remain conﬁdential, or from the loss of vital information (Saﬀady, 2020). Information policies and strategies Policies and strategies, plans and objectives, mission and visions form the framework, albeit one with a very inconsistent use of terminology, for IM; for overviews from diﬀerent perspectives, see Orna (2004), Cornelius (2010) and Evans and Greenwell (2020, chapter 7). Information policies may be applied at widely diﬀerent levels: from a small department or function within an organisation to a large organisation, a grouping of organisations within the public or private sector (e.g. ‘UK higher education’), a region, a nation, a grouping of nations or even the whole world. Organisations began formally to state information policies in the 1980s, coinciding with the widespread adoption of what were then termed ‘new ICTs’ (information and communication technologies). Governments had begun to state national information policies in the previous decade, though elements of what would lat

nd communication technologies). Governments had begun to state national information policies in the previous decade, though elements of what would later be termed information policy can be traced back to at least the start of the 20th century. All countries have de facto some information policy provision, but only a minority have a clear and fully explicit statement of such; the UK has never had one. National policies tend to focus ﬁrst on technological infrastructures, second on skills (oĞen in a rather limited ‘computer literacy’ context) and third on the legal framework, covering copyright, access rights, etc. See Hernon and Relyea (2017) for an account of the historical development of information policy in the United States and Rabina and Johnson (2017) for a similar account for the European Union. At the outset of any policy statement there may be an explicit statement of mission. This is a summary of what the information service is and does, from which everything else can be derived. Mission statements are typically very brief and are oĞen accompanied by a statement of vision: where the service would like to be and what it aspires to. The next level down is the policy, or set of purposes or principles. An information policy is usually a tool for developing information strategies. User needs analysis and information audit For eﬀective IM it is necessary that the needs of the users of an information service are understood and that these are mapped against a full knowledge of the information resources available to meet them. These are the 
===
--- Chunk 487 ---
ormation service are understood and that these are mapped against a full knowledge of the information resources available to meet them. These are the processes of user needs analysis and of information auditing and mapping, respectively. Information needs may be those of an individual, a team, an organisation or a profession. They may be expressed explicitly (what I want to know is . . .) or implicitly (I’m a doctor [so obviously I need to know . . .]). Without a clear understanding of the needs of the users of a service, it is impossible to rationally plan the service’s activities or to evaluate its eﬀectiveness. Information needs analysis is treated in detail by Dorner, Gorman and Calvert (2015). There has been debate about the diﬀerence, if any, between information needs, information demands and information wants. Case and Given (2016) discuss the idea of information need, and its complications and the various deﬁnitions and models derived to explain it, and Ruthven (2019) gives a detailed analysis of various levels of information need. A number of frameworks have been devised for information needs analysis. One long-standing and inﬂuential example, originally due to Nicholas (2000), examines the required information by a series of characteristics: subject; function; nature; level; viewpoint; quantity; quality/authority; date/currency; speed of delivery; spatial coverage; and processing/packaging. An example of a use of this framework is a study of users of a music library

One of the criteria of a resource of any kind is that it may be audited within an organisation; the ﬁnancial audit is most familiar, but other forms of audit are common. Information resources can be audited, and the information audit is a staple tool of IM. At its simplest, an information audit may be a listing, as complete as possible, of the information resources available, with a note of who is responsible for maintaining them. Their cost will also usually be included. More ambitious audits will aĴempt to establish the use and value of the resources and the eﬀectiveness with which information is brought into the organisation and communicated within it. Details and examples of information audits are given by Orna (2004), Buchanan and Gibb (2007; 2008) and Frost and Choo (2017). A variety of methods may be used, including examination of documents and systems, observations, interviews, focus groups and questionnaires and measures of user satisfaction and impact. Information mapping or information ﬂow modelling is a form of information audit which focuses on information ﬂows within an organisation and identiﬁes where information is missing or diﬃcult to access. Valuing information and evaluating information services The demonstration of value and impact of information services is an integral part of IM and information governance (Goulding, 2020; Streatﬁeld, Markless and Paley, 2020). A variety of quantitative and qualitative measures may be used; these will be most eﬀective if they are tied in with key performance indicators, comparable across institutions, and with quality standards. For overviews of these issues see Hernon, Altman and Dugan (2015), Appleton (2017), MaĴhews (2017) and Moss and Thomas (2019); an extensive bibliography is given by Poll (2018). The value of information While the value of information can be simply stated to be the amount that someone would pay to have the information at a particular time, for example to make a decision, there is no generally applicable way to assign a reliable monetary value to information, although the question has been extensively analysed over a long period; see, for example, Braman (2006), Leppãlā (2015) and Stehr and Adolf (2016). This applies to speciﬁc pieces of information, such as facts provided in answer to a reference query or documents retrieved from a database, to collection
===
--- Chunk 490 ---
 applies to speciﬁc pieces of information, such as facts provided in answer to a reference query or documents retrieved from a database, to collections of information and to the totality of an information service. This is due to what Koenig and Manzari (2010, 4305) identiﬁed as the ‘elastic and amorphous nature of information and information services and the diﬃculty of quantifying them and in turn measuring their impact’. Although the cost of providing a particular item or collection of information can be known accurately, its value will depend upon the circumstances of its use and their consequences, which cannot usually be known in advance. Furthermore, it is diﬃcult to determine exactly what results may be said to be due to some particular information being available. This has led in some cases to the abandonment of any aĴempt to provide a quantitative value for information, and reliance on an assessment of the information’s correctness, completeness and relevance to an organisation’s purpose or on asserting a broad, qualitative educational or moral value. Value may also be associated with the use of information, or its ﬁtness for use, and assessed by the extent and adequacy of processes which increase its potential value to a user. This was ﬁrst put forward systematically in Taylor’s well- known ‘value-added’ model (Taylor, 1986), which may be updated in the new networked information environment (Foster and Clough, 2018). Alternatively, some surrogate measure may be used
===
--- Chunk 491 ---
 1986), which may be updated in the new networked information environment (Foster and Clough, 2018). Alternatively, some surrogate measure may be used, such as time saved, which may be related to cost or to expressed user satisfaction. These approaches, however, are not fully convincing, and ways of assessing numerical and cost values are constantly being sought, without resorting to simplistic counting of what is easy to count: ‘social value is all about geĴing the big picture – do not limit the estimate only to the easier ﬁnancial estimates . . . the emphasis is on social value, and the big picture of how local library services contribute to the outcomes of importance to their employing organisations’ (Urquhart, 2020, 3). Reviews of the ways in which library and information services have aĴempted to show return on investment in ﬁnancial terms are given by Aabø (2009), Madden et al. (2016), Urquhart and Turner (2016) and Urquhart (2020). An approach increasingly widely adopted is the idea of contingent valuation, which takes the view that the value of information is what someone would be willing to pay for it, and surveying users as to what they perceive as the value to them for services provided. These methods have been used increasingly widely, as can be seen by examples from various library sectors – national (Pung, Clarke and PaĴen, 2004), academic (Kingma and McClure, 2015), public (Stejskal, Hájek and Rehák, 2019) and special (SaĴerley and Woelhaf, 2020) – and archives
===
