nd PaĴen, 2004), academic (Kingma and McClure, 2015), public (Stejskal, Hájek and Rehák, 2019) and special (SaĴerley and Woelhaf, 2020) – and archives (Moss and Thomas, 2019). Despite some acknowledged shortcomings, contingent valuation methods seem to be among the most acceptable means at present of evaluating the cost-beneﬁt of information services. Away from the library sector, there has been a movement towards treating information more generally as a quantiﬁable asset in • • • monetary terms, for example in company accounts; as an example, see Cummins and Bawden (2010). Eﬀectiveness and impact Evaluation of the eﬀectiveness of information provision is an intrinsic part of IM. There is a long history of such evaluation; see Lancaster (1993) for an inﬂuential summary of practice in earlier years, Rapp (2008) for an account of early evaluations at the US National Library of Medicine, a leader in this area, and Tenopir (2012), Urquhart and Turner (2016), MaĴhews (2017) and Urquhart (2018) for surveys of more recent practice. All evaluations must ‘measure’ something, either by quantitative or qualitative assessment or by a hybrid approach. A useful six-way typology of what may be measured, originally suggested by the American library science professor Wilfred Lancaster, is as follows: Cost: measures what a service costs to provide, a collection to purchase, etc. This can usually be known with accuracy, and replacement costs can be assessed by standard ﬁnancial techniques. It w
===
--- Chunk 493 ---
e, a collection to purchase, etc. This can usually be known with accuracy, and replacement costs can be assessed by standard ﬁnancial techniques. It will be included in an information audit. Eﬀectiveness: shows how well the system is working, compared to what it is expected to do. It may oĞen be measured quantitatively, using, for example, performance metrics or expressed user satisfaction. Beneﬁt: implies a knowledge of the ‘true’ value of a system or service and is notoriously diﬃcult to measure. It is usually approached by qualitative or semi-qualitative measures. • • • Cost-eﬀectiveness: aĴempts to relate the measured eﬀectiveness of a system or service with its known costs. Usually this approach is used on an isolated component of a total information service, and usually in a comparison between two alternatives, e.g. whether to subscribe to information from provider A or B, or whether to outsource some function. Cost-beneﬁt: aĴempts to relate the cost of providing a service to its ‘real’ beneﬁts, through methods such as impact studies and contingent valuation. Cost-performance-beneﬁt: aims at the investigation of the whole set of relationships between the costs, performance and beneﬁts of an information service. Few convincing studies of this type have been carried out. Performance metrics These metrics give quantitative measures of eﬀectiveness, which allow comparison within one information service over time, or between information services if standard sets of performan
===
--- Chunk 494 ---
asures of eﬀectiveness, which allow comparison within one information service over time, or between information services if standard sets of performance indicators are used. An international standard lists indicators meant for various types of library (ISO, 2014a), while another lists indicators speciﬁcally for the national library sector (ISO, 2019). Many national sets of indicators have also been created in past years, though there is an increasing tendency to rely on the international standards. For a detailed discussion of information performance metrics, see Appleton (2017). These indicators are quantitative measures of service eﬀectiveness, such as: number of loans; occupancy of seats in reading rooms; number of accesses to e-resources; availability of required items; speed of retrieval from closed stacks; cost per loan; and rate of satisfactorily answered reference requests. They have the advantage that they should be available from a library’s management information with a minimum of extra work. Drawbacks are that they are oriented towards traditional paper-based library and information services and that they can give liĴle qualitative insight into the reasons for the adequacy or otherwise of the service. User satisfaction, in a necessarily rather limited quantitative fashion, is oĞen included in such metrics. In some sectors, particularly academic libraries, a standard format for assessing this factor is used for comparability. The SERVQUAL protocol, a standard service industry instrument, has been widely used for this purpose, as has LibQUAL+, a protocol derived from SERVQUAL, speciﬁcally devised for assessing user satisfaction in library and information services. In some cases, performance metrics for information services have been explicitly linked with external quality measures, for example the NSS (National Student Survey) or PTES (Postgraduate Taught Experience Survey) student satisfaction measures in the case of UK university libraries. They have also been incorporated into general quality management approaches such as the ‘balanced scorecard’, value scorecard and Holbrook’s value typology (Urquhart, 2015; 2018; Urquhart and Tbaishat, 2016), and into mathematical modelling techniques such as structural equation modelling (Gómez-Cruz, Harari-Betancourt and Vergara-Mendoza, 2020). Impact analysis Impact studies are particularly desirable for service evaluation, since they aim to show the actual impacts made on the users of information services by the information prov
===
--- Chunk 496 ---
icularly desirable for service evaluation, since they aim to show the actual impacts made on the users of information services by the information provided, and on the business of the organisation of which the services are a part; see Streatﬁeld and Markless (2012) for an overview of the issues. In an academic library, for example, we might want to show that use of the library and information services results in students geĴing beĴer grades in assessments, fewer students dropping out, researchers obtaining more grants, lecturers writing more papers, and so on. In a healthcare seĴing we would like to show that information services result in fewer patient deaths, faster recovery, less hospital-acquired infection, etc. In a commercial context we might look for more innovations, and products geĴing to market more quickly. This issue is addressed by two international standards, ISO 16439 for methods for assessing the impact of libraries in general (ISO, 2014b) and ISO 21248 for national libraries (ISO, 2019). ISO 16439 is analysed by Creaser (2017) and de Jager (2017). This standard notes that ‘impact’ may be a variety of outcomes, including improved skills or competencies, changes in aĴitudes or behaviours, greater academic or career success, improved well-being, and social inclusion. Impact may be negative as well as positive, including demotivating people from using an information service. Impact may be: immediate (for example, a student ﬁnding a reference for an assignment) or 
===
--- Chunk 497 ---
ding demotivating people from using an information service. Impact may be: immediate (for example, a student ﬁnding a reference for an assignment) or long term (for example, an improvement in overall information literacy); limited (such as small improvement in a skill) or far-reaching (even changing someone’s life). The population who may be impacted ranges from individual users, through institutions such as universities, to the whole of a society. ISO 16439 recommends three general ways of gaining evidence for impact: inferred (statistics and performance indicators); solicited (user surveys looking speciﬁcally at impact); and observation (direct or via diaries, weblog analysis, etc.). This style of evaluation has been practised most commonly in the health information sector; see, for example, Ayre et al. (2018). For an example of the development of a comprehensive approach to evaluation of quality, value and impact in the public library sector, see Reid (2020). This balance is not always successfully achieved . . . Charles Oppenheim, Adrienne Muir and Naomi Korn (2020, xv) Introduction In this chapter we examine the law and ethics of information. This is a broad topic and we can give only an overview with some relevant examples. In particular, the sections on information law are not in any way intended to provide legal advice. Examples are largely chosen from UK law as of 2021 and may not be relevant at other times, or in other jurisdictions. Ethical issues for speciﬁc aspects of information science are dealt with in the appropriate chapters. The chapter is organised into four sections. The fourth section examines the legal and ethical aspects of two topics, privacy and artiﬁcial intelligence, to illustrate general principles with speciﬁc examples. The legal and ethical context In discussing information law and information ethics we must be aware that there are several related but disti
===
--- Chunk 517 ---
examples. The legal and ethical context In discussing information law and information ethics we must be aware that there are several related but distinct factors. Law, ethics, regulation, standards and good practice, and governance all aﬀect the right handling of information. The distinction between them maĴers, in deciding what is done, how, and by whom. All of these factors, and their interrelations, have been greatly aﬀected by the move to a digital information environment. Law is a set of formal, codiﬁed rules of behaviour imposed on individuals and organisations through social institutions, and enforced by states through legislation. It is applicable within a jurisdiction, either within a nation-state or internationally, through legislation. Ethics is a system of morals or rules of behaviour, objective and codiﬁed, accepted by a social group. Ethics help to determine right behaviour in those cases where there is no law to say what to do, or when it may be justiﬁable to go against the law. Ethics shapes regulation and governance by allowing a consideration of what is socially acceptable or preferable, regardless of what is mandated by law. Floridi (2018) helpfully distinguishes between hard ethics, which come before legislation is in place and shape changes in the law, and soĞ ethics, which apply aĞer the law has been observed, because the law cannot stipulate what is the best thing to do in all cases. Regulation, rules applicable to speciﬁc issues and contexts, derives i
===
--- Chunk 518 ---
ed, because the law cannot stipulate what is the best thing to do in all cases. Regulation, rules applicable to speciﬁc issues and contexts, derives its coercive force from law and is associated with speciﬁc legislation. Compliance with regulation generally requires extensive record keeping, and hence has special relevance for information professionals, and also implications for privacy. Standards and codes of good practice may be local, national or international, and may be institutional or industry wide. They are not generally enforced by law, and most are voluntary, though some may be incorporated into regulations. Information governance, as noted in Chapter 14, is a set of policies, processes, standards, and guidance on good practice which are applied within an organisation to ensure that information is managed correctly, including adherence to all relevant laws and regulations. While there is clearly a strong interrelation between these processes, as Floridi (2018) emphasises (see Figure 15.1), governance, ethics and regulation, while complementary, must be clearly distinguished. This takes us well into the realm of information politics and the governing of the information society, as discussed in Chapter 16. Information law The law is complex, and ensuring adherence to it is a task for the specialist, in the information context as much as in any other. In this section we will give an overview of information law from a lay perspective; for more detailed coverage of these topics, see Oppenheim, Muir and Korn (2020) and Maguire (2018). Legislation can have a very considerable impact, for good or ill, on the development of the information environment. As Floridi (2018) points out, the wrong legislation may kill digital innovation entirely, or destroy whole technological sectors and developments, and simply reacting to technical innovations is a poor approach. There needs to be a proactive decision as to what kind of information environment is needed, and then the construction of legislation to enable it. There are three legal issues of particular importance to information science, because they are focused on data, information and documents: intellectual property, freedom of information and data protection. These will be considered ﬁrst, and then other laws relating to information provision and access will be considered. Intellectua
===
--- Chunk 520 ---
n and data protection. These will be considered ﬁrst, and then other laws relating to information provision and access will be considered. Intellectual property Intellectual property (IP) law is fundamental to the work of the information professions and is arguably the most important aspect of information law. It subsumes the laws of copyright, database rights, patents, design rights, trademarks, and trade secrets. For an overview with an international perspective, see Sinnreich (2019). All IP law is intended to strike a balance between the rights of creators to proﬁt from their creations, including moral rights to be recognised as the creators, and the rights of society to beneﬁt from them. Copyright is the right to prevent unauthorised copying of any work created by intellectual eﬀort, for a deﬁned time period; an analogous database right prevents unauthorised copying of substantial parts of a database. There are exceptions for fair dealing, i.e. allowing a reasonable extent of copying for speciﬁc appropriate purposes. There are problems with orphan works, where the copyright owner is unknown, and complexities due to new forms of licences allowing various degrees of openness of digital materials, most notably Creative Commons licences (Creative Commons, 2020). IP is governed by a variety of international treaties, conventions and directives, typically incorporated into national laws and regulations. IP is a controversial subject with considerable ethical implications, inclu
===
--- Chunk 521 ---
and directives, typically incorporated into national laws and regulations. IP is a controversial subject with considerable ethical implications, including for information professionals, because of the barriers it presents to accessing information, which may be aﬀected by cultural norms. It is a complex area for the practitioner, requiring a specialist understanding; see Padﬁeld (2019), Cornish (2019) and Oppenheim, Muir and Korn (2020, chapters 1 and 6) and, for a US perspective, Crews (2020). Freedom of information Freedom of information (FOI) may be taken to be part of the general movement toward openness of information, including OA, open data, open source and open science. However, FOI generally refers to speciﬁc legislation and regulations. It refers to an obligation placed on public bodies to provide information held by them, or about their activities, on request, with some exemptions. This was ﬁrst recognised as an integral part of a right of freedom of expression by the United Nations in 1946 (Resolution 59). Information professionals in public bodies may be required to provide information on their activities, and information specialists in • • • • • • • general may be well placed to promote and facilitate FOI. For more detail, see Gibbons (2019), Maguire (2018) and Oppenheim, Muir and Korn (2020, chapters 3 and 8). Data protection Data protection, based on a human right to private and family life, home and correspondence, is instantiated in laws and regulations gover
===
--- Chunk 522 ---
 protection Data protection, based on a human right to private and family life, home and correspondence, is instantiated in laws and regulations governing the collection, storage, processing and use of personal data of any kind; personal data being, loosely speaking, any data which may identify an individual. A well-known example is the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Such regulations give individuals the rights to access their data, to correct errors and, to an extent, to erasure, to a ‘right to be forgoĴen’. A set of basic principles apply to collection and processing of personal data: it must be fair, lawful and transparent the purpose must be speciﬁc, explicit and legitimate only the minimum data necessary for the purpose must be collected; it must be adequate, relevant and not excessive stored data must be accurate and kept up to date data must be kept for no longer than necessary security, integrity and conﬁdentiality of data must be maintained there must be responsibility and accountability, and proper records must be kept. Data protection issues aﬀect many contexts of information provision and information management, not merely where data is collected and managed as part of an IM function but also in library services, with respect to user details, borrowing records, browsing histories, etc., and in information research with human subjects. For more detail, see Maguire (2018) and Oppenheim, Muir and Korn (2020, chapters 2 and 8). Other legal maĴers 
===
--- Chunk 523 ---
formation research with human subjects. For more detail, see Maguire (2018) and Oppenheim, Muir and Korn (2020, chapters 2 and 8). Other legal maĴers may aﬀect information providers. Some jurisdictions, including several countries of continental Europe, have a ‘library law’, specifying library provision in detail. The UK has not such comprehensive legislation. Rather, it has a series of laws regarding such things as: the provision of a public library service by local authorities; copyright deposit, a duty on publishers to deposit a copy of everything published in the UK, including digital material, in major ‘copyright libraries’ (Gooding and Terras, 2020); and public lending right, which establishes a right for authors to be paid for the borrowing of their works from public libraries. UK legislation is far from consistent; notoriously, there is a legal requirement to provide a library in a prison, but not in a school. Libraries and other information institutions are also aﬀected by legislation on obscene materials, on prevention of crime and terrorism, on cybercrime and computer misuse, on defamation and libel (for which they may potentially be held responsible for resources which they provide) and on the reuse of government and public sector information. They are also strongly inﬂuenced by legislation on contracts and licences, particularly as the model of purchasing and owning printed materials moves to one of licensing digital resources (Oppenheim, Muir and Korn, 2020, cha
===
--- Chunk 524 ---
 particularly as the model of purchasing and owning printed materials moves to one of licensing digital resources (Oppenheim, Muir and Korn, 2020, chapter 7). Finally, like other institutions, they must comply with general legislation on maĴers such as human rights, equalities and health and safety. Information ethics Ethical issues arise in information research and practice when applicable laws and regulations do not give suﬃcient guidance. Some of the main areas of concern within information ethics include: censorship and intellectual freedom; privacy, conﬁdentiality and data protection; ownership of information, and commercial use of public information; balance in collections, and appropriate metadata; universal access, information poverty and the digital divide; respect for IP, combined with fair use; and issues of balance and bias in information provision, collection development and metadata creation. For a detailed review of principles and applications of information ethics, see Burgess and Knox (2019) and Graﬀ et al. (2020). Speciﬁc ethical issues for information organisation are discussed in Chapter 8, for publishing and social media in Chapter 13, for collection development in Chapter 14 and for information research in Chapter 18. We use the general term ‘information ethics’ here, though much of what follows might equally be denoted ‘data ethics’. The move to ‘dataﬁcation’ and to a ‘Big Data Society’ puts data collection, analysis and search at the heart of many of society’s activities, evoking a need for speciﬁc ethical consideration; for fuller discussion, see ZwiĴer (2014), Hand (2018) and Hasselbalch (2019). Floridi and Taddeo (2016) discuss data ethics as distinct from information ethics, and point out that the ethics of data, algorithms and practices are generally intertwined. Internet search engines are • also a source of ethical concern, due to biases in search and ranking algorithms, in autocomplete functions, etc. (Noble, 2018). While the ethical dilemmas of information science are oĞen dealt with pragmatically as they occur, a more structured and systematic way of deciding such questions is desirable. This is done by drawing either on one of a number of general ethical approaches or on a set of values or code of ethics speciﬁcally designed for the information sector. Types of ethical theory It is usually argued that there are four general types of ethical theory which may be useful. Blackburn (2021) sets them out succinctly, and Fallis (2007) gives examples of their application in information contexts. Existentialism, which emphasises individual freedom and responsibility for whatever we choose to do is sometimes mentioned as a ﬁĞh ethical theory, though one which oﬀers liĴle concrete guidance. The four main types of ethics are: Consequence-based theories: these focus on the outc
===
--- Chunk 526 ---
ethical theory, though one which oﬀers liĴle concrete guidance. The four main types of ethics are: Consequence-based theories: these focus on the outcome, rather than the action itself, arguing that the right action is that which brings about the best outcome for the greatest number. The best-known example is the philosophy of utilitarianism, as originally advocated by John Stuart Mill. This approach may be used in information ethics to argue, for example, that we should not censor potentially oﬀensive materials, even though we know that not doing so will cause distress to some people, since it will be of overall beneﬁt for them to be available. • • • Duty-based, deontological theories: these argue that there are certain ethical duties which must always be obeyed, regardless of their consequences, that there are some actions or values which are always inherently good or bad. These are justiﬁed by our moral intuition; the best-known example is Kant’s idea of the categorical imperative. In an information context we could, for example, argue that we always have a duty to provide full and correct information, which overrides any other consideration. This approach can be reactive to circumstances, giving guidance on what to do in a particular circumstance. Rights-based theories: these suggest that the correct thing to do in any situation is determined by the rights we assign to others. This approach was ﬁrst propounded by John Locke, and recently developed by John Rawls for the ri
===
--- Chunk 527 ---
tion is determined by the rights we assign to others. This approach was ﬁrst propounded by John Locke, and recently developed by John Rawls for the rights of members of society. This approach, which is the justiﬁcation for all human rights legislation, may be particularly useful for ‘code-based’ information ethics, since these are oĞen expressed as the rights which people have: to have access to information, to be treated respectfully and equally by information providers, to have privacy in their information dealings, and so on. Virtue-based theories: these suggest that the right thing to do in any situation is what a virtuous person would do; to live a good life is to become a particular kind of person. It is a proactive and constructionist approach; we can all aim to become beĴer people in all circumstances. These theories, which can be traced back to Aristotle and Confucius, ascribe to the virtuous person traits such as courage, calmness and friendliness, and a quest for a balance • • between excess and deﬁcit in all things. The recent approach of communitarianism is usually understood as a form of virtue ethics, focusing on the idea of the virtuous citizen as part of a strong and functioning community, oĞen associated with promotion of social justice, and hence arguably a particularly suitable approach for the information sciences (McMenemy, 2021). While all of these approaches have some value for the information context, none is a panacea and none is without problems in 
===
--- Chunk 528 ---
iences (McMenemy, 2021). While all of these approaches have some value for the information context, none is a panacea and none is without problems in application to speciﬁc cases. Perhaps the main value of such ethical theories is that they force us to be clear about how we approach speciﬁc ethical dilemmas and to be explicit about how we try to solve them. For an example of how the ethical approach taken may inﬂuence decisions about information provision in practice, see comparisons  of  consequentialist,  rights-based,  virtue,  and communitarian stances to the UK’s free public library service (McMenemy, 2020) and of consequentialist and deontological approaches to the ethics of recommender systems (Milano, Taddeo and Floridi, 2021). Regardless of the ethical system adopted, it must be used conscientiously. Floridi (2019) identiﬁes ﬁve types of ethical risks, all of which can be identiﬁed with respect to information ethics: ethics shopping: choosing ethical principles to justify existing behaviour ethics bluewashing: taking limited and superﬁcial steps to make practices seem more ethically sound than is the case • • • ethics lobbying: using an ethical stance as an argument against legislation or regulation ethics dumping: carrying out unethical activities in countries with a low level of legislation and regulation ethics shirking: avoiding ethical responsibilities when this can be done without consequences. ===
--- Chunk 529 ---
ing: avoiding ethical responsibilities when this can be done without consequences. A new form of information ethics? Some have argued that we need an entirely new form of ethics to deal with information issues, based on the centrality of information as a universal entity. This was ﬁrst suggested by Wiener (1954) and was put forward most fully by Floridi (2013) as a part of his Philosophy of Information. Such an information ethics focuses on information itself, rather than on any particular technologies, and on the idea that a person may use information as a resource, to generate other information as a product, which in turn may transform the informational environment as a target. Floridi argues that all things which exist should be regarded as ‘informational entities’: this certainly includes people, but also animals, plants, paintings, books, stars and stones. Information ethics is that set of principles which enable all information entities to ﬂourish; speciﬁcally, by minimising entropy. Floridi here uses entropy not in the sense of physical, thermodynamic entropy, nor in the sense in which the word is used in Shannon’s theory, but, rather, to mean any destruction or corruption of an informational entity. All entities have some informational value, but not all are equal. Those which contribute most to the well-being of the infosphere have most value, so that we • • • • may reasonably destroy bacteria which threaten human lives, even though the bacteria have informational va
===
--- Chunk 530 ---
osphere have most value, so that we • • • • may reasonably destroy bacteria which threaten human lives, even though the bacteria have informational value in themselves. Floridi derives four main principles of information ethics for the ‘infosphere’ – the universe understood in informational terms: entropy ought not to be caused entropy ought to be prevented entropy ought to be removed the ﬂourishing of informational entities as well as of the whole infosphere ought to be promoted by preserving, cultivating and enriching their well-being. This is an ambitious aĴempt to set up a whole system of ethics with information as its basic concept; not, as Floridi (2013) insists, to replace other ethical systems and principles, but to augment them; it is a ‘nonstandard’ form of ethics. It is related to duty-based ethics, inasmuch as it evaluates the duty of any rational being in terms of a contribution to the well-being and ﬂourishing of the infosphere, but is also related to virtue ethics, as it sees humans, as informational entities, as works in progress, continually seeking to develop ourselves. In Floridi’s scheme, documents have a particular value. He instances both the example of the Italian Library Association’s code, which includes a duty towards information and documents as well as to users and to the profession, and also UNESCO’s recognition that documents can have value in their own right (Floridi, 2013). It remains to be seen whether Floridian ethics will lead to a more cohe

An example of how this might be done is an analysis of the anti-counterfeiting trade agreement (ACTA) in terms of information ethics (Floridi, 2015). Professional values and principles In the speciﬁc context of the information sciences, one approach to ethical decision making is to rely on professional values as a guide. Michael Gorman (2000), for example, lists eight ‘enduring values’ of librarianship: stewardship service intellectual freedom rationalism literacy and learning equity of access to recorded knowledge and information privacy democracy. Rubin and Rubin (2020) set out seven values of LIS: service the importance of reading respect for the search for truth tolerance serving the public good justice • • • • • • cultural excellence. While such value lists may be valuable as a basis for discussion, they are – like the rather similar codes and guidelines mentioned above – of limited value in speciﬁc situations. A more concrete alternative is given by codes of conduct, a number of which have been produced for the information professions since the ﬁrst was introduced by the American Library Association in 1938. To help set the general principles in speciﬁc context, we now look in more detail at the legal and ethical implications for information science of one issue, privacy, and of one technology, AI. Ethics of informational privacy We [. . .] have a private life [and] hold it inﬁnitely the dearest of our possessions Virginia Woolf, Montaigne, in The Common Reader (1925) Privacy has been thought important for many years, as the quotation from Virginia Woolf illustrates, but has gained increased ethical signiﬁcance in a digital information environment, being denoted as ‘a central issue of the information age’ (Wu, Vitak and Zimmer, 2020, 485) and ‘one of the deﬁning issues of our hyperhistorical time’ (Floridi, 2014, 102). It is an issue of particular signiﬁcance for information science, for a number of reasons, including the need to protect the privacy of users of information services, and also more generally the privacy of anyone whose data may be stored and processed. Privacy is deﬁned by the Oxford English Dictionary (2007) as ‘The state or condition of being alone, undisturbed, or free form public aĴention, as a maĴer of choice or right; seclusion; freedom from interference or intrusion’. It has been described as a right to be let alone, or the right to be forgoĴen, and hence is generally treated in the context of rights-based ethics. Privacy is a deceptively simple idea who
===
--- Chunk 534 ---
let alone, or the right to be forgoĴen, and hence is generally treated in the context of rights-based ethics. Privacy is a deceptively simple idea whose nature seems obvious at ﬁrst sight, and the protection of privacy an obvious ethical good, but the issues become complex on investigation (Solove, 2008; Wacks, 2015; DeCew, 2018). It is usually believed, rightly, that privacy is increasingly under threat, due to digital collection and processing of personal information. We may distinguish between anonymity (information about someone has never been recorded) and obscurity (the information has been recorded, but it is too diﬃcult and time consuming to ﬁnd). Both anonymity and obscurity are easily removed in a digital information environment; hence the need for explicit ethical concerns for informational privacy. There have been numerous analyses of the nature of privacy and how it is changing in a digital age. There is something of a paradox here, in that there is an increasing concern about privacy in the digital realm at the same time as many people seem happy to make much of their life digitally public, particularly through social media and the more extreme phenomenon of ‘lifelogging’ (Mai, 2016; Gupta, Crane and Gurrin, 2020). Studies of the concept in a variety of  disciplines  have  produced  many  deﬁnitions,  concepts, frameworks, and models, some of which have clear relevance for information science; for reviews, see Mulligan, Koopman and Doty (2016), Bawden and Robins

for a digital environment. Floridi takes a diﬀerent perspective, seeing privacy as essentially informational, rather than informational privacy as merely of one type. In this view, because personal information plays a crucial constitutive role in who an individual is and who they may become, protection of privacy should be identiﬁed as protection of personal identity, and a breach of informational privacy as an aggression against personal identity and self-development. Defence of privacy should be based directly on the protection of human dignity, rather than on secondary considerations such as a right to property, to freedom of expression or to privacy per se. In this view, ‘my privacy’ is to be regarded as more like ‘my arm’ than ‘my bicycle’, and loss of privacy to be more akin to ‘kidnapping’ than ‘theĞ’. For Floridi’s conception of privacy, see Floridi (2005; 2006; 2016; 2017), and for commentary and discussion see Bawden and Robinson (2019; 2020). Privacy is usually taken to be an individual maĴer, but group privacy is now becoming regarded as equally important, particularly now that groups may be formed algorithmically from data analysis. Such groups need not conform to intuitively understood groupings, and their members will not be aware that they are being treated as belonging to a group which they did not ask to join, and with which they may not necessarily wish to be associated (Taylor, Floridi and van der Sloot, 2017; MiĴelstadt, 2017). There is also a concern for particular demographic groups, such as children (Stoilova, Nandagiri and Livingstone, 2021). Informational friction is an important concept in considering the ethics of privacy. Floridi (2005) argues that privacy itself is a function of informational, or ontological, frictions in the infosphere. An information friction is anything which interrupts the ﬂow of and access to information, including such diverse factors as noise, limited bandwidth, paywalls, copyright, language barriers, access rights, and data protection regulations. ICTs can both increase and decrease frictions, and can therefore both support and damage privacy. It is usually held that the task of information science is always to reduce such frictions and improve information ﬂow and access, but the more frictions are reduced, the more likely it is that privacy will be damaged. Control, not elimination, of frictions is the key to allowing the maximum information ﬂow and access, while maintaining a proper degree of privacy. This is likely to be achieved by a mix of legislation, regulation, codes of conduct for particular seĴings, and an ethical awareness of the right to privacy. These will vary according to the context. For example, some jurisdictions have speciﬁc laws related to privacy, while others do not; the UK, for example, has no speciﬁc privacy legislation, privacy issues usually being  addressed  by  data  protection  law.  Privacy  in library/information seĴings is usually dealt with by codes of practice rather than by law or regulation, with the exception of data protection legislation. The means for protecting privacy will also need adaption to changing technological capabilities, but ideally not in a purely reactive way, but based on clear and lasting ethical principles. While maintenance of privacy is certainly a maĴer for legislation and regulation, it is also important that individuals are aware of the issues and able to take steps to protect their own privacy. Privacy literacy has been suggested as a form of information and digital literacy (Wissinger, 2017). Legal and ethical implications of artiﬁcial intelligence Of all new digital technologies, AI has generated the most controversy  about  the  legal  and  ethical  aspects  of  its implementation. In part this is because of concerns, which would beĴer remain in the realm of ﬁction, about super-intelligences, singularities and killer robots. More realistically, it is because its reach and inﬂuence, and consequent ethical implications, are greater than those of other technologies. As Taddeo and Floridi (2018, 751) put it: [AI] is not just a new technology that requires regulation. It is a powerful force that is reshaping 
===
--- Chunk 539 ---
ogies. As Taddeo and Floridi (2018, 751) put it: [AI] is not just a new technology that requires regulation. It is a powerful force that is reshaping daily practices, personal and professional interactions, and environments. For the well-being of humanity, it is crucial that this power is used as a force of good. Ethics plays a key role in this process by ensuring that the regulations of AI harness its potential while mitigating its risks. Ethical  issues  arising  from  current  AI  systems  include: discrimination and inequalities, due to bias in the datasets from which AI systems learn interacting, and to unanticipated algorithmic judgements; an inability to understand, and hence correct, the behaviour of complex AI systems which are unable to ‘explain themselves’; the loss of privacy, due to extensive data collection and integration; surveillance, both directly through cameras with facial • • • recognition and indirectly through tracking of digital presence; potential job losses, due to the automation of intellectual as well as manual work; and the diﬃculty of assigning responsibility for harms arising from the action of intelligent agents. For overviews of these issues, see Bruneault and Laﬂamme (2020), Coeckelbergh (2020) and Dubber, Pasquale and Das (2020). Ethical issues with AI are oĞen complex and multilevel, and not amenable to simple analysis and solution; as an example, see a review of ethics of AI in healthcare which identiﬁed ethical issues arising on individua
===
--- Chunk 540 ---
menable to simple analysis and solution; as an example, see a review of ethics of AI in healthcare which identiﬁed ethical issues arising on individual, interpersonal, group, institutional and societal levels (Morley et al., 2020). A number of sets of principles have been put forward to ensure that AI is used in a socially beneﬁcial manner, sometimes described as Artiﬁcial Intelligence for Social Good, which may be aligned with the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (Floridi et al., 2020; Cowls et al., 2021). A framework of ﬁve core principles for ethical AI is presented by Floridi and Cowls (2019). The ﬁrst four principles are commonly used in bioethics, showing the value of foundational ethical ideas in this area; the ﬁĞh is developed for the AI context. The principles are: beneﬁcence: AI should be used to promote well-being, preserve dignity and sustain the planet non-maleﬁcence: AI should not do harm, for example by infringing privacy autonomy: a balance must be struck between how much autonomy is given to machines and how much is retained by humans • • justice: AI should be used to promote prosperity, preserve solidarity and avoid unfairness explicability: there should be clarity as to how any AI works and who is responsible for the way it works. There is inevitably a gap between such typically high-level statements of principle and practical guidance on incorporating ethical considerations in the design of systems. This problem may be overcome by the idea of

nts of principle and practical guidance on incorporating ethical considerations in the design of systems. This problem may be overcome by the idea of ‘ethics as a service’, including codes of practice, ethics advisory boards, ethics-based system audits and full documentation (Morley et al., 2021; Mōkander and Floridi, 2021). Following such recommendations, AI systems should become just another tool, to be used in a transparent, responsible and trusted way, as in the intended use of AI in public services by the cities of Amsterdam and Helsinki (Floridi, 2020b). Summary The new digital information environment has raised a host of new issues requiring careful governance if new technologies are to be beneﬁcial to humanity. These issues involve information, data and algorithms in a complex and interrelated landscape, and require an equally complex and interrelated set of laws, regulations, standards, governance, and ethics. A variety of laws relate to information and information provision, varying between jurisdictions; the most signiﬁcant bodies of information law relate to IP and the balance between the rights of creators and users, to access to information and to the privacy of the information and data of groups and individuals. There is no single accepted form of information ethics; rather, several traditional ethical approaches have been adopted, augmented by • • • • speciﬁc systems of ethics designed to deal with information issues. Of all information-related ethical issues, privacy has received the most aĴention, and AI the most aĴention of all technologies. Law and ethics have not kept up with technology in the new infosphere. To ensure the proper treatment of information and data requires a mix of law, ethics, regulation, standards and good practice and governance. Currently the most important information laws relate to IP, especially copyright, freedom of information and privacy and data protection. All the main ethical systems have been applied to information issues; Floridi’s information ethics is the most fully developed of systems speciͅcally for the information environment. DOI: 10.1177/2053951714559253. 16 Information Society We can see now that information is what our world runs on: the blood and the fuel, the vital principle. James Gleick (2011, 8) We are so familiar with the talk of ‘the information society’ that we sometimes forget there is no such thing, but rather a multitude of societies, unalike from each other, some of which may qualify as information ones in diﬀerent ways and degrees. Luciano Floridi (2016, 1) Introduction Since the later years of the 20th century it has become commonplace for commentators to declare that we are living in an ‘information society’. In this chapter we will ﬁrst consider the nature of, and criteria for, an information society. We will then look at some of the frameworks and infrastructures which

Understanding information society Information society is not a recent phenomenon. As Floridi (2014a; 2016) reminds us, it would be reasonable to say that information society emerged in the Bronze Age with the introduction of wriĴen communication and records. The contributors to Rayward (2008) identify origins of our present information society in the early 20th century. However, we tend to think of the development of information society as synonymous with the widespread use of digital information systems (Gleick, 2011, chapters 14 and 15; Floridi, 2014a; Lindgren, 2017). While information use has been a feature of all historic societies, in our current situation of hyperhistory (Floridi, 2014a), our use of information and communication technologies deﬁnes our society as one rooted in the infosphere. Put simply, as Gleick points out in our opening quotation, information is what our world runs on. There are diﬀerent kinds of information societies, but a mature information society is one ‘whose members assume the digital as a foregone phenomenon’ (Floridi, 2019, 183). Considered in more detail, however, there are a number of diﬀerent criteria by which we may recognise and deﬁne information society. We will consider these in outline; for detailed analysis, see 
===
--- Chunk 552 ---
 a number of diﬀerent criteria by which we may recognise and deﬁne information society. We will consider these in outline; for detailed analysis, see Feather (2017), Webster (2014), Floridi (2016) and Beaulieu and Leonelli (2021). Types of information society An economic information society is one in which most of the economic activity and wealth of a society is based on intangible, information- based goods, rather than on manufacture and agriculture. This viewpoint builds on the studies of scholars such as Fritz Machlup, Peter Drucker and, particularly, Marc Porat, who pioneered the idea of the ‘information economy’ in the 1970s (Machlup, 1972; Porat, 1977). Since, for example, more than 70% of the economic activity of the G7 group of developed countries is associated with intangible, i.e. information-based, goods, in this view these may be counted as information societies. An occupational information society is one in which most people are employed as ‘information workers’, however this may be deﬁned. This viewpoint was pioneered in the 1960s by the American sociologist Daniel Bell, with his idea of the ‘post-industrial society’ (Bell, 1976), and developed in the 1990s in the ‘knowledge society’ idea of the German sociologist Nico Stehr, who examined the extent to which non-information occupations were increasingly knowledge based (Stehr, 1994). A technological information society is one built around, and dependent upon, widespread ICTs. The problem here is to determine wha
===
--- Chunk 553 ---
ased (Stehr, 1994). A technological information society is one built around, and dependent upon, widespread ICTs. The problem here is to determine what counts as an ‘information technology’ and how much of it there must be to create an information society. The presence of a digital infrastructure, particularly access to broadband and to digital devices, can readily be measured, but their inﬂuence on society may be varied. Three key aspects are social media, e- commerce (both online retail and business-to-business transactions) and e-government; widespread adoption of these is taken as indicative of an information society. A political information society is one in which information and ICT issues become the subject of political debate, and of action at local, national and international levels. Here there is the problem of how much debate is necessary, and also whether the political aĴention needs to be positive. Governments, and powerful individuals, have engaged  in  censorship  and  propaganda  since  wriĴen communication became widespread. Should these be counted as progress towards an information society? For thoughts on the politics of mature information societies, see Floridi (2019). Sociocultural factors have also been proposed as the basis for an information society. Most notable is the idea of the network society put forward in the 1990s by the Spanish sociologist Manuel Castells (1996). Such concepts point to the power of information, and speciﬁcally of information n
===
--- Chunk 554 ---
ward in the 1990s by the Spanish sociologist Manuel Castells (1996). Such concepts point to the power of information, and speciﬁcally of information networks, to change our perceptions of time and distance and to change the way we behave and interact in all aspects of our social dealings (Graham and DuĴon, 2019). This was anticipated by Karl Popper, who in 1945 foresaw an abstract society, in which people practically never meet face to face, with business conducted by individuals in isolation, who communicate by typed leĴers or by telegrams (Popper, 2020, 166) – an idea which has resonance in the COVID pandemic of 2020–21 (Chmielewski, 2020). The rise of social media since such ideas were ﬁrst advanced has only served to further promote this idea. It seems undeniable that society, in those parts of the world aﬀected by these trends, has changed greatly; but it is problematic to say exactly when, and why, it became an information society. See Graham and DuĴon (2019) for analyses of the inﬂuence of the internet on society. Finally, the British sociologist Frank Webster has argued for the idea of a theoretical information society, one in which the main guide to practical action is abstract theoretical knowledge, recorded in documents, rather than tradition, experience, and tacit knowledge (Webster, 2014). This is similar to Michael Buckland’s suggestion that it would be beĴer to speak of a document society rather than an information society, as it is increase in use of recorded 
===
--- Chunk 555 ---
 Buckland’s suggestion that it would be beĴer to speak of a document society rather than an information society, as it is increase in use of recorded information which demarcates our society from others (Buckland, 2017, 17). All of these conceptions of an information society oﬀer some insight, but none in itself is fully satisfactory as a deﬁnition. It is reasonable to say, following Floridi, that there are many kinds of information society, but the deﬁning feature of any mature information society is the unreﬂective and implicit expectations of its citizens that they will be able to access, communicate and process whatever information they want at any time. We can mention one other concept which, though not a theory of the information society, has some resonance with it. This is Karl Popper’s idea of open society, which he initially proposed in the 1940s as an alternative to the closed societies of fascism and communism. Popper’s open society is a society based on the rule of law, in which everyone knows the law and is equal before it, in which those who are responsible for making the laws can be changed without the use of force, and in which society is advanced by rational argument and open criticism of the status quo. It is therefore a form of society dependent on the free ﬂow of information, and Popper’s principles can be used as a guide for information providers (Robinson and Bawden, 2001). Popper’s protégé, the ﬁnancier and philanthropist George Soros, used these ideas

Popper’s protégé, the ﬁnancier and philanthropist George Soros, used these ideas as the basis for his Open Society Institute (OSI) (Tamkin, 2020). OSI has always supported library and information programmes as an important strand of its work; for one example, support for the professional development of information specialists in countries in transition, see Robinson and Glosienė (2007). With these ideas of the nature of an information society in mind, we look at some of the infrastructures which govern information within societies. Information society infrastructures National and international policies have a major eﬀect in determining the form of information society in parts of the world aﬀected by them. National governments and international bodies have the power to enact the laws and regulations which provide the framework for information societies. These control the nature of IP and copyright, data protection and privacy, freedom of information and censorship in any region. These aspects of information society are covered in Chapters 14 and 15. Governments and international bodies may also choose to fund the development of the physical and digital information infrastructure, promote education and training for digital literacy, advocate e-procurement and e-commerce and so on. They are able to lead by example, since governments are among the  largest  producers,  collectors,  preservers  and  users  of inf
===
--- Chunk 557 ---
ommerce and so on. They are able to lead by example, since governments are among the  largest  producers,  collectors,  preservers  and  users  of information, and can promote e-government, giving citizens digital access to government information and services. Public libraries, established in most of the developed world in the 19th century and described as ‘the prototypical spaces of the knowledge society’ (Mainka et al., 2013, 295), have the potential to be an eﬀective support for many aspects of information society, if given the opportunity to do so (McMenemy, 2008; Leorke and WyaĴ, 2018). A recent marker of the development of information society is the smart city or, as Castells termed it, the informational city, whose physical and digital infrastructure is designed to promote an onlife existence, as well as managing the city’s resources to best eﬀect (Mainka, 2018). Such a city may act as an information repository and a knowledge hub, though with consequent concerns about surveillance and privacy (Simeone, 2020; Israilidis, Odusanya and Mazhar, 2021; MaĴern, 2021). The nature of information policies varies greatly between countries and regions. The UK and the USA, for example, have had rather partial and reactive policy provisions, while the countries of continental Europe have adopted a more co-ordinated approach (Hernon and Relyea, 2017; Rabina and Johnson, 2017). The technical infrastructure for an information society comprises the ICTs outlined in Chapter 9. A variety of standard metrics are available for international comparison of progress. A well-known example is the ICT Development Index (IDI) of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), which is designed to measure the level and progress over time of ICT developments in both developed and developing countries, the digital divide between countries in terms of their levels of ICT development and the development potential of ICTs and the extent to which countries can make use of them to enhance growth and development (GerpoĴ and Ahmadi, 2015). The IDI  uses  indicators  under  three  headings:  ICT  readiness (infrastructure and access), such as proportion of households with a computer and with internet access, and reach of broadband and mobile networks; ICT use, such as proportion of individuals using a mobile phone and using the internet; and ICT capability (skills), such as duration of formal education and percentage of individuals with speciﬁed digital skills. With all such indicators, there are disagreements as to the most appropriate metrics and ways of measurement. Social informatics Metrics such as the IDI give a simple quantitative assessment of the extent and, to a degree, the nature, of information society. A more nuanced assessment is given by the discipline of social informatics, most simply understood as ‘the systematic study of social aspects of computerization’ (Kling, Rosenbaum and Sawyer, 2005, 3). It uses an eclectic and ﬂexible mix of methods, from the analytical and technical to the ethnographic, and also includes a strong element of action research (Fichman and Rosenbaum, 2014; Smutny and Vehovar, 2020). Focusing on tasks, practices, communities, tacit knowledge, and the ways in which these are aﬀected by ICTs and, in turn, aﬀect the way ICTs are used, social informatics has an overlap with ideas of knowledge management (discussed in Chapter 14). Information poverty and digital divide These are closely related ideas which denote the diﬀerential levels of engagement of individuals and groups with the information society. Both of these are contested concepts, with lack of agreement as to their exact scope and meaning. ‘Information poverty’ has been, and is, understood in various ways: as lacking money to pay for information; as living in a region where access to information sources is limited; as living under a government which deliberately restricts access to information; or as lacking the basic education or the information literacy necessary to use a range of information resources. See Feather (2017, chapter 5), Haider and Bawden (2007), Duﬀ (2015) and Marcella and Chowdhury (2020) for analyses of the concepts of information rich and poor. Duﬀ regards information poverty as a deﬁciency in ‘normal democratic information’, and hence an issue aﬀecting full membership of society; Marcella and Chowdhury consider it to be
===
--- Chunk 561 ---
ty as a deﬁciency in ‘normal democratic information’, and hence an issue aﬀecting full membership of society; Marcella and Chowdhury consider it to be a lack of access to the information necessary for survival, self- suﬃciency, sustainability or development. Note that the term is sometimes also used in respect of those who, though not ﬁĴing any of the categories above, have problems in ﬁnding necessary information for some tasks, as in a study of healthcare information managers (MacDonald, Bath and Booth, 2011). Where information poverty is a term mainly used in respect of individuals and distinct groups, referring to all forms of information, digital divide is typically used on a larger scale, and speciﬁcally in respect of digital information, although the implications of the terms are much the same. Digital inclusion and exclusion are also used for the same idea. Divides have been identiﬁed between the developed and developing worlds, between continents, regions and countries, and between rural and urban areas. The divide is generally taken to be between those who have access to digital resources, the money to pay for them and the ability to use them eﬀectively and those who lack one or more of the requisites. See van Dĳk (2020) and Flanagan (2018) for reviews of the issues, and Stevenson (2009) for a critique of the whole concept. It is argued that people of diﬀerent ages form distinct generations with diﬀerent aĴitudes and behaviours (Edmunds and Turner, 2005; Wacheider, 2016). This might be expected to include information behaviour, due to their growing up in very diﬀerent information environments. The baby boomer generation, brought up with the novelties of television, vinyl records and paperback books, will be very diﬀerent from the Millennials, brought up with the web, the mobile phone and the computer game, from the Google Generation and so on. Inasmuch as this is the case, it may be a problem in various ways: diﬀerent generations may need diﬀerent forms of information provision; older generations, unfamiliar with new ICTs, may form a group of ‘information poor’ in their own right; and the younger generations, while very conﬁdent

It has to be said that many concerns are based on anecdote and opinion, rather than on research. Studies have not shown any consistent generational diﬀerences in aĴitudes and behaviour ﬁxed over a lifetime; indeed, digital technologies may be inﬂuencing the concept of generation itself (Au, 2020). There may well be typifying generational aĴitudes and preferences in information behaviour; see, for example, Benselin and Ragsdell (2016), Herrando, Jimenez- Matinez and Martin-De Hoyos (2019) and Deyrup, Bekbalaeva and Tammaro (2020). It is not viable to categorise people by age in this respect; other factors may be of more importance, there are always outliers and people change over time. In particular, the idea of digital natives, the newer generations brought up in a world of ubiquitous digital technology and therefore supposedly intuitively capable in the use of ICTs, has been largely discredited. Information overload and anxiety The phenomenon of information overload has been known by many diﬀerent names, including infoglut, data smog, information fatigue and cognitive overload. There is no single, generally accepted deﬁnition, but it is usually understood as that situation which arises when there is so much relevant and potentially us
===
--- Chunk 564 ---
no single, generally accepted deﬁnition, but it is usually understood as that situation which arises when there is so much relevant and potentially useful information available that it becomes a hindrance rather than a help. Overload has been claimed both to be the major issue of our time and to be a complete non-issue. Its nature has not changed with changing technology, though its causes and proposed solutions have changed much. It is not a new problem, although, as Gleick (2011) points out, it has always felt new. For almost as long as there has been recorded information, there has been a perception that humans have been overloaded by it, and concerns about ‘too much to read’ have been expressed for many centuries (Blair, 2010). These have become more urgent since the arrival of ubiquitous digital information in the late 20th century. Originally seen as a problem primarily aﬀecting scholars and academia, it was then claimed to aﬄict business and the information-intensive professions such as medicine, and has been more recently seen as aﬀecting the whole of society, including education, government, home life and leisure, and citizenship, and has even inﬂuenced literature. For reviews, see Bawden and Robinson (2020), SchmiĴ, Debbeit and Schneider (2018), Koltay (2017), Groes (2017) and Case and Given (2016, 122–7). Information anxiety is a closely related issue, described by Wurman (1989, 34) as ‘the ever-widening gap between what we understand and what we think we should un
===
--- Chunk 565 ---
anxiety is a closely related issue, described by Wurman (1989, 34) as ‘the ever-widening gap between what we understand and what we think we should understand . . . the black hole between data and knowledge’. It has remained an issue of concern: see, for example Wurman (2001), Hartog (2017) and Naveed and Anwar (2020). The irony is that increasing volumes of data and information may cause a lack of knowledge and understanding; overload and anxiety are linked. The causes of overload are primarily associated with having ‘too much information’ (TMI), particularly when it comes through a diversity of media and when it appears interesting and potentially useful. Lack of time to deal properly with information is oĞen cited as a cause; see, for example, Savolainen (2006). So is the ‘paradox of choice’, the paralysis of action caused by too many alternatives, for information as much as for anything else. It has been blamed for many consequences, including ineﬃcient working, poor decision making and ill-health. On the other hand, it is suggested that overload, for many people at least, does not exist; it is a ‘phantom’, a ‘myth’ and something which may be avoided simply by ignoring most available information; Bawden and Robinson (2020) give examples of this viewpoint. Floridi suggests that we should no more complain about there being too much available information and data than we would complain about there being more food provided at a banquet than we can eat; in both cases, it is a 
===
--- Chunk 566 ---
 much available information and data than we would complain about there being more food provided at a banquet than we can eat; in both cases, it is a maĴer of thoughtfully deciding what we should consume (Floridi, 2014b). There are many suggested solutions to information overload and anxiety (Bawden and Robinson, 2020). The best ways of avoiding overload, individually and socially, appear to lie in a variety of coping strategies, such as ﬁltering, withdrawing, avoiding and ‘satisﬁcing’ (Savolainen, 2007; Lauri, Virkus and Heidmets, 2020). BeĴer design of information systems, eﬀective personal information management (PIM) and the promotion of digital and media literacies also have a part to play. Overload may perhaps best be overcome by seeking a mindful balance in consuming information. Summary • • • It is generally agreed that we live in an information society, but there is no general agreement about exactly what this means, other than that information is somehow central to the way in which the society works. A variety of theories invoke technology, politics, economics, occupations and roles, networks and communication, knowledge and abstract theory, and other factors, as the basis for the idea. It is probably best understood in terms of a combination of these. Despite the wealth of information available in the digital environment of the infosphere, the pressure of ‘too much information’ and the inequitable nature of access have led to concerns about information overload, in
===
--- Chunk 567 ---
ent of the infosphere, the pressure of ‘too much information’ and the inequitable nature of access have led to concerns about information overload, information anxiety, the digital divide and the rest. Whether these will fade away into insigniﬁcance as societies adapt to their new nature, or whether they will continue to require active treatment through IM and digital literacy remains to be seen. Information society is a concept with no single agreed deͅnition; it may be understood in a number of ways, expressed as theories or frameworks. It can be said that an information society has existed for as long as there has been recorded information, but modern information society has been catalysed by digital technologies, and by the move into hyperhistory and onlife. The idea of information society is closely related to other concepts: network society, knowledge society, information economy and post- industrial society. • Perceived problems of information societies include information overload, information poverty and the digital divide. Barbara Fister (2021, 5) Introduction The ability to use information eﬀectively, in all formats, in a largely digital information environment is a vital life skill for everyone. This ability is variously termed information literacy, digital literacy and media literacy, with numerous other literacies having been mentioned. We will use digital literacies as an overall term, linked to the concept of onlife, for reasons explained later, using the other terms where appropriate. What constitutes each of these literacies, how they relate to each other, and how they can best be taught and promoted, has caused much debate. The promotion of digital literacies has been seen as an important task for information professionals in all sectors. Indeed, CILIP i

Indeed, CILIP includes, as one of its seven principles for ethical information professionals, a commitment to uphold the development of information skills and information literacy. Identiﬁed as an important issue since the 1990s, it has gained in importance as a claimed solution to the pathologies of the current information environment (Bawden and Robinson, 2009; 2011; 2020): information overload, misinformation, disinformation, information anxiety, etc. While information literacy training has largely been centred in libraries in secondary and tertiary education, as a replacement for traditional bibliographical instruction, there is an increased interest in its promotion in the workplace, and in society generally. The question of whether this can be a generic ability or whether it can be promoted only in the context of a speciﬁc subject is still debated, while the issue of multicultural information literacy has gained aĴention. In this chapter, aĞer explaining why we prefer the ‘digital literacies’ term, we will look at the variety of literacies of information. We will outline some of the more important concepts and models, consider the contexts in which they may be applied and the relation of generic and subject-speciﬁc digital literacies and how it may be aﬀected by linguistic and cultural factors. These topics have generated a very large literature, and our coverage here is necessarily selective and the examples only illustrative. Why ‘digital literacies’? Paul Gilster (1997), introducing the concept of digital literacy as the term is now generally used, explained it as an ability to understand and to use information from a variety of digital sources, and regarded it simply as literacy in the digital age. He emphasised that digital literacy is about mastering ideas and concepts, not keystrokes, thus distinguishing his conception from the more limited ‘technical skills’ view of digital literacy. It is ‘the ability to understand and use information in multiple formats from a wide variety of sources when it is presented via computers’ (Gilster, 1997, 1). Gilster speciﬁcally notes that digital literacy involves an understanding of how to complement digital resources with such things as reference works in libraries, printed newspapers and magazines, radio and television, and printed works of literature. There is a clear analogy with Floridi’s conception of onlife (Floridi, 2014), with its seamless blending of physical and digital. Indeed, there is an analogy between Gilster’s digital literacy as literacy for the digital age with Floridi’s PI as philosophy for the information age. For this reason, we have chosen this term as most appropriate, but make it plural to distinguish it from some narrower conceptions called digital literacy. [We were tempted to write of onlife literacy or infosphere literacy, which would best ﬁt our perspective, but the area is bedevilled by too many terms as it is.] A variety of literacies The terminology here is unclear, with a substantial and potentially confusing variety of ‘literacies’ of information, and of changing understandings of the same literacy (Bawden, 2001; 2008; Pinto, Cordon and Diaz, 2010; Koltay, 2011; Julien, 2016; Carrington, 2018; Sample, 2020). A bibliometric study of the information literacy literature identiﬁed over 70 diﬀerent literacies associated with information between 1975 and 2018 (Onyancha, 2020). One clear trend has been a move away from seeing these literacies as primarily skills based, in essence lists of things people should be able to do, to more broad and holistic conceptions, including aĴitudes and values, and social and ethical factors. Walsh (2015) describes them as ‘competence’ and ‘relational’ models, respectively, suggesting that the second type begins with the work of Christine Bruce (1997). Although the relational models are generally regarded as more realistic and comprehensive, the competence models are still of pragmatic value for structuring resources and instruction. They are of importance because they provide the basis for all training and promotion in this area. . Information literacy Information literacy is generally agreed to be a successor to traditional bibliographic instruction or library orientation. The term library literacy has also been used. The concept of information literacy was introduced by Paul Zurkowski in 1974, in a report on the likely impact of the digital computer on information work, in which he wrote ‘People trained in the application of information resources to their work can be called information literates’. It was ﬁrst given a deﬁnite content in the inﬂuential American Library Association (ALA) deﬁnition of 1989: ‘To be information literate, a person must be able to recognize when information is needed and have the ability to locate, evaluate, and use eﬀectively the needed information.’ This set a trend for information literacy to be expressed as a series of linear steps to be carried out, somewhat reminiscent of the process models for information behaviour considered in Chapter 12. It may be noted that there has been surprisingly liĴle explicit linkage between the conceptions and models of information literacy and of information behaviour, although the two clearly have much in common (Julien, 2016). Similar was the ‘Seven Pillars’ model produced in 1999 by the UK Society of College, National and University Libraries (SCONUL). This saw information literacy as consisting of understanding and competencies in each of seven ‘pillars’ or ‘headline skills’: recognise information need; ﬁnd ways of meeting the need; 
===
--- Chunk 581 ---
nsisting of understanding and competencies in each of seven ‘pillars’ or ‘headline skills’: recognise information need; ﬁnd ways of meeting the need; construct strategies for locating information; locate and access; compare and evaluate; organise, apply, and communicate; synthesise and create. In 2011, SCONUL revised their approach, making their pillars concept broader and more general: ‘Information literacy is an umbrella term which encompasses concepts such as digital, visual and media literacies, academic literacy, information handling, information skills, data curation and data management. Information literate people will demonstrate an awareness of how they gather, use, manage, synthesise and create information and data in an ethical manner and will have the information skills to do so eﬀectively.’ This was a non-linear model, without the prescriptive sequential process and with ‘lenses’ for context; for example, a research lens, and a graduate employability lens. In the United States ACRL produced a similar formulation in their Standards of 2000. Their six steps were: determine the extent of information needed; access the needed information eﬀectively and eﬃciently;  evaluate  information  and  its  sources  critically; incorporate selected information into one’s knowledge base; use information eﬀectively to accomplish a speciﬁc purpose; understand the economic, legal, and social issues surrounding the use of information; and access and use information ethically and leg

In 2015, ACRL introduced a new approach, their Framework, based on the idea of information literacy as a social practice rather than a set of competencies (Foasberg, 2015). The deﬁnition, ‘Information literacy is the set of integrated abilities encompassing the reﬂective discovery of information, the understanding of how • • • • • • information is produced and valued, and the use of information in creating new knowledge and participating ethically in communities of learning’, is non-linear and inclusive, and accompanied by a series of six ‘frames’ or threshold concepts (Oberlies and MaĴison, 2018). Media literacy Media literacy, also termed mediacy, and subsuming social media literacy and news literacy, is generally regarded as the skills needed to access and evaluate information from a variety of media and to understand the nature of diﬀerent media (Livingstone, 2004; PoĴer, 2021). Creating media is also commonly included, and the concept has been associated with visual literacy, the ability to critically and ethically view, understand, use and create images and visual media (Brown et al., 2016; Michelson, 2017; Thompson, 2020), with critical thinking or critical skills (Dodd, 2017; GoodseĴ, 2020) and with civic literacy, data citizenship and digital citizenship (Carmi et al., 2020; Hintz, Dencik and Wahl-Jorgensen, 2019). Media literacy and information literacy, though clearly having much in common, developed independently and have been combined only relatively recently (Lee and So, 2014). Digital literacy Digital literacy is generally taken as an all-embracing successor to a variety of technical literacies, including computer literacy, IT literacy, internet literacy and network literacy, together with the more recent idea of algorithmic literacy, understanding the nature of algorithmic decision making and its potential for inaccuracy and bias (Carrington, 2018; Lloyd, 2019; Ridley and Pawlick-PoĴs, 2021). These earlier concepts typically related to a basic ability to use computing hardware and soĞware. More recently they have come to mean an ability to cope in a digital environment, including using search engines eﬀectively, evaluating digital information, creating and sharing digital information, using social media appropriately and avoidi

using search engines eﬀectively, evaluating digital information, creating and sharing digital information, using social media appropriately and avoiding online risks, and behaving ethically online. The term information ﬂuency has also been used for this idea (Bawden, 2014; EmmeĴ, 2016). IFLA’s 2017 statement on digital literacy is of this nature: ‘To be digitally literate means one can use technology to its fullest eﬀect – eﬃciently, eﬀectively and ethically – to meet information needs in personal, civic and professional lives . . . the deﬁnition of digital literacy remains ﬂuid . . . digital literacy overlaps with other areas of competence, notably media and information literacy . . . and ﬁnally digital literacy is a lifelong learning process’. Marcum and O’Shea (2017) use the term information technology literature to describe this kind of broad, multidimensional set of skills and knowledge, regarding it as more complex than information literature and heavily dependent on the context. Digital literacy also typically includes data literacy, the ability to ﬁnd, understand, use and communicate data in all its forms, including visualisations, and incorporating an understanding of how to create, control and protect our personal data (Pangrazio and Selwyn, 2019). Metaliteracies Finally, we may mention metaliteracies of information. The metaliteracy model (Mackey and Jacobson, 2014; Jacobson and Mackey, 2016) is an open, non-linear and ﬂexible framework that uniﬁes information literacy with related literacies, in particular with media literacy and with computer literacy; it places great importance on collaboration and reﬂection and on an ability to critically self- assess diﬀerent competences. It regards skills-based models as inadequate for the present digital information environment, especially its emphasis on open learning, social media and participation/creation/collaboration. Foregrounding the importance of information literacy for lifelong learning, it also recognises that, since the information environment is constantly changing, courses and learning materials based on the metaliteracy model must also constantly be revised.  This is slowly changing, as they are increasingly seen as worth promotion in schools (Laubersheimer, Ryan and Champaign, 2016; Walton, Pickard and Dodd, 2018), in workplaces (Forster, 2017) and in society generally (Goldstein, 2020). To be fully eﬀective, this is likely to require diﬀerent concepts of digital literacies and diﬀerent methods of promotion. Clearly, much information literacy is discipline and context speciﬁc: as examples, see Bawden and Robinson (2017) for chemistry and Houlihan, Click and Wiley (2020) for business and, for a comparison over several disciplines, Dreisiebner and Schlōgl (2019). Indeed, there has been a long-lasting debate whether there is such a thing as generic information, digital or media literacy, or whether it must always be context bound. The evidence suggests that there is a core of basic principles, but these are best presented in the relevant context, as is current good practice. Most conceptual and pedagogic development of digital literacies has been carried out in the developed Anglophone world and there has been relatively liĴle consideration of what adaptions may be necessary for diﬀerent cultural seĴings. This issue has been recognised for many years (Bruce, 1997). As Johnson and Webber (2003, 112) put it: ‘in terms of local and national culture, the information literate person is a self- and socially-conscious being, rather than a simple repository of skills and knowledge.
