There have been many descriptions of information literacy education in diﬀerent seĴings, but liĴle analysis of the needs of diﬀerent cultural groups, and liĴle agreement on good practice. Suggestions have included using locally relevant examples, considering whether individual or group working is more acceptable and using models such as Hofstede’s cultural dimensions (ACRL, 2017; Nowrin, Robinson and Bawden, 2019). An extensive set of studies are those of Dorner and Gorman, drawing on analyses of the contexts of Asia and Oceania (Dorner, 2012; 2017, Dorner and Gorman, 2011). They argue for explicit consideration of cultural factors, using Hofstede’s dimensions, and in favour of models using a critical form of information literacy, and suggest, for example, that student-centred learning may not be appropriate and that collaborative group working will be beĴer accepted than individual work. Evaluating information and avoiding mis- and disinformation Evaluation of information has been a part of all formulations of digital literacies. The need for explicit evaluation of information has always been important but it has become more pressing in a largely digital information environment, for several reasons: more information is available, so a greater degree of selectivity is needed a greater proportion of information is generated outside the formal ‘publication chain’ and therefore may have liĴle or no initial quality control web browsers have a homogenising eﬀect. All information has a similar ‘look and feel’, whereas previously the diﬀerences between, say, a textbook, a legal case report, a newspaper article and a Post-It note were immediately obvious the origin of information, the motives of its originator(s) and its trustworthiness may be unclear many people rely on social media sources, rather than on formal media, for news, and even for information on topics such as health technology increasingly allows the easy creation of ‘deep fakes’, false images and videos. The result has been a concern for the proliferation of misinforma

--- Chunk 593 ---
logy increasingly allows the easy creation of ‘deep fakes’, false images and videos. The result has been a concern for the proliferation of misinformation (false information), disinformation (deliberately false information) and malinformation (true information presented for malicious motives) and for the phenomena of fake news (Buschman, 2019; Rubin, 2019; O’Connor and Weatherall, 2019; Carmi et al., 2020; Zimdars and Kembrew, 2020) and of post-truth and alternative facts (Cooke, 2017). This has led to a revival of the long-established practice of ‘fact checking’ and, of particular relevance here, to initiatives for training in the evaluation of information and information sources, oĞen within a framework of information or digital literacy (Revez and Corujo, 2021; Agosto, 2018; Cooke, 2018). A somewhat naïve view was held for a long time that all that was necessary to defeat these problems was more training in information, media and digital literacies. This optimistic view has been dispelled by the realisation that the reasons why such problems exist are far more complex than a simple lack of digital literacy. The commonly used checklist methods of information evaluation, such as the widely used CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) list, applied within a source, are of limited value beyond a basic appreciation of evaluation criteria. It is also clear that many of those who provide false information, for whatever motives, have a very sophisticated understanding of information handling. Improvement in levels of digital literacies will therefore be a help, but it will require more sophisticated approaches than heretofore, involving a variety of actors (Bontcheva and PoseĴi, 2020) and focusing on promoting a broader understanding of ‘how information works’ (Polizzi, 2020; Fister, 2021). Promoting digital literacies How to teach and promote information literacy is a continuing debate, and many diﬀerent approaches have been tried and are in use (Robinson and Bawden, 2018; Saunders and Wong, 2020). There has been a general reliance on traditional classroom seĴings, supported by online tutorials and LibGuides (Courtney and Wilhoite-Mathews, 2015; Miller, 2015; Burkhardt, 2016; Saunders, 2018). Other methods have been considered, including MOOCs (Dreisiebner, 2019; Dreisiebner et al., 2021), games (Urban, 2019; JerreĴ, Bothma and de Beer, 2017; Walsh, 2015), peer-led learning (Aylward, Sbaﬃ and Weist, 2020) and activities such as source evaluation, creation of resource lists, reﬂective writing, and ﬂipped classrooms  (Rodriguez,  2016;  Johnson  and  BarreĴ,  2017; Humrickhouse, 2021). Zora Neale Hurston, American novelist and anthropologist Introduction Research is generally regarded as the creation of new knowledge; more speciﬁcally, as the creation of knowledge which is new to everyone, not just to the researcher, in a form which can be communicated through objective information, and which builds on existing knowledge. Communication to the wider community is the vital ﬁnal stage of research, through the processes of scholarly communication and further dissemination discussed in Chapter 13. Research is oĞen described in terms of major discoveries by brilliant individuals. But it is usually more realistic to think of it as the creation of new knowledge within a discipline by an evolutionary and impersonal process, with contributions by many individuals, most of whom will never be credited with a major advance (Scerri, 2016). n associated professional activity, such as information science, research has two purposes: academic, to improve the discipline’s knowledge base; and professional, to improve practice. Information research may be carried out by university researchers, advanced students, research institutes and consultancies, government agencies, system and service designers and suppliers and practitioners. Research has been an important aspect of information science since the discipline’s beginnings. In this chapter we will consider ﬁrst the somewhat troubled research/practice interaction, then consider information research and methods and ﬁnally mention research ethics. There are several textbooks for this area, and the coverage here will not be detailed. Research and the practitioner Interaction between academics and researchers on the one hand, and practitioners on the other, is as desirable in the information disciplines as in any other academic area with an associated professional discipline. Practitioners may be in a position to carry out research themselves, and should certainly be aware of, and make use of, research results. It is beneﬁcial for both if practitioners carry out their own research and use research results and if researchers are aware of practice issues in planning and carrying out studies, as has been recognised for many years; see, for example, Williamson (1931). In the information sciences there has in the past, as with other disciplines, been a divide between academic

The laĴer have been held to be uninterested in research results, still less in carrying out research themselves; the counter prejudice has been that information researchers undertake ‘useless’ research, ignoring the needs of practice. As long ago as 1983, Blick presented this as a kind of contest or conﬂict between practitioners and researchers in information science, and the nature of the divide has been investigated, and solutions proposed, since then: see, for example, Haddow and Klobas (2004), Hall (2010), Finlay et al. (2013), Partridge et al. (2014), Pilerot (2016) and Mizrachi (2018). There is an analogy with the use, or non-use, of theory by practitioners; see, for example, Pinﬁeld, et al. (2020, chapter 4). The gap may be bridged by research embedded in a practice context, where the aim of the research is the improvement of practice as much as the extension of the disciplinary knowledge base, typically termed action research. The description use-inspired research has been applied to research which is an academic study of real- world problems, producing fundamental understanding but also beneﬁĴing practice. Information research approaches All research is based in a philosophical viewpoint or paradigm, although this is not always explicitly recognised by researchers, and the viewpoint determines the research approach (Creswell and Creswell, 2018). A rough distinction can be made between studies conducted from a positivist viewpoint, where it is assumed that an objective reality exists, which the researcher may identify and study, and those conducted from a constructivist or interpretivist viewpoint, which assumes that reality is subjective and must be constructed or interpreted by the researcher. For information research, the former assumes, for example, that concepts such as the meaning or relevance of a piece of information to a user, or the proper role of an inform
===
--- Chunk 614 ---
, the former assumes, for example, that concepts such as the meaning or relevance of a piece of information to a user, or the proper role of an information service, are objective facts which may be determined correctly; the laĴer assumes that they are subjective, and created and modiﬁed by those involved. The former assumes that the researcher is detached from the context studied; the laĴer allows for them to be involved, and may be termed participatory research. There is also a pragmatic viewpoint, which assumes no philosophical position. This should be a deliberately chosen stance, not a thoughtless, seemingly easy default. While information researchers need not be philosophers, it is important to recognise what assumptions are implicit in the methods used, and what assumptions or viewpoints the researchers themselves hold which may aﬀect their approach. A detailed discussion  of  the  relation  between  research,  philosophies, approaches and methods is given by Creswell and Creswell (2018); see Berryman (2019) and Polkinghorne and Given (2021). A common distinction is between quantitative and qualitative research,  approximately  corresponding  to  positivist  and interpretivist viewpoints. These describe a diﬀerence in general approach: whether the focus is on measuring, counting and testing formally stated hypotheses or on an interpretation of the meaning of events, issues and opinions, in an aĴempt to gain understanding. Each has its own ways of analysing the data generated in the research process, and qualitative data collection and analysis are no less rigorous than quantitative methods. Mixed methods studies, corresponding to a pragmatic viewpoint and incorporating both qualitative and quantitative methods, have become increasingly common in information research. They have advantages in the richness of data collected, but require careful analysis and synthesis of the results (Tashakkori, Johnson and Teddlie, 2021; Granikov et al., 2020). Information research methods: general aspects A wide range of research methods and techniques are used in the information disciplines (Ullah and Ammen, 2018). These methods are explained in detail in textbooks such as Pickard (2013), Connaway and Radford (2021), Williamson and Johanson (2017), Denscombe (2017) and Billups (2020). We consider methods in four categories: document-based research; experiment and observation; evaluation and design; and surveys. These are not mutually exclusive, and mixed method studies are increasingly common. The term triangulation is used to describe studies which mainly rely on one method but then use a second method to check the validity of the results; for example, questionnaire surveys which include some interviews. Research methods (1): document-based research Document-based research, commonly termed desk research, involves research carried out by any form of analysis of documents of any kind. This is a part of all research, in the form of a literature search to establish the context and to identify previous relevant work. It may provide the methods for studies in their own right, which are entirely valid research, inasmuch as they have the potential to provide new knowledge. Document research may also be referred to as literature research or internet research, although both these terms are too narrow to cover all forms of document research. Several styles can be distinguished, although the distinctions are not sharp, and the terms are oĞen loosely used; some studies cross the boundaries between styles. Literature reviews are the most common form, and may form a study in their own right as well being a precursor to other research methods (Fink, 2014; Hart, 2018). They may be designated as comprehensive or selective, according to whether an aĴempt is made to cover all relevant material or only a subset which the reviewer ﬁnds signiﬁcant. A systematic review carefully deﬁnes and justiﬁes the research question, the sources and search strategies and the relevance criteria to be used, before material is identiﬁed. A scoping review or mapping review or narrative review is a comprehensive examination of the scope, extent and content of the literature in a particular topic, without the very speciﬁc criteria of a systematic review. For a comparison of diﬀerent forms of comprehensive review that may be done, see the reviews of eye-tracking research on search engine use by Lewandowski and Kammerer (2021) and by Strzelecki (2020). A review may be objective, simply reporting what is in the literature, or subjective, in that the reviewer gives a judgement on the quality of the material and its content; the laĴer may be called a critical review. Reviews focused on an emergent or developing technology and its prospects may be termed technology assessments. Meta-analysis is a speciﬁc kind of literature review, in which quantitative data from a number of sources are combined and analysed together; necessarily it requires comparable numeric datasets. Meta-synthesis is the equivalent term for systematic analysis of multiple qualitative studies (or sometimes a mix of qualitative and quantitative studies), using interpretivist methods such as thematic analysis and grounded theory, rather than statistical analysis, to combine the ﬁndings of the studies (Braun and Clarke, 2006; Bawden, 2012; Kie et al., 2020). Conceptual analysis and philosophical analysis are used to analyse and clarify terms, concepts and issues (Furner, 2004). Conceptual analysis relies on examining usage of concepts in documents; philosophical analysis may be more abstract. Historical research analyses developments over time, using documentary and archival evidence, personal recollections, etc. For the information sciences, this has typically been focused on the development of libraries and other information institutions, or information systems, services, processes and concepts, and of information phenomena in society. Content analysis is a varied form of research, involving some kind of quantitative assessment of the content of a set of documents to assess the extent to which concepts and issues are mentioned, or not (White and Marsh, 2006; Armann-Keown and PaĴerson, 2020). It may include a qualitative dimension, to record how concepts and issues are described. Discourse analysis is a form of content analysis, focusing on the way in which spoken or wriĴen language is used. It is used to analyse, oĞen in detail, the way in which concepts and issues are mentioned and what this shows about how they are understood (Budd, 2006). Research methods (2): experiment and observation This category of research covers a variety of methods. At one end of the spectrum are those described as experimental, based in a positivist, scientiﬁc worldview. Observation research was originally located within this approach as a largely quantitative technique counting how many people did what and how oĞen; it now embraces methods within an interpretivist approach, based in the traditions of ethnography and similar disciplines. These methods are also oĞen subsumed into mixed method approaches. They are typically used to understand information behaviour and to understand in detail how information systems and services are used and how well they work, so as to provide a basis for the improvement of information systems and services. The experimental style of research in library/information science derives from the approach of the physical sciences. The topic to be studied is isolated, so far as possible, from the complexities of the real world so that all the variable factors in the situation can be held constant, apart from the one being studied. It is therefore particularly suitable for comparisons of algorithms and interfaces. Its opposite is operational evaluation, analysing the totality of an information service and including all the messiness of the real-world context. The experimental approach was pioneered in information retrieval research (Sparck Jones, 1981; Robertson, 2008) and is still most commonly used there, and in HCI studies, using methods such as eye-tracking (Lund, 2016). Where users are involved, data on their success in using the system may be augmented by data gathered from special equipment, such as eye-tracking devices to see where they look on the screen, and by user opinions given by conventional interview or by ‘talk/think aloud’ or ‘talk/think aĞer’ features of the experiment. At the other extreme, observation is usually regarded as a technique for understanding a real-world situation without aﬀecting or inﬂuencing it at all; hence a phrase commonly used in the past, unobtrusive observation, when the subjects are not aware that they are being studied. Research methods (4): surveys, interviews and Delphi Methods of this kind, and particularly questionnaires and interviews, are the most widely used information science studies and are commonly used in mixed-methods research, typically combining a survey with some form of observation or document- based research. Longitudinal studies are carried out over a period of years so as to assess changes over time; as examples see Tenopir et al. (2009) and Borgman et al. (2021). Most library/information surveys are small scale, rarely involving more than one hundred participants, and are usually aimed at a closely deﬁned group of people. They do not therefore usually adopt the rigorous methods of sampling and analysis used for purposes such as public opinion polling or large-scale market research. Questionnaires  are  usually  regarded  as  being  in  the positivist/objective style of research, since they assume that researcher and participants share a common perspective of the situation. A series of short, structured questions with prescribed answers (yes/no, Lickert scale, multiple choice) are generally used, with limited opportunity for expressing extra information, giving reasons or raising other topics. This approach is appropriate for geĴing large numbers of responses quickly and simply and for giving results which can be analysed quantitatively. However, the value of the results relies in the researcher’s having understood all the relevant factors and expressed them in a way which the participants  can  understand.  For  a  basic  introduction  to questionnaire design, see Kara (2019). Questionnaires are now usually administered electronically rather than in printed form. This is convenient and gives greater reach, but may mean that the population sampled, the response rate and any bias in response are unknown. If such a survey is placed on a website, for example, all that can be known is those who replied to it; the number who saw it and did not respond cannot usually be established, nor whether there is anything diﬀerent about those who responded and those who did not. Interviews are regarded as appropriate for geĴing a greater, and richer, amount of information from a smaller number of participants; they may be carried out in person or by telephone, video, or e-mail. At the opposite extreme unstructured interviews have no predeﬁned structure and resemble a free-ﬂowing conversation; they are most appropriately used in an exploratory way, in situations where the interviewer does not have a good understanding of the issues or context. An intermediate form, and oĞen regarded as most appropriate for most library/information research, is the semi-structured interview, where a number of predeﬁned questions are always asked, but subsequent questioning will depend on the responses given. Interviews are usually carried out one to one. Group interviews may be used on grounds of practicality and time saving. They may also be useful in allowing interviewees to discuss the questions asked, reach consensus and spark ideas oﬀ each other; but equally they run the risk of being dominated by a small number of participants, such that other views are not heard. This approach avoids very general and bland responses and is particularly useful in assessing the impact of information systems and services. When a survey is begun, a pilot study may be carried out with a small number of participants to check the validity of the survey questions and allow for changes to be made for the main study. In a large-scale study, particularly if it is to be analysed quantitatively, the results of the pilot study would not be included, though in smaller surveys they may be. Sampling, data analysis and statistics A full treatment of statistics and data analysis is beyond the scope of this book. There are many good resources available for these topics, so here we reiterate some central points, making some remarks about sampling and about the question of ‘how much is enough’. For basic introductions, s

For basic introductions, see Frey (2015), Campbell and Swinscow (2009), Rowntree (2018) and Spiegelhalter (2020) and from an LIS perspective Walters (2021). A fundamental distinction is between quantitative and qualitative data analysis. Qualitative analysis, not primarily involving numbers, has its own rigorous methods, typically involving repeated coding, categorising and comparing of data. Quantitative analysis is typically divided into descriptive and inferential statistics. The former seeks to describe and summarise a set of collected data through numeric calculations and through diagrams and visualisations. The laĴer seeks to decide what may be reliably concluded and generalised from a set of data; this is the realm of statistical signiﬁcance and hypothesis testing. What kind of statistical tests are appropriate will depend upon the nature of the data available: • nominal (categories or groups); ordinal (ordered); ratio (positive numbers); interval (numbers). The ready availability of easy-to-use statistical analysis packages makes it important that we are aware of which tests are appropriate to use, in view of the kind of data we have, and how to interpret the results. The aim of sampling is to choose a sample representative of the larger population from which they are drawn, so that the results obtained have a more general validity beyond the particular entities which were studied. The issue of sampling very oĞen arises in information research, regardless of the method used. It is oĞen thought of in the context of surveys – how should we choose our participants? – but is equally applicable in, for example, the choice of documents for content or discourse analysis, or the choice of place and time for observations. It raises two questions: what kind of sample is to be used; and how to know when it is enough. This is a complex subject, and only some simple points are made here. Texts on research methods and on statistics cover the topic more thoroughly. Four general kinds of sample may be taken. A complete sample, where we include all examples of the population. For example, in a study of archiving policies in local government in London, an archivist in each of the 33 government units could be interviewed. • • • A random sample of our population. This has to be done formally, typically using tables of pseudo-random numbers. Many samples described as ‘random’ are no such thing, having simply been picked arbitrarily. A purposive sample, chosen to include examples of diﬀerent types within our population
===
--- Chunk 632 ---

For example, to get a sample of users of a website, we might choose to select by age, gender, nationality, education level, place of residence, occupation, etc. Having chosen these groups, we might then select individuals within them randomly. This is a complex process and must be done carefully, according to the nature of the research. This may be referred to as a systematic, clustered, quota or stratiﬁed sample, according to the exact procedure used. If the participants are individually chosen by the researchers, it may be termed a judgement sample. A convenience sample, where a set of appropriate participants are selected because they are available: family, friends, fellow students, regular users of an information service, etc. This may be an appropriate method for small-scale and exploratory studies, provided that (1) it is declared as such and (2) no aĴempt is made to generalise the results or to claim statistical validity; both of the laĴer would need a more formal sampling process. A snowball sample is a convenience sample where participants are asked to select others. The question of how large a sample is needed is oĞen asked, but is diﬃcult to answer exactly. In the case of qualitative studies, the usual process is to continue to saturation, the point when no new information is being found. Research ethics Ethics are of relevance to all research, if only because of the idea that it is unethical to waste resources by doing poor research and producing potentially misleading results. The principles of research ethics are the same as those for ethics in general, as discussed in Chapter 15, but there are certain ethical issues speciﬁc to the research context; for a basic introduction, see Poth (2021). For information research, some of the main issues are: recognising potential preconceptions and prejudices on the part of the researcher transparency: making clear issues such as the natur
===
--- Chunk 634 ---
main issues are: recognising potential preconceptions and prejudices on the part of the researcher transparency: making clear issues such as the nature and purpose of the research, who may beneﬁt from it, who is funding it and how the results will be disseminated • • • • • • informed consent: making sure that all research participants are fully aware of the nature of the research and have the chance to decline to take part and to withdraw from the study at any time ensuring anonymity and conﬁdentiality as necessary protecting participants’ rights, particularly for vulnerable groups such as children or those in ill-health dealing correctly with documents, both in the study and in its dissemination, including observing copyright and avoiding plagiarism not collecting more data than necessary, and ensuring that data is stored and disposed of correctly choosing samples, analysing data and presenting results in ways which, so far as possible, avoid bias and distortion. Digital research brings its own particular ethical issues, such as those around the collection of data or observation of behaviour without those aﬀected being aware that they are being investigated. Care needs to be taken to observe the rules of digital environments, particularly social media platforms, regarding data collection. Researchers will oĞen be required by their institutions or funders to observe processes of research integrity, for example by observing codes of conduct, by collecting only that data which

eir institutions or funders to observe processes of research integrity, for example by observing codes of conduct, by collecting only that data which is strictly necessary for the research, by observing norms of data protection and so on. Summary Research is fundamental to the information disciplines and professions. Without it, the academic knowledge base will stagnate • • • and improvements in practice will be made more diﬃcult. Academics and practitioners have a joint duty to carry out appropriate research, to be aware of and make use of existing research ﬁndings and to communicate across the academic– practitioner divide on these issues. The range of methods available for and used in information research has expanded greatly, and novel methods still arise. Research is likely to be even more important in the future, to help deal with dramatic changes in the information environment. Research is essential for the future of the information disciplines and professions. Practitioners and academic researchers have a joint responsibility to carry out appropriate research and to make use of existing research. Robert Storm Petersen, Danish poet and philosopher – also aĴributed to the physicist Niels Bohr Introduction In this ﬁnal chapter we give an overview of some ideas about the future of the discipline and profession of information science. This has been a source of debate almost since the beginnings of the discipline, and of its sibling, library science. Much of the debate has been negative, with a narrative around disciplines and professions permanently in crisis. And, indeed, if o

And, indeed, if one worries about the structure of academic departments and the names of professional associations one might ﬁnd cause for concern. If one takes a longer view and thinks, with Lord Dunsany, about the power of recorded information and the continuing need for disciplines and professions to deal with it, the concerns come into beĴer focus. Predicting and prophesying Karl Popper distinguished between prediction, when suﬃcient knowledge is available to make reasonable conclusions about future events, and prophecy, when statements are made about the future without the necessary knowledge being available for them to be rational or realistic. We have seen examples of both of these relating to information science, but, because of the great and rapid changes in the information environment, most fall under the heading of prophesy, and much of it bad prophesy. David Deutsch (2011) builds on Popper’s view to argue that the continuous development of knowledge of all kinds reduces all speculation about the future to prophesy, and almost inevitably in error. Arthur C. Clarke, writer of popular science books and science ﬁction novels and originator of the concept of the communications satellite, identiﬁed two general problems in predicting the future. A ‘failure of imagination’ occurs when future developments are unforeseen because some necessary
===
--- Chunk 646 ---
ntiﬁed two general problems in predicting the future. A ‘failure of imagination’ occurs when future developments are unforeseen because some necessary piece of knowledge was as yet unavailable; more common is the ‘failure of nerve’, in which all the relevant facts are known, yet they are not followed to their logical conclusion (Clarke, 1999). Again, we have seen examples of both of these relating to the information sciences. Speculations about a future likely to be inﬂuenced by the growth of knowledge and by the new technologies and capabilities arising from it are likely to be just that: speculations, possibly interesting, but almost always wrong. The future of the information environment and the information disciplines is most certainly of this kind, and it is straightforward, if a liĴle unkind, to reﬂect on the many poor predications of the value and use of information and communication technologies and to point out that authors of ﬁction were oĞen more successful; see Bawden (1997) and the equivalent chapter of the ﬁrst edition of this book (Bawden and Robinson, 2012, chapter 15) for examples. Having  acknowledged  the  diﬃculties  of  speculating  on information futures in detail, we will now consider the changes in the  information  environment  which  will  inﬂuence  future developments. In the ﬁrst edition of this book we expressed these as a series of drivers for change; we are now able to summarise them more coherently as the advent of the infosphere. Curating the

Curating the infosphere Throughout this book we have emphasised the signiﬁcance of Luciano Floridi’s ideas of the fourth revolution, the infosphere, and onlife (Floridi, 2014). Humankind has passed through a once-only transition into a new information environment and a new form of society, with far-reaching implications. It is hardly surprising that this has caused disruption to the disciplines and professions focused on the handling of recorded information. To give just one example, from the 1970s to the 1990s one of the most important roles for information professionals was online searching, carrying out searches in digital sources on behalf of clients. This was necessary because the nature of the digital sources and their interfaces, and the cost of searching, required specialist expertise and equipment. Since the advent of the internet and web search engines, this role has largely disappeared and online searching is the remit of everyone with a smartphone, including primary school children. It is true that much could be said about the quality of most search and the continuance of the intermediary searcher role in some environments, but that is beside the point; this typiﬁes the way in which the move to the infosphere has disrupted much of what was assumed to be the raison d’être of the information disciplines and professions. In our view
===
--- Chunk 648 ---
 the move to the infosphere has disrupted much of what was assumed to be the raison d’être of the information disciplines and professions. In our view, this is not a cause for lamentation but, rather, oﬀers new opportunities. The importance of documents in the keeping of the human record is not diminished in the infosphere, it is just reframed. We have argued that the information professions may gain a new role as ‘curators of the infosphere’ (Bawden and Robinson, 2018). This involves agreement with the view expressed by Floridi at the 2017 CILIP annual conference that the library and information community are experiencing a profound evolution of their role from keepers to curators of the infosphere. It involves an active role of curation and ontic stewardship of the new information environment (Fyﬀe, 2015; Van der Veer Martens, 2017), a novel, and we think appropriate, orientation of the information professions for the infosphere and onlife. The future of a multidiscipline If the information professions are to have a future as curators of the infosphere, what of the academic disciplines which support them? We suggested in Chapter 1 that information science is a multidisciplinary ﬁeld of study focused on recorded information. As information and data become more signiﬁcant in many, if not all, academic disciplines, it is not surprising that we see even more interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary activity, not all of it necessarily under the heading of ‘information science’, ‘
===
--- Chunk 649 ---
rising that we see even more interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary activity, not all of it necessarily under the heading of ‘information science’, ‘information studies’ or ‘library and information science’. At a time when many academic disciplines are experiencing a change in their boundaries and interactions, it would be surprising if information science, • arguably the most multidisciplinary of the multidisciplines, kept a tidy and exclusive place. Rather, we are likely to see research, scholarship and teaching in the subject developing, as they always have, in diﬀerent academic sectors, and partnering with a variety of related areas. We cannot, and should not try to, claim all information science issues as belonging to that discipline; rather, we should seek to ensure that their importance is recognised in the wider world. We can see three diﬀerent, though not incompatible, places for information science in the changing academic ﬁrmament. One is a closer alignment with the informatics and data science areas; this is essentially the route taken by the iSchools movement. Another is an alignment with media, communications, journalism, publishing and similar subjects. A third is an alignment with cultural studies and the digital humanities. Examples of all three can be seen, and all seem to be viable. It is important, however, not to choose one of these and declare that this is the future of the information sciences. They, and others which will emerge in the future, are simp
===
--- Chunk 650 ---
not to choose one of these and declare that this is the future of the information sciences. They, and others which will emerge in the future, are simply aspects of the multidiscipline, emphasising diﬀerent perspectives on the central focus of documents and the human record. The big issues In the ﬁrst edition of this book we proposed a series of seven rather general, research questions which, we argued, would, and should, inﬂuence the future of information science. They are: What is the best theoretical basis for the information sciences (if indeed there is a single such basis)? • • • • • • • How is the concept of information in the information sciences related to the ideas of information in other domains? How can principles of information science be applied to all sectors where documents and information resources (widely understood) are used? How can lessons from the past be applied to current and future information environments? How can we best operate in a world where an information glut, previously unimaginable, will be the norm? How can we best show the impact and value of knowledge and information resources and services in changing environments? How can information research and information practice best be linked, so that each informs the other? We believe these still to be valid, and would not change any of them. We would, however, subsume them under a wider question: How can individuals and societies best operate, in information terms, so as to best adapt to the new in
===
--- Chunk 651 ---
 however, subsume them under a wider question: How can individuals and societies best operate, in information terms, so as to best adapt to the new infosphere and pursue what Floridi terms ‘the human project’? This implies investigation of the ontology, epistemology and ethics of the section of the infosphere of particular relevance to LIS: essentially, that involved with documenting the human record, particularly in light of developments with big data and new forms of document. We believe that it is important to keep these big questions and their wider context in mind, so as not to be overly focused on issues of the moment. Currently important general issues for the information sciences are such things as sustainability and climate change, global and local inequalities, democracy and social justice, OA and open scholarship, the ethics of algorithms and AI, privacy and big data, and more. These are, of course, of great importance and should be priorities. Some will no doubt remain signiﬁcant issues in the long term; for example, issues of sustainability of information provision (Chowdhury, 2016; Fedorowicz-Kruszewska, 2021). But we should not be misled into thinking that any one of them is what information science is, or should be, about. Our subject should, perhaps more than most, take a long view and ﬁt the concerns of the moment into this. Summary No one knows in detail what the future will be like. ent into this. Summary No one knows in detail what the future will be like. This applies particularly to a discipline such as information science, which will be greatly changed by new knowledge, in ways which it is not possible to imagine. Given the rapid and dramatic changes in the information infrastructure, due to the move to onlife and the infosphere, we should not be surprised that the professions and disciplines centred on the communication of information should feel a sense of disorientation, and even crisis. This does not mean that they have become irrelevant or outmoded, but it does mean that it is necessary to focus on the big issues, rather than try to defend particular roles. It is equally necessary to align with other information-related disciplines and professions, some of which are experiencing equally challenging changes. • • • We believe that information science has a bright future, though its details cannot be known. Rather than aĴempting to defend their present disciplinary niche, academics and practitioners alike should concentrate on ensuring that the insights of information science are recognised and applied in wider contexts. The detailed future of information science is inherently unpredictable, since it will depend on the growth of new knowledge. The future role of the information professions may be as curators of the infosphere, and that of the information disciplines as providers of supporting scholarship and research.
